PART 1 / UNIT 01 / CHAPTER 1.1

From a program to a system

Prerequisites: Basic programming4 original figures
Reading the figures: boxes name parts or states; arrow labels explain how they relate. Dashed arrows show a code dependency or a change in the level of detail. Each caption explains the example.

Imagine that you have written a small to-do program. You enter “Read the design notes,” and the program adds it to your list. You close the program. When you open it the next morning, the list is empty.

The program could add a task, but it could not keep one. To make it useful, we must decide where tasks are stored and what should happen when the program stops. These are our first system design questions.

In this chapter: We will identify the parts of this application, follow a change in its data, and decide when it is safe to display “Saved.”

1.1.1 · What makes a program part of a system?

A software system consists of parts that work together to perform a task. In our example, the program accepts a title, checks it, stores a task, and displays the list. Once we add permanent storage, the program and the stored data must work together.

It helps to state what we are designing. Our first application is for one person using one machine. The person can add tasks, list them, and mark them complete. A task reported as saved must still be present after the program restarts. For now, we assume that the machine’s disk remains intact.

We can draw a line around the application and its storage. This is the system boundary: it tells us which parts we are considering together. The person uses the system from outside this line.

The boundary depends on the question. To investigate a slow function, we may study only the running program. To investigate a missing task, we also need to examine storage. When drawing a boundary, state which question it helps answer.

System design is the work of deciding how these parts should be organised and how they should interact to meet the requirements. For our application, this includes choosing where to store tasks, which code checks their titles, and when to tell the user that a task has been saved.

START WITH THE USER’S EXPECTATION

If the screen says “Saved,” what should the user be able to rely on?

1.1.2 · Follow one task through the program

Let us first keep tasks in memory. Memory holds the data used by a running program. In this example, the program creates a new, empty dictionary each time it starts.

The following Python code assumes that calls run one at a time, that the title is text, and that the caller supplies a positive integer identifier. It checks the title length and prevents two tasks from using the same identifier.

tasks = {}

def create(task_id, title):
    title = title.strip()
    if not 1 <= len(title) <= 200:
        raise ValueError("title must contain 1–200 characters")
    if task_id in tasks:
        raise ValueError("task id already exists")

    tasks[task_id] = {"title": title, "done": False}
    return {"id": task_id, **tasks[task_id]}

print(create(7, "  Read  "))
# {'id': 7, 'title': 'Read', 'done': False}

The call create(7, " Read ") first removes spaces from the ends of the title. It checks that the resulting title is between 1 and 200 characters long and that identifier 7 is unused. It then adds one task and returns its details.

Before the call, tasks is empty. After the call, it contains task 7. This is a state change. The state of a system is the information it currently holds that affects what it will do next. If we now ask for the task list, task 7 will appear because the state has changed.

We can use this one operation to distinguish four related ideas. The title “Read,” the number 7, and the value False are data. The collection of tasks currently stored is state. Trimming and checking the title are computation. Passing the title into the function and returning the result are communication. Later, communication may also involve files or a network.

Some rules must hold whenever the task collection is valid: each task must have a unique identifier, and each title must contain 1–200 characters after trimming. A rule of this kind is called an invariant. If validation fails, the function raises an error before changing the collection.

To complete task 7, we would check that it exists and set tasks[7]["done"] = True. Setting that flag to True again leaves the task completed. Creating another task is different: it adds another entry. We will return to this distinction when we discuss repeated requests.

A closer look · Describing a state change with notation

We can write an operation as T(S, c) → (S′, result). Here, S is the state before the operation, c is the command, and S′ is the state afterward.

For our example, S is an empty task collection, c is “create task 7 with title Read,” and S′ contains that task. If the title is empty, the result is an error and S′ = S. This notation describes the intended change. By itself, it says nothing about crashes or two callers running at the same time.

1.1.3 · Decide what “saved” means

The dictionary works while the program is running. When the program restarts, it creates a new dictionary and loses the old list. To meet our restart requirement, we need persistent storage: storage that keeps data after the program stops.

For this application, we will use SQLite, a database that can store its data in a local file. The application groups a write into a transaction. Completing the transaction successfully is called a commit. We will report success only after the database has committed the task.

The order matters. Suppose the application displays “Saved” and then tries to write the task. If it crashes between these events, the user has been told that a task was saved even though it is missing after restart. Waiting for commit avoids this particular failure.

This is a promise about restarting the program while its committed storage remains intact. If the only disk is destroyed, a local database cannot recover the data from that disk. The SQLite atomic-commit documentation explains how its commit mechanism works and which storage assumptions it relies on.

TRY IT · INTERACTIVE MODEL

What survives a restart?

Choose when the application reports success. Use “Next event” to follow the request, then restart the process and check whether the task remains.

    This model follows one request. A commit either finishes completely or does not happen. Restart removes memory but preserves committed storage. No real files are written.

    Try the policy that reports success before commit. Advance until the user receives “Saved,” then restart the process. Now repeat with commit before success. The different results come from the order of two events.

    The model removes memory when the process restarts and keeps committed storage. It does not simulate a damaged disk or a power failure. The runnable Python example lets you create a task, close the real database connection, and read the task through a new connection.

    1.1.4 · Give each part a clear contract

    A component is a part of the system with a defined responsibility. We will soon separate the code that accepts input, the code that applies task rules, and the code that stores tasks. These components can all run inside the same program.

    Components need a way to use one another. An interface describes the operations they offer, such as create(title) or list_tasks(). A contract explains how those operations behave.

    For example, the name create(title) does not tell us whether blank titles are accepted or whether the result has already been saved. We must state those rules. The following contract describes the persistent version of our application, which will assign identifiers itself.

    Table 1.1.1 · The contract for creating a task
    SituationRequired behaviourHow to check it
    The title has leading or trailing spaces.Remove those spaces before checking and saving it.Submit “ Read ” and check that the title is “Read.”
    The trimmed title is empty or longer than 200 characters.Reject it without adding a task.Compare the task list before and after the attempt.
    Creation succeeds.Return the new identifier after commit.Restart the program and find the task.
    The database write fails.Report the error instead of reporting success.Make storage fail and inspect the result.
    The task is committed, but its reply is lost.The task remains saved; the caller may be unsure what happened.Interrupt the reply after commit.

    The last row introduces a problem we will examine in Chapter 1.4. Saving a task and delivering its reply are separate events. The application must account for both.

    1.1.5 · Look at the same design at two levels

    We can now ask two sets of questions. Where does the application store tasks, and how does it communicate with that storage? Within the application, which functions validate a title and perform the write?

    High-Level Design (HLD) usually describes the main parts of a system and how they work together. For our application, it shows the user, application, and persistent store. It also states that the application waits for commit before reporting success.

    Low-Level Design (LLD) describes how a part is implemented: its functions, classes, interfaces, data structures, and algorithms. Here, it explains how the task service checks a title and calls the storage code.

    Software architecture concerns the major choices that shape the system and the reasons for them. Choosing to keep tasks in a local database is one such choice. Different teams use HLD, LLD, and architecture somewhat differently; the useful distinction is the level of detail being discussed.

    Both levels must agree. The high-level design may say “save before replying,” but the code must actually wait for the save to finish.

    CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING

    Putting a dictionary in a class does not make it persistent. Adding a database does not make a reply arrive. A successful restart test does not show what happens when the disk is destroyed. Each result depends on a different part of the design.

    Remember: Start with what the application must do. Identify the parts and the data they hold. Then trace the events that must happen before the user receives success.

    Before continuing: The application reports “Saved,” then crashes before writing to storage. Which event must move earlier to prevent the task from being lost?

    PART 1 / UNIT 01 / CHAPTER 1.2

    Organising code into modules

    Prerequisites: 1.1 · From a program to a system4 original figures
    Reading the figures: boxes name parts or states; arrow labels explain how they relate. Dashed arrows show a code dependency or a change in the level of detail. Each caption explains the example.

    Our to-do application can now save tasks between runs. We add a web form and a command-line interface. Both contain code that checks the title. Later, we change the title limit from 80 characters to 200, but update only the web form.

    The same application now accepts a title through one entry point and rejects it through another. To fix the cause, we need to decide where the rule belongs.

    In this chapter: We will divide the application into modules, examine the dependencies between them, and follow a change through the revised design.

    1.2.1 · Why does one change require several edits?

    A first version of the web handler may do everything in one place: read the request, check the title, write SQL, and build the response. For a small program, this is easy to follow. The difficulty appears when another feature needs some of the same behaviour.

    Suppose the command-line interface copies the title check. A CSV exporter also reads the database table directly. We now have two copies of a rule and several places that know how tasks are stored. Changing either the rule or the table can affect several features.

    Coupling describes the dependencies between parts of a system. In this example, the exporter is coupled to the database layout: it must know the column names. Rename a column, and its query may stop working.

    A dependency is often necessary. The task service needs some way to store a task. The design question is how much it needs to know. Calling repository.insert(title) requires less knowledge of storage than constructing SQL and opening database files throughout the application.

    Cohesion describes how closely the work inside a module belongs together. Checking task titles and completing tasks serve a shared purpose. Password handling, CSV formatting, and database connection setup have different purposes; placing them in a single “helpers” module gives that module little focus.

    Coupling asks how one module depends on another. Cohesion asks whether the work within one module belongs together. These ideas help us decide where to put code.

    1.2.2 · Separate input, task rules, and storage

    Let us give the application three main responsibilities.

    • The input adapter translates an incoming request into a call the application understands. A web adapter reads an HTTP request; a command-line adapter reads command-line input.
    • The task service applies task rules. It checks the title and asks storage to create a task.
    • The repository provides operations for storing and retrieving tasks. Our SQLite implementation contains the database queries and commits each change before returning.

    This division is an example of separation of concerns: giving different kinds of work their own place. The web adapter handles web details, the service handles task rules, and the repository handles storage details.

    Here is the essential structure. This is pseudocode, so it shows the responsibilities without implementing a complete web server.

    interface TaskRepository:
    insert(title) -> saved Task, or StorageError
    list() -> list of Task records
    set_done(id) -> saved Task, or NotFound, or StorageError

class TaskService:
    constructor(repository):
        self.repository = repository

    create(raw_title):
        title = trim(raw_title)
        require 1 <= length(title) <= 200
        return self.repository.insert(title)

handle_http(request, service):
    title = parse_json(request.body)["title"]
    task = service.create(title)
    return response(201, json(task))

    Follow a request through this code. The web adapter reads the title from JSON. The service checks it. The repository inserts and commits the task. The saved task returns through the service to the adapter, which builds the response.

    The command-line adapter can call the same service.create(title). When the title limit changes, we update the shared rule. Each adapter still checks its own input format: for example, whether a web request contains valid JSON. Task rules and input-format rules have different jobs.

    The real Python example implements the service and repository. It also checks that a title is text. A complete HTTP adapter would additionally handle missing fields, invalid JSON, and storage errors.

    1.2.3 · Hide details that callers do not need

    The service needs to request a saved task. It does not need to know the table name, SQL statement, or file path used to store it. The repository presents a simpler operation, insert(title), while hiding those details. This is abstraction.

    The contract still matters. In our design, insert must return only after commit. The service relies on that behaviour when it returns success. An abstraction should hide implementation details while explaining the behaviour callers depend on.

    ONE OPERATION, SEVERAL HIDDEN STEPS

    The service asks “store this task.” The repository handles the query and commit needed to carry out that request.

    Encapsulation controls access to a component’s internal data. If every part of the application can change the repository’s records directly, it can bypass the rules we have just defined. Returning a separate task record, rather than a reference that callers can use to edit internal state, helps preserve that control.

    Modularity is the organisation of a system into parts with clear responsibilities and interfaces. Separate files can help, but the division is useful only if it limits what each part must know about the others. Ten files that all edit the same internal data can still be difficult to change.

    At application startup, we create the SQLite repository and pass it to the service: TaskService(SQLiteTasks(path)). Supplying a dependency this way is called dependency injection. The startup code that creates and connects these objects is sometimes called the composition root. Unit 6 examines these ideas in detail.

    Read the dashed arrows in the figure as code dependencies: the service uses the repository contract, and the SQLite adapter implements it. During execution, the service calls that adapter. All of this can happen in one process, without a network call.

    1.2.4 · Check the design by changing it

    We can judge the division by asking where an edit would be needed. Consider four changes to the application.

    Table 1.2.1 · Where should a change be made?
    ChangeMain place to editWhat else needs checking?
    Accept a web form instead of JSON.Web input adapter.Does it pass the same title to the service and display errors correctly?
    Increase the title limit.Task service.Can the database store the longer title? Update any matching database constraint.
    Rename a database column.SQLite repository and the procedure that updates existing data.Can old records still be read after the change?
    Recognise a repeated create request.Input contract, service, and repository.Can the application identify the request and recover its earlier result?

    The last change affects several parts because it adds new behaviour. A caller must identify a repeated request, and storage must keep enough information to recognise it. Good modules help us see where agreement is needed; they cannot make every change fit inside one file.

    TRY IT · INTERACTIVE MODEL

    Where would you make the change?

    Choose a change and compare the parts that need editing in the two designs.

    The results follow our example’s division of responsibilities. They show where edits are needed, without estimating how long those edits take.

    1.2.5 · Understand what a layer hides

    We can also arrange the application as a series of abstraction layers. Each layer uses the operations offered by the one below it. A user asks to remember a task. The application turns that into a storage operation. The storage implementation uses the operating system to read and write files.

    Each step lets us work at a different level of detail. When writing title validation, we do not need to reason about disk blocks. When investigating a damaged database file, those lower-level details may become important.

    Some details must be visible in the contract. For example, suppose a repository returns results one at a time and keeps a database connection open until the caller finishes reading. A slow caller can then hold that connection for a long time. The caller needs to know when and how to close the result. Alternatively, the repository could return a bounded page of records and release the connection before returning.

    A closer look · Why a test substitute cannot check persistence

    We can test title validation using a simple repository that stores tasks in memory. This makes the test quick and easy to control. But the substitute loses its tasks when it is discarded. It cannot demonstrate that SQLite saves a task across a restart.

    For that check, use the real repository: create a task, close the connection, open a new connection to the same database, and read the task. The two tests answer different questions. Matching method names does not mean that two implementations have the same behaviour in every situation.

    1.2.6 · Use the amount of structure the application needs

    In this example, separating the title rule helps because both the web and command-line interfaces use it. Keeping SQL in a repository helps because several features need tasks without needing to know the table layout. These are concrete reasons for the boundaries.

    Every added interface also takes work to understand and maintain. A short, temporary script may need only a few functions. As the program grows, introduce a boundary where it protects a rule, hides a storage detail, or allows a real change to be made safely.

    The modules still run in one application. If that process crashes, all of them stop. Code organisation improves how we understand, change, and test the application; keeping it running through a machine failure requires further design work.

    COMMON MISTAKES

    Separate files do not necessarily have separate responsibilities. An interface does not automatically hide useful details. And fewer dependencies are not always better: the application needs well-defined dependencies to get its work done.

    FURTHER READING

    Parnas’s 1972 paper examines how the same system can be divided into modules in different ways. It asks which design decisions each module should hide. Our storage example gives a small application of that question. Paper record and abstract ↗

    Remember: Give related work a clear home. Let other modules use it through a contract. To check the division, follow a likely change and see which parts need editing.

    Before continuing: Both the web form and command-line interface check the title limit. Where should the shared rule move, and which checks should remain in each adapter?

    PART 1 / UNIT 01 / CHAPTER 1.3

    From requirements to design choices

    Prerequisites: 1.2 · Organising code into modules4 original figures
    Reading the figures: boxes name parts or states; arrow labels explain how they relate. Dashed arrows show a code dependency or a change in the level of detail. Each caption explains the example.

    The team asks us to make the to-do application “fast, safe, and easy to maintain.” These are reasonable goals, but they leave important questions unanswered. How fast should a task list appear? Which failures should saved tasks survive? What changes should be easy to make?

    Before choosing a design, we need to turn these goals into requirements that people can understand and check.

    In this chapter: We will write a small set of requirements, compare storage choices, and record why one choice fits our application.

    1.3.1 · State what the application must do

    A requirement states something the system must do or a condition it must satisfy. “A user can mark a task complete” describes behaviour. “A saved task remains after the application restarts” describes a condition that behaviour must meet.

    Requirements about what the system does are called functional requirements. Requirements about qualities such as speed, security, and ease of maintenance are commonly called nonfunctional requirements. Both influence the design.

    Consider a shared version of our application. For this example, assume a team of 20 people, one application machine, and a small budget. During normal use, the application receives at most 5 requests per second. These are teaching assumptions, rather than measurements of a real service.

    The team needs to create, list, and complete tasks. Each person’s tasks are private. A successful save must survive an application restart, provided the committed storage remains intact. At least 95% of list requests should finish within 300 milliseconds under an agreed test workload.

    The timing requirement gives us something to measure. If a test sends 1,000 list requests, at least 950 must finish within 300 milliseconds. To make results comparable, we must also specify where the test runs, how many tasks it lists, and how much traffic it sends. Unit 2 develops this measurement process.

    Table 1.3.1 · Making a requirement precise
    Starting statementQuestion to askA requirement we can check
    “The app is fast.”Which operation, under how much load?At least 95% of list requests finish within 300 ms under the agreed workload.
    “Tasks are safe.”Which failure should they survive?A task reported as saved can be read after the process restarts, with committed storage intact.
    “Tasks are private.”Who is allowed to do what?Users cannot read or change another person’s tasks through any task endpoint.
    “The code is easy to change.”Which change should be easy?Add a command-line interface that reuses the task service and repository.

    Qualities such as performance, security, reliability, and maintainability are also called quality attributes or architectural characteristics. Their names help organise a review. A concrete scenario tells us what each one means for this application.

    Some requirements fit more than one category. Checking whether a user may complete a task is application behaviour and part of its security. The classification is useful for organising work; the important step is to implement and check the requirement.

    1.3.2 · Separate constraints, assumptions, and risks

    Suppose the team says that the first version must run on an existing machine. That limits the choices available to us. Such a limit is a constraint. A fixed budget or a delivery deadline can also be a constraint.

    We have assumed that the disk remains intact when the process restarts. An assumption is something we treat as true while making a decision. Writing it down makes clear where the reasoning applies.

    Now suppose the only disk fails. We may lose the saved tasks. This is a risk: a possible event that could prevent the system from meeting its needs. The team must decide whether to accept it or change the design, for example by keeping recoverable copies elsewhere.

    These terms answer different questions. A constraint asks what limits our choices. An assumption asks what our reasoning relies on. A risk asks what could go wrong. They often connect: relying on one intact disk exposes us to the risk of losing that disk.

    1.3.3 · Compare choices against the requirements

    We have three storage candidates. We could keep tasks only in memory, use an embedded database such as SQLite, or run a separate database service. An embedded database runs as part of the application rather than as a separate server; here, it stores data in a local file.

    First check the mandatory restart requirement. Memory alone fails it. However easy the code is to write, that option cannot meet the agreed need.

    The other two candidates can meet this requirement with suitable commit behaviour and storage settings. We can then compare their costs and benefits. Embedded storage keeps deployment small. A separate database can be accessed by multiple application machines, but also needs a network connection, access controls, and operating work.

    A choice between competing benefits and costs is a trade-off. Which cost is worth paying depends on the requirements and on the people who will operate the system.

    Table 1.3.2 · Example preference scores: 1 = poor fit, 5 = strong fit
    CandidateSurvives process restart?Simple to run hereSupports multiple app machinesStorage separate from app machine
    Memory onlyNo; reject.511
    Embedded storeYes, under our storage assumptions.521
    Separate databaseYes, with suitable commit settings.244

    The scores express judgments about fit for this example. They are not performance measurements. The low score for separating an embedded store from its application machine reflects our local-file setup, rather than a claim about every possible use of SQLite.

    We can assign a weight to each preference. A higher weight means that preference matters more to the decision. A weighted score multiplies each preference score by its weight, adds the results, and divides by the sum of the weights.

    If simplicity has weight 5 and the other two preferences have weight 1 each, the embedded store receives (5×5 + 1×2 + 1×1) / 7 = 4.00. The separate database receives (5×2 + 1×4 + 1×4) / 7 ≈ 2.57. With these priorities, the embedded store ranks higher.

    TRY IT · INTERACTIVE MODEL

    Which preferences matter most?

    The scores come from Table 1.3.2. A higher weight gives that preference more influence. Every acceptable choice must still preserve tasks across a process restart.

    Try increasing the importance of multiple application machines and separate storage. The ranking may change. This is useful: it reveals how the decision depends on priorities. The memory-only option still fails the restart requirement, regardless of its score.

    1.3.4 · Record the decision and its reasons

    A few months later, someone may ask why the team chose a local database. A short Architecture Decision Record (ADR) can preserve the answer. It records the situation, the decision, and the consequences. It should also say when the team needs to reconsider.

    ADR 001 · ACCEPTED FOR THIS EXAMPLE

    Use a local database and commit before reporting success

    Situation
    A small team uses one application machine. Tasks must survive a process restart. The current requirement does not include keeping the service available after that machine fails.
    Decision
    Use SQLite on the application machine. Keep input handling, task rules, and storage code in separate modules. Wait for commit before returning success.
    Alternatives
    Memory alone fails the restart requirement. A separate database is possible, but its extra operating work is not yet justified by the requirements.
    Consequences
    Deployment is small, and the application has a clear point at which a task is committed. Losing the machine stops the service. Losing its only disk can lose data. We still need backups, restore checks, access controls, and monitoring.
    Reconsider when
    The application must run on several machines, measured storage contention causes unacceptable delays, or tasks must survive loss of the machine or disk.
    Checks to run
    Create a task and restart the process. Simulate a storage error. Restore a backup. Measure request times with representative data and traffic.

    An ADR need not be long. It needs enough detail for a later reader to understand why the choice made sense. Michael Nygard’s article on documenting architecture decisions describes this practice.

    If the requirements change, keep the old record and write a new one that replaces it. The earlier decision helps explain which assumption or need has changed.

    1.3.5 · Distinguish the qualities we are checking

    Some quality terms sound interchangeable. We need to separate them because they require different checks.

    Availability concerns whether the system can provide the required service when needed. If users cannot list their tasks while the application restarts, it is unavailable for that operation during that interval. When measuring availability, define which requests count and what a useful response is.

    Durability concerns whether committed data survives specified failures. Our restart test checks whether a saved task remains after the process stops and starts. It says nothing about losing the only disk.

    Reliability usually refers more broadly to providing correct service over time. Teams sometimes use it differently, so a requirement should explain the failures and outcomes it covers.

    Consistency concerns which observations of state the system allows. For example, after completing a task, should the user’s next list request show it as complete? If the application later has several copies of the data, we must specify when each copy may show the change. Unit 14 examines precise consistency models.

    These distinctions explain two possible outcomes. An application may keep replying to requests yet lose tasks it held only in memory. A database may preserve every committed task while refusing requests during recovery. The first has a data-loss problem; the second has a period of unavailability.

    A closer look · What makes a design simple enough?

    Count the work needed to understand, change, operate, and recover the system. One large function may use few components yet be hard to maintain. A separate managed database may add a network connection while reducing backup work for a team.

    The simplest sufficient design meets the agreed requirements with manageable work. Low traffic does not remove the need for access controls or correct saves. At the same time, an imagined future need does not automatically justify extra infrastructure today. Record likely changes and the conditions that would make them necessary.

    COMMON MISTAKES

    A high preference score cannot compensate for a failed requirement. More users do not, by themselves, tell us which part needs scaling. And a good uptime figure does not show whether saved data survives a failure.

    Remember: Write requirements that can be checked. Reject choices that fail them. Compare the remaining choices, then record the reasons and the conditions for reconsidering.

    Before continuing: The team still has only 20 users, but it now requires tasks to survive destruction of the only disk. Which part of ADR 001 must be reconsidered?

    PART 1 / UNIT 01 / CHAPTER 1.4

    Drawing the system at different levels

    Prerequisites: 1.3 · From requirements to design choices4 original figures
    Reading the figures: boxes name parts or states; arrow labels explain how they relate. Dashed arrows show a code dependency or a change in the level of detail. Each caption explains the example.

    A diagram shows three boxes: input adapter, task service, and repository. A reviewer asks whether the application needs three servers. The author intended all three to be modules inside one program.

    Both readers saw the same boxes but gave them different meanings. A useful system diagram must make its level of detail clear.

    In this chapter: We will draw the to-do application from several viewpoints, trace a request, and use the drawings to find possible failures.

    1.4.1 · Choose a view that answers a question

    Suppose we want to explain the application to a new team member. We might begin with the person who uses it and the task system as a whole. A developer changing validation needs a closer view of the modules. Someone investigating a machine failure needs to see where the application and data run.

    These are different views of the same system. Each selects the details needed for a particular question.

    The C4 model names four levels for describing system structure: context, containers, components, and code. Moving through them is like zooming in on the application.

    Table 1.4.1 · Choosing a diagram
    ViewQuestion it answersWhat it shows here
    System contextWho uses the system, and which other systems interact with it?A team member uses the task system.
    ContainerWhich applications and data stores make up the system?Browser client, server application, and task store.
    ComponentHow is an application divided internally?Input adapter, task service, and storage adapter inside the server application.
    CodeHow is a selected component implemented?Task records, service methods, and the repository interface.
    SequenceIn what order do events occur in one scenario?The application validates a request, saves the task, commits, and replies.
    DeploymentWhere do the application and data run?One machine runs the application and holds the database file.

    A container has a particular meaning in C4: an application or data store. It can be a browser application, a server application, or a database. It does not have to be a Docker container. The C4 container definition explains this terminology.

    Sequence and deployment views add information about order and location. They support the four structural levels rather than adding more levels of zoom. We can use whichever views help explain the design.

    TRY IT · INTERACTIVE MODEL

    Zoom in on the same application

    Select a level to see which parts it shows. Figure 1.4.1 and Table 1.4.1 explain all four levels without using these controls.

    1.4.2 · Show where the program and data live

    Our first version was an in-memory script. The second used modules and a local database. Now the team needs to access tasks from several computers, so we add a web interface. A browser sends requests to the server application, which uses the task service and repository.

    The deployment view shows an important detail: the server application and SQLite file are on the same machine. The browser is elsewhere. If the server machine fails, both the application and access to its database are affected.

    Parts that can fail together because of one cause belong to a failure domain. Here, the machine is a shared failure domain. Drawing the service and repository as separate boxes does not give them independent machines.

    The browser also introduces a trust boundary. The server cannot assume that a request is valid merely because it came from the application’s usual web page. A user can construct requests directly.

    The server must establish who the caller is; this is authentication. It must then check whether that caller may access the requested task; this is authorization. Every task operation needs the relevant check. Hiding another person’s task from the web page does not prevent a direct request for it. Unit 18 develops these checks in detail.

    1.4.3 · Trace a request from input to reply

    Let us create a task through the web interface. The browser sends POST /tasks with a JSON body containing {"title": "Read"}. The following sequence describes the intended API; the local Python example is not an HTTP server.

    1. Identify the caller from a validated session.
2. Read the title and check the input.
3. Begin a database transaction.
4. Insert the task with the caller as its owner.
5. Commit the transaction.
6. Return:
   201 Created
   Location: /tasks/7
   {"id": 7, "title": "Read", "done": false}

    The 201 Created response tells the client that creation succeeded. The Location header identifies the new resource. HTTP’s specification defines this response. Waiting for the database commit is an additional rule of our application.

    Now interrupt the sequence. If title validation fails, the application writes no task. If the transaction fails before commit, the application reports an error. If the process crashes after commit but before the reply, task 7 exists even though the browser has not received success.

    What should the browser conclude after waiting too long for a reply? It cannot tell whether the task was saved. The request might never have reached the application, or the task might have been committed and the reply lost.

    If the browser sends a fresh create request, the application may add task 8. The user intended one task but now has two. To recognise retries, the client and server need a stable identifier for the original operation. The server must store that identifier with its result so that a repeated attempt can retrieve the earlier result. Chapter 8.2 develops this mechanism, called request deduplication.

    This is why event order belongs in the diagram. A drawing with only “request” and “response” can hide the commit that determines whether a task exists.

    1.4.4 · Label arrows and copies of data

    An arrow can mean a function call, a network request, a code dependency, or a step in a sequence. Label it with the actual relationship. For example, “HTTPS request,” “calls insert,” and “implements interface” describe different things.

    Use a legend when colour or line style carries meaning. In this atlas, dashed arrows often show dependencies or zoom relationships, while solid arrows show the labelled action. Read the labels and caption to find the meaning in that particular view.

    Also show where copies of data are held. The browser may display a task list it fetched a minute ago. The application may hold a task record in memory. The database contains the committed record. If another user completes a task, the browser’s old list does not update itself. We must decide when it fetches or receives new data.

    A diagram that distinguishes these copies makes the freshness question visible. A single label saying “task data” does not tell us which copy a reader is seeing.

    A closer look · Four ways to review a diagram
    1. Stop a component. What stops with it? If several modules share one process, a process crash affects all of them.
    2. Delay a call. Who is waiting? Decide how long that caller can wait and what happens when the time runs out.
    3. Repeat a request. Does it add another task? Point to the code and stored information that recognise a retry, if that behaviour is required.
    4. Change a data format. Which readers and writers must change together? Check how old and new versions will work during the update.

    These questions help uncover omissions. Tests are then needed to check the actual behaviour.

    1.4.5 · Change the design when there is a reason

    Each change in our example answered a particular need. Persistent storage let tasks survive a process restart. Modules gave shared rules a clear home. A web interface let people use the application remotely. None of these changes made it survive failure of its only machine.

    Suppose the application becomes slow. Before adding another server, measure where requests spend their time. A slow database query may need a better query or index. Adding application servers could send even more work to that same query. If computation in the application is the bottleneck and storage has spare capacity, additional workers may help.

    Adding a second machine also changes our storage assumptions. If each machine has its own unrelated task database, a user may see different lists depending on which machine handles the request. We need a design for shared or coordinated data; a load balancer alone cannot supply it.

    The drawings help us review these consequences together. A structure view assigns responsibilities. A sequence view shows event order. A deployment view shows where execution and data live. They should describe a consistent design.

    COMMON MISTAKES

    Three module boxes need not mean three servers. A timeout does not establish that a write failed. And another application machine does not automatically provide another usable copy of the data.

    Remember: Choose a diagram for a specific question. Label what the boxes and arrows mean. Check that the code structure, request sequence, and deployment tell the same story.

    Before continuing: Which view would help you find a reply sent before commit? Which view would show that the application and its only backup are on the same disk?

    PART 1 / UNIT 02 / CHAPTER 2.1

    Turn user journeys into workloads

    Prerequisites: Introduction to System Design4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Opening a feed looks like one action, but it can fetch many images and update several records. Begin by finding out what people need to do and which work each journey causes.

    2.1.1 · Gathering and prioritizing requirements

    Suppose we are asked to build a social feed. Before estimating servers, we need to know what people will do: publish posts, follow accounts, read updates, or report harmful content. These journeys lead to different work inside the system.

    Write the required outcome for each important journey. “Keep an accepted post and show it to followers within five seconds” is specific enough to discuss and test. Then separate essential behaviour from desirable improvements. Investigate requirements whose failure would cause the greatest harm or whose feasibility is uncertain. Record exclusions too: private messaging should not silently enter an estimate for a public feed.

    2.1.2 · User journeys and workload characteristics

    Opening a feed appears to be one action. In an assumed session, however, the browser sends one feed request, fetches twenty images, and records one analytics event. These requests differ in size and in the work they cause.

    A workload describes that mixture of operations and how often they arrive. For each operation, estimate its rate, payload size, and dependencies. A small response can still require expensive computation; an image can require little computation but substantial transfer. Keep these workloads separate when finding bottlenecks. The first estimates are assumptions. Replace them with measurements once the application is running.

    2.1.3 · Read-heavy vs write-heavy systems

    Assume users read ten feeds for every post they publish. At the public API, this looks read-heavy. But if publishing copies the new post into a thousand follower feeds, that one action causes a thousand additional storage writes.

    A read/write ratio therefore needs a boundary: are we counting user actions, API requests, or database operations? Creating follower feeds in advance moves work to publication time. Building them when requested moves work to reading time. The choice depends on how often users publish and read. Read replicas can help some reads, but delayed replicas may not immediately show a user's new post.

    Think further · How would simultaneous retries change an estimate based on average user sessions?

    Retries add attempts without adding new user intentions. Model their timing, maximum amplification, and the failing dependency separately from normal sessions. A correlated retry wave can exceed a peak factor based on independent arrivals. Bound attempts and admission, then test useful completion and recovery under that burst.

    Remember: Count work at the boundary being designed, including operations caused by one user action.

    Try applying it: Which requests and storage writes would a new image-upload feature add to the estimate?

    PART 1 / UNIT 02 / CHAPTER 2.2

    Measure the experience

    Prerequisites: 2.1 · Turn user journeys into workloads4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Averages can make a slow service look healthy. Follow offered requests, completed work, individual waits, and errors to choose measurements that reflect what users receive.

    2.2.1 · Latency, throughput, QPS, RPS, TPS

    Suppose a server receives 200 requests each second and completes 180. If the remaining requests stay queued, twenty more accumulate every second. Reporting only the completion rate would hide the growing wait.

    Latency is the time one operation takes. Throughput is the amount of work completed per unit time. RPS usually means requests per second, QPS queries per second, and TPS transactions per second. State which work each number counts, since one request may cause several queries. Measure offered work, successful completions, errors, and rejected requests together. Otherwise, an apparently steady throughput can conceal users who are waiting or giving up.

    2.2.2 · Average vs median vs p95/p99 latency

    Consider 100 assumed request times: 99 requests take 10 milliseconds each, and one takes 1,000 milliseconds. The mean is (99×10 + 1,000)/100 = 19.9 milliseconds. That average tells us little about the user who waited a full second.

    The median describes the middle of a sorted set. A percentile such as p95 or p99 describes a point near its upper end; the precise estimate depends on the percentile convention. Use the distribution to study slow requests. To find a fleet-wide p99, combine compatible observations or histograms. Averaging individual servers' p99 values does not produce the fleet p99. Account for timeouts rather than discarding them.

    2.2.3 · Availability, reliability, durability, consistency

    A payment status page can respond quickly while showing yesterday's information. Its ability to respond and the freshness of its answer are separate properties.

    Availability concerns providing the required service when needed. Durability concerns whether committed data survives specified failures. Reliability usually concerns correct service over time; state how it is being measured. Consistency defines which observations of state are allowed. For example, must the next read show a completed payment? Choose the requirement for each operation. A popularity count may tolerate delayed updates, while selling the last ticket requires stronger coordination. A single label such as “reliable database” leaves these decisions unanswered.

    2.2.4 · SLI, SLO, SLA, and error budgets

    Suppose a service handles one million eligible requests in a month. A target of 99.9% successful requests allows 0.1%, or 1,000, to fail. This allowance is its event-based error budget for that population and period.

    An SLI is the indicator we measure, such as the fraction of successful requests. An SLO is its target and measurement window. An SLA is an agreement with stated obligations and possibly consequences. Define eligible requests honestly; excluding failures merely to improve the number defeats the purpose. A time-based objective uses time as its denominator and gives a different budget. Use budget consumption to guide release and reliability work, while also considering the harm of a concentrated outage.

    Think further · How would simultaneous retries change an estimate based on average user sessions?

    Retries add attempts without adding new user intentions. Model their timing, maximum amplification, and the failing dependency separately from normal sessions. A correlated retry wave can exceed a peak factor based on independent arrivals. Bound attempts and admission, then test useful completion and recovery under that burst.

    Remember: Measure useful outcomes and their distribution, with an explicit population and observation window.

    Try applying it: A service reports a low mean while some users wait a second. Which additional evidence would you request?

    PART 1 / UNIT 02 / CHAPTER 2.3

    Estimate the resources

    Prerequisites: 2.2 · Measure the experience4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Suppose ten million people use the service daily. We will turn explicit activity assumptions into requests, stored bytes, transfer, and headroom, keeping each resource's calculation separate.

    2.3.1 · Capacity and growth planning

    Suppose stored data grows by an assumed 10% each month. Starting with one unit, a year of this growth gives 1.1¹² ≈ 3.14 units. That is a planning scenario, not evidence that request traffic and CPU usage will also triple.

    Plan each important resource separately: stored history, frequently accessed data, background jobs, and spare capacity during failures. Include temporary space needed while old and new data layouts coexist during a migration. A useful capacity plan names the resource likely to fill first, the time needed to add capacity, and the observation that triggers action. Revisit the assumptions as measurements arrive.

    2.3.2 · Storage, memory, bandwidth, and CPU estimates

    Assume ten million daily users each make fifty API requests. The daily total is 10,000,000×50 = 500,000,000 requests. Divide by 86,400 seconds per day to obtain about 5,787 requests per second on average.

    If each user publishes one 2 kB post daily, raw post growth is 20 GB/day. If each views ten 200 kB images, image delivery totals 20 TB/day. These calculations use decimal units and describe different resources. Add indexes, extra copies, retained history, and transfer overhead separately. Memory depends on the data kept active; CPU depends on the work per request. Neither can be inferred from the user count alone. These are assumed workloads, not company benchmarks.

    2.3.3 · Peak vs average load

    A daily average spreads all requests evenly across 24 hours. Real users may arrive together after a notification or event. Suppose, for planning, that peak API traffic is five times the preceding average. The estimate becomes 5×5,787.04 ≈ 28,935 requests per second.

    Also ask how long the peak lasts. Extra instances that take several minutes to start may arrive after a short spike has ended. Admission limits and existing spare capacity must handle the gap. Image traffic and posting traffic may peak differently, so a common multiplier is only an initial assumption. Retries during an outage can create another peak that ordinary user averages miss.

    INFRASTRUCTURE WORKSHEET · ASSUMED CAPACITY

    At 28,935.19 peak requests/s, a hypothetical tested instance capacity of 600 requests/s and a 60% utilization target imply ceil(28,935.19 / 360) = 81 active instances. Reserving capacity for one lost instance gives 82. This does not size the database, image delivery path, or failure domains. Validate each separately; the 600 figure is an assumed input, not a reported benchmark.

    Think further · How would simultaneous retries change an estimate based on average user sessions?

    Retries add attempts without adding new user intentions. Model their timing, maximum amplification, and the failing dependency separately from normal sessions. A correlated retry wave can exceed a peak factor based on independent arrivals. Bound attempts and admission, then test useful completion and recovery under that burst.

    Remember: Workload estimates are inputs to capacity testing; per-instance capacity and failure needs require their own evidence.

    Try applying it: If users view twice as many images but publish the same number of posts, which estimates change?

    PART 1 / UNIT 02 / CHAPTER 2.4

    Queues, bottlenecks & defensible decisions

    Prerequisites: 2.3 · Estimate the resources5 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A queue grows even though all workers are busy. We will relate waiting, parallel work, and dependent calls before comparing the designs that could meet the requirements.

    2.4.1 · Little's Law and queueing intuition

    Imagine a stable service completing 500 operations per second. Each operation spends an average of 40 milliseconds inside the boundary being measured. Little's Law gives average work in progress as L = λW: 500/s × 0.04 s = 20 operations.

    Here L is the average number in the system, λ the long-run arrival/completion rate, and W the average time inside it. If that average time rises to 0.4 seconds while stable throughput stays 500/s, L becomes 200. Use consistent boundaries and units, including waiting time where applicable. This relation describes stable averages; it does not predict p99 or make an overloaded queue become stable.

    2.4.2 · Amdahl's Law and bottlenecks

    Suppose a job spends 20% of its time in work that must run sequentially. The other 80% can be divided perfectly among workers. With four workers, the ideal time becomes 0.2 + 0.8/4 = 0.4 of the original. The speedup is therefore 1/0.4 = 2.5 times.

    This is Amdahl's Law for a fixed amount of work. Even infinitely many workers cannot remove the sequential 20%, so the ideal ceiling is five times. Coordination can reduce the real benefit further. Find the stage that limits progress before adding workers. After improving it, measure again: another stage may become the new bottleneck.

    2.4.3 · Tail latency and latency budgets

    A page request may start fifty calls in parallel and need all their results. Its completion then depends on the slowest required call. Assume each call independently has a 1% chance of exceeding a threshold. The chance that all are fast is 0.99⁵⁰; the chance that at least one is slow is 1−0.99⁵⁰ ≈ 39.5%.

    This example shows how fan-out can worsen tail latency. Shared dependencies can also correlate delays, so independence must be justified. Divide the overall deadline among network travel, waiting, computation, and returning the reply. Sending duplicate calls to reduce waiting spends extra capacity and is appropriate only when repeated execution is safe.

    2.4.4 · Cost, security, operational complexity, and maintainability as constraints

    Suppose two designs both handle the expected traffic. One is cheaper but allows a tenant's cached result to reach another tenant. It fails a security requirement and should be rejected before comparing prices.

    Other differences may be preferences: one design costs more money but takes less operating work. Include staffing, maintenance, migration, and recovery in the comparison. A team also needs the skills to run what it builds. Compare candidates against the same workload and failure requirements. A price advantage obtained by dropping backups or weakening isolation represents a different service, rather than a like-for-like saving.

    2.4.5 · Decision matrices and trade-off analysis

    After rejecting designs that fail mandatory requirements, we may still have several reasonable choices. A decision matrix lists the criteria, gives each candidate a score, and weights the criteria according to their importance. It makes the team's judgments visible.

    Try changing uncertain scores and weights. If a small change reverses the result, the decision needs better evidence or a choice that is easy to reverse. Record the reason and the condition for reconsidering it in an ADR. The weighted total helps discussion; tests are still needed to establish performance and correctness. A high score cannot make an unsupported requirement true.

    Try the mechanism in code

    Python · examples/mechanisms.py

    from mechanisms import capacity, amdahl
print(capacity())
print(amdahl(.8, 4))

    The defaults produce about 5,787.04 average requests/s and 28,935.19 at the assumed peak. Dividing by 600×0.6 and rounding up gives 81 active instances; allowing one to fail gives 82.

    The worksheet sizes only its assumed request-serving resource. Database, image delivery, and the chosen failure placement still need their own capacity tests.

    Estimate capacity for the social application

    Start with the stated daily workload, then change one input. Each user views ten 200 kB images and writes one 2 kB post per day. GB and TB use decimal units. The instance capacity is an assumption; database capacity and capacity after a larger outage need their own checks.

    Think further · How would simultaneous retries change an estimate based on average user sessions?

    Retries add attempts without adding new user intentions. Model their timing, maximum amplification, and the failing dependency separately from normal sessions. A correlated retry wave can exceed a peak factor based on independent arrivals. Bound attempts and admission, then test useful completion and recovery under that burst.

    Remember: More concurrency helps only where work and resources permit it; compare feasible choices with their assumptions visible.

    PART 1 / UNIT 03 / CHAPTER 3.1

    Addresses, sockets & transports

    Prerequisites: Introduction to System Design4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A browser has a website name, but packets need a destination and a transport. Trace how addresses, ports, sockets, and protocol behaviour connect the application to another machine.

    3.1.1 · How the internet works from the application perspective

    Type a website address into a browser. Before the page appears, the browser may resolve the name, establish a connection, negotiate security, send a request, and fetch additional resources. The server must also perform its application work, and the browser must render the result.

    Some steps can reuse earlier work. A cached address avoids a lookup; an existing connection avoids setup. Follow the path used by the actual request before assigning a single “network time.” A fast server can still produce a slow page when images are large or connection setup takes several round trips. The request is a sequence of dependent activities.

    3.1.2 · IP addresses, ports, sockets, routing

    To contact a web server, a client needs an address and a transport port. Routing moves packets toward the destination address. The port helps the destination operating system direct transport traffic to the appropriate endpoint. A socket is an endpoint the operating system provides for communication.

    An application might listen on port 443 but remain unreachable because it is bound to the wrong address, a firewall blocks the path, or replies cannot return. Investigate the whole route. An address or port also provides no proof of permission: reaching a service and being authorised to use it are different requirements. Private addressing alone does not establish that a caller is trusted.

    3.1.3 · TCP vs UDP vs QUIC

    Suppose an application sends two messages. With TCP, the receiver gets an ordered stream of bytes; it must use an application rule to discover where each message ends. UDP provides datagrams but does not supply TCP's ordered, reliable stream behaviour.

    QUIC runs over UDP and provides its own secure transport with separate streams and connection identifiers. Loss affecting one stream need not block delivery on another as a missing TCP byte can. The streams still share congestion constraints and may have application dependencies. Choose a transport by the required behaviour and supported infrastructure. Using UDP does not by itself make an application faster, reliable, or secure.

    Think further · What changes when a local dependency becomes a cross-region call?

    The call adds travel, connection, timeout, trust, and partial-failure behaviour. A local exception and an unknown remote outcome are different. Revisit deadlines, operation identity, encoding, credentials, and fallback, measuring the whole path. Preserve the business meaning while changing the communication arrangement.

    Remember: Choose communication mechanisms by their actual delivery and ordering rules.

    Try applying it: Where would you investigate if the application listens on its port but no remote client can reach it?

    PART 1 / UNIT 03 / CHAPTER 3.2

    A secure request, one round trip at a time

    Prerequisites: 3.1 · Addresses, sockets & transports5 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    The first secure request is slower than the next, even with identical server work. Follow name lookup, setup, encryption, and connection reuse to account for the difference.

    3.2.1 · DNS resolution and DNS caching

    A browser knows a name such as example.org, but it needs a usable network address. A DNS resolver obtains the relevant records, often using cached answers rather than asking authoritative servers each time. A record's time to live, or TTL, guides how long it may be cached.

    Now change the address during failover. Some clients still hold the earlier answer; others already have open connections and do no new lookup. Negative answers may also be cached. The change therefore does not redirect every client immediately. Test DNS refresh and connection lifetimes together when designing failover. The authoritative record is only one part of how clients choose a destination.

    3.2.2 · TLS and HTTPS

    When a browser opens an HTTPS connection, it needs to establish that it is talking to the intended server and protect the traffic. TLS provides peer authentication under its trust configuration, along with confidentiality and integrity protection. The client must validate the certificate and its relationship to the requested hostname.

    Trace where encryption ends. If a reverse proxy terminates TLS, the proxy-to-application connection needs its own policy. Protect the relevant keys as well. TLS protects the connection; the application must still check whether a signed-in user may read a particular task. A secure transport does not supply resource ownership rules.

    3.2.3 · HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, HTTP/3

    A page often needs many resources. HTTP/1.1 clients may use multiple connections to avoid waiting behind other responses. HTTP/2 carries multiple streams over one TCP connection. If a TCP byte is lost, later bytes wait for recovery, which can delay several HTTP/2 streams.

    HTTP/3 uses QUIC streams and changes that transport behaviour. The protocols retain HTTP's application meanings, such as methods and status codes, while carrying messages differently. Performance depends on loss, negotiation, proxies, and payloads. Upgrading the protocol can reduce some waiting, but the request still spends time in application queues and the database. Measure the complete path rather than attributing every delay to the HTTP version.

    3.2.4 · Connection establishment and connection reuse

    The first request to a server may need a new connection; a later request can reuse one. A new TCP connection normally performs a handshake, and secure setup adds exchanges whose number depends on the protocol and reuse options. Existing connections avoid some of this work.

    Connection reuse needs limits. A connection left idle may be closed by an intermediary. A very long-lived connection may continue using an endpoint that discovery has replaced. Conversely, closing connections too often wastes setup work and CPU. Choose lifetimes and pool sizes that fit the infrastructure and workload, and handle replacement safely when an old connection no longer works.

    3.2.5 · Latency caused by network round trips

    Assume a simplified cold request spends 20 ms on DNS, 40 ms on TCP setup, 40 ms on TLS setup, and 55 ms on the request, server work, and reply. In this sequential model, the total is 20+40+40+55 = 155 ms.

    This is an assumed example, not a benchmark. Cached DNS, connection reuse, security resumption, and overlapping work change the calculation. It illustrates why a small amount of server computation can still accompany substantial delay. Moving a service closer can reduce network travel time. Reuse or batching can reduce the number of exchanges. First identify which exchanges the actual request needs.

    Think further · What changes when a local dependency becomes a cross-region call?

    The call adds travel, connection, timeout, trust, and partial-failure behaviour. A local exception and an unknown remote outcome are different. Revisit deadlines, operation identity, encoding, credentials, and fallback, measuring the whole path. Preserve the business meaning while changing the communication arrangement.

    Remember: A request includes setup and travel as well as server execution; reused work changes the path.

    Try applying it: Which parts of the 155 ms cold example can disappear with a usable warm connection?

    PART 1 / UNIT 03 / CHAPTER 3.3

    Intermediaries & persistent connections

    Prerequisites: 3.2 · A secure request, one round trip at a time4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A proxy, gateway, and balancer can all sit between a browser and an application. Assign each a purpose, then compare the work involved in polling and streaming updates.

    3.3.1 · Reverse proxies vs forward proxies

    An organisation may send employees' outbound traffic through a forward proxy. A website may place a reverse proxy in front of its application servers. The first acts on the client side of the exchange; the second presents the servers to incoming clients.

    A reverse proxy can terminate TLS, route requests, and apply limits, but it also introduces another component that can fail or time out. Decide which forwarded metadata the application may trust. For example, accepting a client-supplied identity header as if a trusted proxy had checked it can bypass authentication. The design must identify who creates the header and which callers can reach the receiving endpoint.

    3.3.2 · Load balancers vs API gateways

    Suppose incoming requests must be sent to one of several application instances. A load balancer chooses a backend. An API gateway often adds API-specific functions such as authentication integration, quotas, or request transformation. A product can perform both roles.

    Assign responsibilities explicitly instead of relying on product names. A gateway can reject an oversized request or apply a coarse rate limit, while a domain service checks ownership of a payment. Moving every business rule into the gateway makes many teams depend on changes there. Also trace downstream capacity: distributing traffic across more application instances does not repair a database that is already overloaded.

    3.3.3 · L4 vs L7 load balancing

    To route a connection by its destination port, a balancer can work with transport information: this is Layer-4 routing. To route an HTTP request by its host or path, it must inspect application messages: this is Layer-7 routing.

    Application-aware routing supports richer decisions but adds parsing, processing, and trust requirements. The placement of encryption termination determines which component can see those messages. Also distinguish requests from connections. A long-lived connection can remain attached to one backend even while new connections go elsewhere. Choose the routing level by the information needed for the decision and the connection behaviour the application expects.

    3.3.4 · WebSockets, Server-Sent Events, and polling

    Assume 1,000 clients ask for updates every five seconds. Even when nothing changes, polling creates 1,000/5 = 200 requests per second. Each response gives the client another snapshot.

    Server-Sent Events lets a server stream events to a client over HTTP. WebSockets supports messaging in both directions after connection setup. Streaming avoids repeated empty polls but keeps connections open. Plan heartbeats, buffers, reconnects, and what happens to missed updates. A live connection is a delivery path, not a durable message history. If clients must recover updates after a disconnection, the application needs event identities and a replay or resynchronisation rule.

    Think further · What changes when a local dependency becomes a cross-region call?

    The call adds travel, connection, timeout, trust, and partial-failure behaviour. A local exception and an unknown remote outcome are different. Revisit deadlines, operation identity, encoding, credentials, and fallback, measuring the whole path. Preserve the business meaning while changing the communication arrangement.

    Remember: Label the responsibility and trust of each intermediary rather than inferring behaviour from a product name.

    Try applying it: Which policy belongs at the gateway, and which needs the service's knowledge of resource ownership?

    PART 1 / UNIT 03 / CHAPTER 3.4

    Discover, route & survive the network

    Prerequisites: 3.3 · Intermediaries & persistent connections5 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    The server commits, but the client receives no reply. Follow routing, discovery, caches, and bounded connection use to understand why a healthy destination does not guarantee a known result.

    3.4.1 · NAT, firewalls, ingress, egress

    A client opens an outbound connection, but no reply arrives. The problem may lie outside the remote application: a firewall may block traffic, or a network address translation table may have exhausted or expired its mappings.

    NAT rewrites network addressing. A firewall applies traffic rules. Ingress is traffic entering a boundary, and egress is traffic leaving it. Show these functions when tracing the path in and out. Choose connection lifetimes and outbound policies together. Segmentation can reduce which services are reachable, but an allowed connection must still authenticate and authorise its requests, particularly in a shared tenant environment.

    3.4.2 · Service discovery

    An application wants to call “the payment service” even as instances are replaced. Service discovery maps that logical name to usable endpoints. It may rely on DNS, a registry, or the platform's control plane.

    Discovery information can be stale. An instance might fail after being advertised, or a healthy instance might already lack spare capacity. Cache results to avoid making every call depend on a lookup, but refresh them deliberately. A client must still cope with a bad endpoint, using bounded retries within its deadline. Successful discovery establishes a possible destination; it does not establish that the operation will succeed.

    3.4.3 · CDN and edge networking

    A user requests a public image. A nearby CDN cache can return it without contacting the origin server. On a miss, the edge fetches the image and stores a representation according to its caching policy.

    The cache key determines which requests share a copy, and freshness rules determine when that copy may be reused. These are correctness decisions. A missing tenant or authorisation dimension can make a cache serve someone else's content. Public images and private account pages need different policies. CDNs reduce some network travel and origin traffic, while adding copies whose expiry, purge, and failure behaviour must be understood.

    3.4.4 · Network partitions, timeouts, packet loss

    A client sends a request and waits until its deadline. It sees a timeout. Did the server receive the request, perform it, or commit its write? The timeout alone cannot answer these questions. The request or its reply may have been delayed or lost.

    A network partition prevents some participants from communicating even while other paths work. Treat such partial failures as normal possibilities. Distinguish connection-setup, idle, and overall request limits. Unbounded waiting can exhaust resources; blind retrying can repeat an effect. Use operation identifiers or status queries where the client needs to recover an uncertain outcome, and keep retries inside an overall deadline.

    3.4.5 · Connection pooling and keepalive

    A database connection pool lets requests borrow existing connections. Suppose there are twenty connections and each is held for an assumed average of 50 ms. If every connection remains busy, the simple service-capacity calculation is 20/0.05 = 400 operations per second before overhead and variability.

    A request can also wait to borrow a connection, so include that wait in its deadline. Oversizing the pool may merely overload the database; a leaked connection gradually reduces usable capacity. Keepalive can help detect some broken connections, but says little about whether a business operation will succeed. Measure queueing and hold times before changing the pool size.

    Try the mechanism in code

    Python · arithmetic model

    cold = dict(dns=20, tcp=40, tls=40, request_and_work=55)
assert sum(cold.values()) == 155
warm = dict(request_and_work=55)
assert sum(warm.values()) == 55

    The cold path totals 155 ms. The warm model reuses the assumed DNS, TCP, and TLS setup, leaving the same 55 ms request/work stage.

    Real reuse depends on cache, protocol, connection state, and overlap. This code performs arithmetic; it does not open a connection or measure a protocol.

    The call adds travel, connection, timeout, trust, and partial-failure behaviour. A local exception and an unknown remote outcome are different. Revisit deadlines, operation identity, encoding, credentials, and fallback, measuring the whole path. Preserve the business meaning while changing the communication arrangement.

    Remember: A timeout limits waiting; it does not identify whether remote execution occurred.

    Unit 4 assessment → Explained solutions →

    Concept coverage

    4.1 · The runtime owns your resources
    • Program vs process vs thread.
    • Memory, stack, heap, and object lifetimes.
    • Scheduling and context switching.
    • CPU-bound vs I/O-bound workloads.
    • Synchronous vs asynchronous execution.
    4.2 · Tasks, threads & event loops
    • Blocking vs nonblocking I/O.
    • Concurrency vs parallelism.
    • Event loops, tasks, futures, promises.
    • Thread pools and worker pools.
    4.3 · Shared memory & coordination
    • Shared memory vs message passing.
    • Race conditions and critical sections.
    • Mutexes, semaphores, atomics, condition variables.
    • Deadlocks, starvation, livelocks.
    4.4 · Visibility, cancellation & overload
    • Memory visibility and happens-before relationships.
    • Thread safety and immutability.
