    PART 1 / UNIT 04 / CHAPTER 4.1

    The runtime owns your resources

    Prerequisites: Introduction to System Design5 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A thousand uploads can wait on storage or compete for CPU. First identify the process, threads, memory, and resource ownership before selecting an execution model.

    4.1.1 · Program vs process vs thread

    The same program can run twice at the same time. Each running instance is a process, with its own address space and resources. Inside a process, threads provide separate paths of execution. They commonly share heap memory but have their own stacks and scheduling state.

    These runtime boundaries differ from source files and modules. A crash of one process can stop all its threads, even if they execute different modules. Separate processes can provide useful isolation, while threads make sharing data convenient. Sharing introduces coordination needs: neither choosing threads nor dividing code into classes automatically makes concurrent updates safe.

    4.1.2 · Memory, stack, heap, and object lifetimes

    When an upload request calls functions, the runtime keeps call information on a stack. Dynamically managed objects, such as a large upload buffer, commonly live on the heap. The details depend on the language and runtime.

    An object's lifetime need not end when the initiating function returns. If a background task still holds a reference to the buffer, the buffer can remain in memory. Track who keeps each resource and when that ownership ends. Files and database connections need timely cleanup as well. A garbage collector managing memory does not establish when every external resource is closed. Bound the number and size of outstanding uploads.

    4.1.3 · Scheduling and context switching

    A machine may have more runnable threads than available cores. Its scheduler chooses which thread runs next. A context switch saves one execution state and restores another, and may disturb useful CPU-cache contents.

    More threads help when some are waiting and others can use an idle CPU. When the CPU is already saturated, more runnable threads can add overhead and waiting. A blocked I/O call can leave the CPU free for another thread; a busy-wait loop consumes it. Inspect CPU utilisation, runnable queues, and lock contention before choosing a thread count. Starting a thread for every incoming request allows resource use to grow without a bound.

    4.1.4 · CPU-bound vs I/O-bound workloads

    Assume 1,000 uploads each spend 100 ms waiting for storage and require negligible CPU work. Handling them sequentially takes about 100 seconds of waiting. Allowing fifty independent waits at once gives an ideal waiting-time lower bound near two seconds, before overhead and bandwidth limits.

    This workload is I/O-bound: waiting is the main limit. Compression may instead be CPU-bound because useful time is spent computing. Extra asynchronous tasks do not create extra CPU cores. For computation, investigate algorithms and actual parallel execution. For waiting, concurrency can use idle periods, provided the storage service and connections can support it. Measure which resource limits the real workload.

    4.1.5 · Synchronous vs asynchronous execution

    A caller can start an operation and wait for its result before proceeding; this is synchronous interaction. With an asynchronous interface, initiation and later completion are represented separately, so the caller can arrange other work while waiting.

    A different question is whether the thread itself blocks. An async function can still call a blocking library operation and stall the thread running it. Trace the implementation beneath the interface, including drivers. Choose a model that keeps waiting and resource usage manageable for the workload. The word “async” describes an interface or execution arrangement; it does not establish that every operation underneath is nonblocking.

    Think further · Who should own accepted upload work after its initiating request is cancelled?

    If cancellation only ends the connection but the business still requires processing, a durable job or workflow must retain identity, input, and progress. Cancel and release request-owned resources without discarding that obligation. If the work itself should stop, persist the chosen cancellation and block inappropriate later completion.

    Remember: Match concurrency to the limiting resource and account for what remains alive while work waits.

    Try applying it: Which resource changes first if uploads become CPU-heavy compression jobs?

    PART 1 / UNIT 04 / CHAPTER 4.2

    Tasks, threads & event loops

    Prerequisites: 4.1 · The runtime owns your resources4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    One event-loop callback computes for two seconds while other tasks are ready. Trace readiness and execution to see how nonblocking I/O and bounded pools affect progress.

    4.2.1 · Blocking vs nonblocking I/O

    An event loop starts a network read and arranges to be notified when progress is possible. While the I/O waits, the loop can run another ready task. Nonblocking I/O avoids holding the thread idle throughout that wait.

    The mechanism still needs readiness or completion notifications. Repeatedly checking an unfinished operation without yielding can consume CPU instead of saving it. Use the platform's intended interface. If a required library blocks, it may need a separate, bounded executor. Limit both active blocking jobs and queued jobs, and define cancellation and cleanup. Nonblocking submission does not mean the requested work has finished.

    4.2.2 · Concurrency vs parallelism

    Imagine two uploads on one core. Upload A starts, then waits for storage. The core works on B during that wait. Both activities are in progress over overlapping periods, so they are concurrent.

    If two cores execute A and B at the same instant, there is parallelism as well. Concurrency concerns overlapping progress; parallelism concerns simultaneous execution. A one-core program can still have a race if operations are interleaved between a read and its matching write. Decide separately how much work may be in progress and how much can execute at once. Both choices affect resource use, while coordination determines correctness.

    4.2.3 · Event loops, tasks, futures, promises

    A task awaits a future representing a pending result. The event loop runs other ready work. When the result becomes available, the task's continuation becomes eligible to run. A promise or future is the runtime's representation of that later result; exact behaviour depends on the runtime.

    Now suppose one callback computes continuously for two seconds on the only event-loop thread. Other ready callbacks must wait, even if their I/O already finished. Keep long computation away from the loop or split work appropriately. Scheduling a future also does not make the work durable: if its process dies, a memory-only task may disappear.

    4.2.4 · Thread pools and worker pools

    Suppose eight workers process uploads. The pool limits active execution to eight jobs, but accepting a thousand large buffers into a waiting queue can still exhaust memory. Execution limits and admission limits solve different problems.

    Use a bounded queue as well as a bounded worker count. Where practical, store large upload bytes separately and queue compact references. Decide what happens when the queue is full: reject, wait until a deadline, or use another supported path. A durable queue is needed if accepting the work promises survival across process loss. Count queued payloads, active buffers, and open resources when choosing the limits.

    Think further · Who should own accepted upload work after its initiating request is cancelled?

    If cancellation only ends the connection but the business still requires processing, a durable job or workflow must retain identity, input, and progress. Cancel and release request-owned resources without discarding that obligation. If the work itself should stop, persist the chosen cancellation and block inappropriate later completion.

    Remember: Overlapping tasks do not necessarily execute in parallel, and an event loop still needs short runnable turns.

    Try applying it: Why can adding async tasks leave a CPU-bound loop unresponsive?

    PART 1 / UNIT 04 / CHAPTER 4.3

    Shared memory & coordination

    Prerequisites: 4.2 · Tasks, threads & event loops4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Two increments leave a counter at one. Trace each read and write, then choose a coordination boundary that covers the whole rule rather than only one assignment.

    4.3.1 · Shared memory vs message passing

    Two threads can update a shared inventory map directly, provided they coordinate access. Alternatively, one owner can keep the map private and process inventory commands sent by other tasks. These are shared-memory and message-passing approaches.

    A single owner can make some local rules easier to preserve, but its messages may repeat and the owner can fail. Define delivery and recovery behaviour. Sending a pointer to an object that both sides can still mutate has not transferred exclusive ownership. Choose the arrangement by where state belongs and how much communication it needs. Both approaches need clear rules for concurrent access and failure.

    4.3.2 · Race conditions and critical sections

    Start a counter at zero. A reads zero. B reads zero before A writes. A adds one and writes one; B also adds one to its earlier value and writes one. Two increments have produced a final value of one.

    This is a lost update caused by a race: the outcome depends on how operations interleave. Protect the complete read–modify–write sequence as a critical section, using a suitable lock or atomic operation. Locking only the final assignment leaves the earlier reads unprotected. The protection must be shared by all relevant writers. A mutex inside one process cannot coordinate unrelated processes writing a database.

    4.3.3 · Mutexes, semaphores, atomics, condition variables

    Different coordination tools answer different questions. A mutex allows one holder into a protected section. A semaphore permits a limited number of holders. An atomic operation makes a specified action indivisible under its defined memory-order rules.

    A condition variable lets a thread wait for a condition while releasing a lock, then reacquire it before proceeding. Recheck the condition in a loop: waking does not establish that it is still true. Choose the protected state by the invariant. If a transfer changes two balances together, making each balance individually atomic does not automatically make the whole transfer atomic.

    4.3.4 · Deadlocks, starvation, livelocks

    A holds the inventory lock and waits for the payment lock. B holds the payment lock and waits for inventory. Neither can continue. This circular wait is a deadlock.

    Starvation occurs when a participant repeatedly fails to obtain the service or resource it needs. Livelock occurs when participants remain active but make no useful progress, for example by repeatedly yielding and retrying in the same pattern. Consistent lock ordering can prevent the illustrated deadlock. Shorter critical sections or different ownership may help too. A timeout needs cleanup and rollback; repeating the same failed coordination indefinitely can merely replace one problem with another.

    Think further · Who should own accepted upload work after its initiating request is cancelled?

    If cancellation only ends the connection but the business still requires processing, a durable job or workflow must retain identity, input, and progress. Cancel and release request-owned resources without discarding that obligation. If the work itself should stop, persist the chosen cancellation and block inappropriate later completion.

    Remember: Protect the complete invariant at the actual shared-state boundary.

    Try applying it: Which lock must both callers use, and why would separate per-caller locks fail?

    PART 1 / UNIT 04 / CHAPTER 4.4

    Visibility, cancellation & overload

    Prerequisites: 4.3 · Shared memory & coordination4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A request ends while its child work still holds a large buffer and a connection. Connect publication, ownership, cancellation, and admission to keep shared state and resource use controlled.

    4.4.1 · Memory visibility and happens-before relationships

    A thread constructs an object and publishes a reference to another thread. For the reader to use it correctly, the language's memory model must guarantee visibility of the initialised fields. An earlier wall-clock time alone does not supply that guarantee.

    Happens-before is an ordering relation used by memory models to describe which effects must be visible. Synchronisation mechanisms, such as an appropriate channel or lock, can establish the required relationship. Use the rules of the actual language and runtime rather than assuming all machines behave the same way. The Go memory model is one specified example. Safe publication matters even when the object will not change afterward.

    4.4.2 · Thread safety and immutability

    Suppose task records never change after construction. Readers can share those immutable values without competing to modify their fields. But a mutable dictionary that holds the records can still have concurrent inserts and removals.

    Thread safety is a claim about allowed concurrent use of the whole operation or object. Immutability removes some mutation problems; publication and surrounding containers still need coordination. Other approaches include keeping data inside one owner, copying values, or using locks. State which access is allowed and who protects it. Returning a writable internal collection lets callers bypass the rules even if each record looks safe on its own.

    4.4.3 · Resource exhaustion and backpressure

    Assume jobs arrive at 150 per second while workers complete 100 per second. If every job is accepted, the waiting queue grows by fifty each second. A larger queue postpones running out of space but leaves the mismatch unchanged.

    Backpressure slows or limits upstream work according to downstream capacity. Use bounded queues, admission deadlines, and clear overload responses. Keep queued payloads compact. Monitor the age of the oldest job as well as the number waiting: a short queue of stuck jobs may still be harmful. When a dependency slows, unlimited concurrency turns its delay into memory, connection, and thread exhaustion elsewhere.

    4.4.4 · Cancellation and structured concurrency

    An upload request starts several child tasks. If its deadline expires, someone must cancel work that is no longer needed and release local resources. Structured concurrency gives those child tasks a parent scope responsible for their completion and failure.

    Cancellation is a request to stop, with behaviour defined by the runtime and operation. It cannot prove that a remote side effect was undone. A payment may already have committed. Use reliable local cleanup for files and connections, and a status or reconciliation process for uncertain remote effects. If accepted work must continue after the request process dies, give it a durable job record and an explicit owner.

    Try the mechanism in code

    Pseudocode · bounded upload ownership

    queue = bounded_queue(capacity=100)
start_workers(count=50)
for upload in arrivals:
    reference = persist_upload_or_reject(upload)
    queue.put_with_deadline(reference)
worker():
    while reference = queue.take():
        try: process(reference)
        finally: release_owned_resources()

    The queue holds at most one hundred waiting references, and fifty workers limit active jobs. The large bytes remain in storage.

    A failed handoff still needs an explicit durable-job or rejection policy. A process-local queue alone cannot promise to resume accepted work after its process disappears.

    Download the executable mechanism collection ↓ · Follow the connected complete design →

    THE WORKBENCH · TRY CHANGING THE INPUTS

    What happens when jobs arrive faster than they finish?

    The queue starts empty. Jobs arrive and finish at constant rates, treated as a continuous flow. Increase the waiting limit and compare waiting with rejection. The model omits startup time, scheduling, and differences between individual jobs.

    1,000 uploads · compare the resource that dominates

    Assume each independent upload needs exactly 100 ms of waiting for storage and no meaningful CPU work. Ignore startup, connection limits, bandwidth, queue overhead, and variance. Sequential execution then needs 100 seconds; allowing 50 independent waits at once has an ideal lower bound of 2 seconds. These are constructed lower bounds, not measurements.

    Same I/O workload, different execution and recovery boundaries
    Execution modelIdeal elapsed timeWhat must be boundedCrash recovery
    Sequential100 sOne active upload; backlog elsewhereRequires a durable record
    50 threads with blocking I/O2 sThreads, stacks, connectionsMemory alone loses accepted work
    Async I/O with 50 in flight2 sTasks, buffers, socketsMemory alone loses accepted work
    Durable queue, 50 workersAt least 2 s, plus queue overheadAdmission, queue age, worker countDurable intent plus retry and idempotent completion

    Change the workload: each upload instead requires 20 ms of CPU and negligible I/O. The batch needs 20 CPU-seconds. One executing core therefore needs at least 20 seconds; eight truly parallel cores have an ideal lower bound of 2.5 seconds. An event loop creates no extra cores. Runtime restrictions can also prevent CPU-heavy threads from running in parallel. Measure overhead and contention before choosing threads or processes. A durable queue changes acknowledgment and recovery behavior; it does not erase service demand.

    Think further · Who should own accepted upload work after its initiating request is cancelled?

    If cancellation only ends the connection but the business still requires processing, a durable job or workflow must retain identity, input, and progress. Cancel and release request-owned resources without discarding that obligation. If the work itself should stop, persist the chosen cancellation and block inappropriate later completion.

    Remember: Safe concurrent use includes visibility, lifetimes, and bounded waiting as well as individual state updates.

    Try applying it: What must happen to local resources and required durable work when the parent request is cancelled?

    PART 2 / UNIT 05 / CHAPTER 5.1

    Model behavior with objects and values

    Prerequisites: Introduction to System Design5 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    One payment class checks orders, creates an SDK, and stores results. Divide the responsibilities, then examine which object relationships and contracts let those decisions change safely.

    5.1.1 · Abstraction, encapsulation, polymorphism, inheritance

    Imagine one payment class that checks an order, constructs a provider SDK, calculates fees, and writes audit records. A fee change and a provider change both require editing it. Begin by separating those kinds of work.

    Abstraction lets callers request a payment without knowing the provider protocol. Encapsulation controls access to payment state so changes follow its rules. Polymorphism lets different implementations satisfy the same sending contract. Inheritance is one way to specialise behaviour, but the other benefits can also be achieved with composed objects or functions. Keep rules such as valid amounts and allowed payment transitions under application control.

    5.1.2 · Composition vs inheritance

    Suppose callers use an Account contract that permits withdrawal. A ReadOnlyAccount subclass that always rejects withdrawal changes an assumption those callers rely on. Sharing fields through inheritance has not established a valid behavioural relationship.

    Composition assembles collaborators instead. A payment service can receive a fraud policy and a gateway, varying either without creating a subclass for every combination. It adds wiring and contracts, so use it where those variations are real. Inheritance remains useful when the specialised object consistently fulfils the inherited contract. Judge the relationship by what callers may do, rather than by similar fields or convenient code reuse.

    5.1.3 · Interfaces and contracts

    What does charge(100) mean? It might mean one hundred dollars, one dollar expressed in cents, or another currency entirely. A gateway interface needs more than a method signature.

    State the currency, amount units, operation identity, and possible outcomes. A payment may be approved, declined, or uncertain, with a provider reference when available. A timeout after submission is uncertain because the provider may already have charged. This behavioural contract lets the application replace adapters without silently changing payment meaning. Test the real adapter as well as a substitute: a fake returning “approved” cannot establish how the provider handles lost replies or repeated operations.

    5.1.4 · High cohesion and low coupling

    A fee rule belongs with related payment rules. An SMS receipt formatter has a different reason to change. If adding SMS requires editing ledger arithmetic, the responsibilities are entangled.

    Cohesion describes how closely the work inside a module belongs together. Coupling describes its dependencies on other modules. A focused payment module can use a narrow gateway contract without knowing provider field names. Test the arrangement with likely changes: where would a new receipt format or provider go? Avoid dividing work so finely that a simple action becomes difficult to follow. Extract a module when it protects a rule, hides changeable details, or gives a real change a clear home.

    5.1.5 · SOLID principles, including their limitations

    SOLID collects five design ideas. Single responsibility asks whether a module has a focused reason to change. Open/closed encourages useful extension points. Substitution requires implementations to preserve callers' expected behaviour. Interface segregation favours contracts suited to their callers. Dependency inversion places important policy behind abstractions it controls.

    For example, the payment service can use a small gateway interface implemented by a provider adapter. These are guidelines for judging a design, not a demand for an interface around every class. An elaborate extension system can cost more to understand than a direct edit. Apply each idea to an actual change or testing problem.

    Think further · Which payment rules should remain the same when objects are replaced by pure functions?

    Currency, units, allowed transitions, operation identity, and uncertainty remain business rules regardless of representation. Pure decision functions can make them easier to test. A separate effect interpreter still needs authorisation, transactions, provider identity, and reconciliation. Refactoring should preserve observed outcomes, not merely move methods into functions.

    Remember: Organise payment rules and provider details so callers rely on meaningful behaviour.

    Try applying it: Which part should change when the provider renames a field but the payment rule stays the same?

    PART 2 / UNIT 05 / CHAPTER 5.2

    Principles under pressure

    Prerequisites: 5.1 · Model behavior with objects and values4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Two pieces of code look alike, but do they express the same rule? Apply design heuristics to actual changes instead of treating every repetition or method chain as a defect.

    5.2.1 · DRY, KISS, YAGNI

    Suppose every gateway contains a copy of the same currency-conversion rule. A policy change can leave the copies disagreeing. This is duplicated knowledge: the concern behind DRY, “Don't Repeat Yourself.” Two similar-looking checks for genuinely different policies need not be merged.

    KISS asks us to keep the required design understandable. YAGNI, “You Aren't Gonna Need It,” discourages building speculative features before there is a need. Together, these ideas suggest a practical approach: identify the rule and its owner, share that knowledge where appropriate, and keep the implementation small enough to change. Similar syntax alone is weak evidence that two responsibilities belong together.

    5.2.2 · Law of Demeter

    Consider order.customer.account.settings.currency. The caller now knows the shape of several objects. Changing the account's settings representation may force that caller to change too.

    The Law of Demeter encourages limiting such knowledge of distant collaborators. An operation such as order.paymentCurrency() can express what the caller actually needs. The value is the reduced dependence on internal structure. Counting dots is not the objective: a fluent builder or a deliberate traversal of data can be clear. Avoid adding forwarding methods that hide nothing useful. Ask which representation details the caller would otherwise have to understand and maintain.

    5.2.3 · Tell, Don't Ask

    A caller reads an account balance, subtracts an amount, and writes the result. It has taken responsibility for a rule that belongs with the account. Another caller may implement the rule differently, and simultaneous updates can conflict.

    “Tell, Don't Ask” suggests asking the owner to reserve(amount). The owner can check the allowed balance and perform the change under the appropriate coordination. Reading balances for a report remains useful. Keep reads predictable and effects explicit. Moving a method onto an object also does not supply concurrency control: when several processes share the account, its storage boundary must enforce the rule atomically.

    5.2.4 · Command-query separation

    A call named payment.status() should report the payment's state. If reading status unexpectedly charges a card, callers cannot use it safely as a query.

    Command-query separation distinguishes operations that change state from those that report information. A create command may still return a useful result, such as the new identifier, provided its effect is clear. Document that convention. CQRS goes further by giving commands and queries different models where their needs justify it. Ordinary command-query separation does not require separate databases, services, or event histories. Begin with clear operation meanings before considering a larger architecture.

    Think further · Which payment rules should remain the same when objects are replaced by pure functions?

    Currency, units, allowed transitions, operation identity, and uncertainty remain business rules regardless of representation. Pure decision functions can make them easier to test. A separate effect interpreter still needs authorisation, transactions, provider identity, and reconciliation. Refactoring should preserve observed outcomes, not merely move methods into functions.

    Remember: Share knowledge that has one meaning and owner; keep effects and intentions explicit.

    Try applying it: When would merging similar validation code create a dependency between unrelated policies?

    PART 2 / UNIT 05 / CHAPTER 5.3

    Side effects, domain models & collaboration

    Prerequisites: 5.2 · Principles under pressure4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A payment keeps its identity while its status changes; a Money value is defined by its amount and currency. Use these differences to organise collaboration and test observable outcomes.

    5.3.1 · Immutability and side-effect management

    Suppose several helpers edit the same payment summary. To understand its final value, a reader must track every mutation. An immutable value gives a simpler alternative: calculate a new summary and leave the old one unchanged.

    Keep pure calculations, such as fee arithmetic, separate from effects such as provider calls and database writes. Inputs and returned values then make the calculation easier to test. Copying and allocation have costs, which should be measured when significant. Immutability also has a limited scope: an immutable payment command can still be executed twice, and it cannot undo an external charge. Execution still needs authorisation and an operation identity.

    5.3.2 · Domain models, entities, value objects

    Payment 42 is still the same payment after its status changes. Its identity matters, so it is an entity. Two Money values with the same currency and minor-unit amount can represent the same value without separate identities; they are value objects.

    A domain model expresses business concepts and their rules. Money arithmetic should reject incompatible currencies unless an explicit conversion rule applies. A domain service can express a rule that does not belong naturally to one entity. Put important rules where callers can consistently use them. Simple transport data need not become an elaborate object model, but scattering payment invariants across controllers makes them difficult to preserve.

    5.3.3 · Object collaboration

    During checkout, an orchestrator asks inventory to reserve items, asks payments to authorise, and records the order's progress. Each collaborator owns its own rules and returns an explicit result.

    An object collaboration describes these requests and responsibilities, rather than only the fields each object holds. Inventory should not quietly edit payment records. If one step fails after another succeeds, the orchestrator needs enough information to recover or compensate. Also consider where calls run. Many small in-process calls may be cheap; moving the same conversation across a network adds waiting and partial failures. Design a remote contract for that boundary rather than automatically copying the object interface.

    5.3.4 · Testability and design for change

    To test a declined payment, give the service a test gateway that returns “declined.” The test can then check the order's resulting state without contacting a real provider. Controllable inputs and visible outcomes make such tests useful.

    A test that only expects a particular sequence of private method calls may fail after a harmless refactor while missing a business error. Prefer checks of the required result and state. Keep integration checks for the real boundaries: encoding, transactions, timeouts, and cleanup. A substitute gateway helps test orchestration but cannot establish the actual provider's behaviour. Choose evidence appropriate to the claim being checked.

    Think further · Which payment rules should remain the same when objects are replaced by pure functions?

    Currency, units, allowed transitions, operation identity, and uncertainty remain business rules regardless of representation. Pure decision functions can make them easier to test. A separate effect interpreter still needs authorisation, transactions, provider identity, and reconciliation. Refactoring should preserve observed outcomes, not merely move methods into functions.

    Remember: Keep identity, values, effects, and coordination distinct enough to reason about their changes.

    Try applying it: Which checks can a fake gateway establish, and which require the real storage or provider boundary?

    PART 2 / UNIT 05 / CHAPTER 5.4

    Design for change, testing & functions

    Prerequisites: 5.3 · Side effects, domain models & collaboration4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Refactoring a payment class should preserve approval, decline, and uncertainty. Follow those behaviours through structural changes and compare object-based and functional ways to express the decisions.

    5.4.1 · Refactoring and recognizing code smells

    Before reorganising a large payment class, capture its important behaviours: successful payment, decline, timeout, and storage failure. In particular, keep an uncertain provider outcome distinct from a definite decline.

    Refactoring changes structure while preserving the intended behaviour. Extract input parsing, fee calculation, provider communication, and storage in small steps, checking those behaviours after each change. A long method or repeated conditional suggests a place to investigate; it does not automatically call for a design pattern. Tests focused on outcomes allow code to move without tying the design to every old internal call. If the business behaviour changes, describe and test that change explicitly.

    5.4.2 · Functional programming alternatives to object-centric design

    We can express payment decisions using functions as well as objects. A pure function decide(state, command) can return a new state, events, or requests for external actions. Another part of the application carries out the database write or provider call.

    Because the decision function has explicit inputs and no hidden effects, it is easier to test and replay. The effect-performing part still needs durable progress, ownership, and duplicate handling. Calling a pure decision function twice is different from charging a provider twice. Choose functions and objects according to which makes the rules and collaboration easiest to see; they can be used together in the same design.

    Try the mechanism in code

    Python · injected collaborator

    class RecordingGateway:
    def __init__(self): self.calls = []
    def charge(self, command):
        self.calls.append(command)
        return "uncertain"

def pay(command, gateway):
    return gateway.charge(command)

gateway = RecordingGateway()
assert pay({"amount_minor":100,"currency":"USD"}, gateway) == "uncertain"

    The recording gateway receives the command and returns uncertainty. Passing it as an argument makes this behaviour easy to exercise without a real provider.

    A complete payment service also checks money, persists progress, and reconciles outcomes. This small example isolates the dependency; it does not implement those other obligations.

    Think further · Which payment rules should remain the same when objects are replaced by pure functions?

    Currency, units, allowed transitions, operation identity, and uncertainty remain business rules regardless of representation. Pure decision functions can make them easier to test. A separate effect interpreter still needs authorisation, transactions, provider identity, and reconciliation. Refactoring should preserve observed outcomes, not merely move methods into functions.

    Remember: Improve structure while preserving the required outcomes and making external effects visible.

    Try applying it: What regression test would catch a timeout accidentally being reclassified as a decline?

    PART 2 / UNIT 06 / CHAPTER 6.1

    Dependencies, inversion & composition

    Prerequisites: Object-Oriented and Modular Software Design6 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A notification service constructs its own provider and is difficult to test. Move that choice to startup, then distinguish supplying a dependency from choosing the interface policy relies on.

    6.1.1 · Dependency, dependency direction, and inversion

    A notification service that imports an email provider's SDK must understand that provider's types and errors. A provider change can then reach the application's notification rules. The source dependency points from the service to the SDK.

    Dependency inversion changes which interface the service relies on. Define a Sender contract in the application, then make the provider adapter implement it. Runtime calls still execute that adapter, but the notification policy no longer needs the SDK's details. Check the boundary's data and errors as well as its imports. Moving a constructor into a helper does little if provider-specific meanings still pass through every caller.

    6.1.2 · Inversion of Control (IoC)

    In an ordinary function call, our code decides when to invoke another function. With an event loop, we register a callback and the loop decides when to call it. Some control has moved to an external coordinator. This is Inversion of Control, or IoC.

    Frameworks also invoke request handlers or arrange their construction. Dependency Injection is one technique that can be used within these arrangements; IoC is the broader idea. Understand the framework's callback lifetime, ordering, and error behaviour. Delegating control changes where these decisions are made, while the application still needs to choose and use them correctly.

    6.1.3 · Dependency Injection (DI)

    Compare a notification service that constructs EmailSender internally with one created as NotificationService(sender). In the second version, another part of the program supplies the collaborator. This is Dependency Injection, or DI.

    The supplied sender might be an email adapter, an SMS adapter, or a test sender that records messages. Ordinary constructor or function arguments are sufficient; a container is optional. Keep the dependency focused. Passing one enormous infrastructure object can still expose far more knowledge than the service needs. The value of injection comes from visible collaborators and a meaningful contract, rather than the presence of a particular framework.

    6.1.4 · Constructor, property/setter, and method injection

    If an object cannot work without a sender, constructor injection supplies it before the object is used. Setter injection supplies a dependency later, which may suit optional configuration but introduces a period when the object is not fully ready.

    Method injection passes a collaborator for one operation. This can express a per-call dependency without storing it for the object's whole lifetime. Choose by validity and ownership. For example, a long-lived service should not retain a request's database session after that request ends. Different frameworks provide different facilities, but the design question remains: when is the dependency required, and how long may the receiver keep it?

    6.1.5 · Dependency inversion principle vs DI

    Suppose Service(provider_sdk) receives its SDK through a constructor. This uses DI, but the service may still depend on provider-specific request types and exceptions. Injection alone has not isolated its policy from the provider.

    The dependency inversion principle concerns the direction of knowledge: important policy relies on suitable abstractions, while implementations conform to them. DI concerns how collaborators are supplied. The two often work together but answer different questions. Inspect the actual interface, outcomes, and resource handles crossing the boundary. A manually assembled service can respect dependency inversion without a container; constructor syntax alone cannot establish that its contract is well chosen.

    6.1.6 · Composition roots and DI containers

    At startup, we can write repository = SQLiteRepository(path), then service = NotificationService(repository, sender). Keeping these construction choices together makes the application's object relationships visible. This part of the program is the composition root.

    A DI container automates construction and manages registered lifetimes. It can simplify a large graph, but also hide which dependency is resolved and postpone some mistakes until runtime. Validate registrations early and make resource ownership clear. For a few collaborators, explicit construction may be easier to read. Use a container where its actual wiring and lifetime support justify the additional machinery.

    Think further · How should resources be owned when a job outlives its request and user session?

    Give the job an explicit lifetime and scope, with durable identifiers rather than captured request objects. Create or borrow resources under a documented owner and close them at the appropriate boundary. Define whether current membership must be rechecked; a long-lived job must not silently inherit expired user authority.

    Remember: Injection supplies collaborators; inversion determines which abstractions and meanings the policy depends on.

    Try applying it: Can a constructor receive an SDK while still exposing provider details throughout the service?

    PART 2 / UNIT 06 / CHAPTER 6.2

    Lifetimes, ownership & cleanup

    Prerequisites: 6.1 · Dependencies, inversion & composition6 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A background job uses a connection after its request scope has closed. Track creation, reuse, ownership, and disposal across the lifetimes involved.

    6.2.1 · Transient, scoped, singleton, and framework-specific lifetimes

    Resolve a scoped object twice in request one: both references should point to A. Resolve it twice in request two: both should point to B. That is reuse within a scope. A transient resolution creates a new instance, while a singleton is reused within the framework's stated container or application boundary.

    Those words describe lifetimes, not universal global identities. Another process can have its own singleton. A shared singleton must also be safe for its allowed concurrent callers. Check the framework's exact naming, resolution, and disposal rules. A lifetime label does not establish thread safety or mean that the object can outlive its dependencies.

    6.2.2 · Request scopes, session scopes, and custom scopes

    An HTTP request finishes and its scoped database session is closed. A background job that kept that session now tries to use it. The job has outlived a resource it borrowed.

    A request scope covers one request. A session scope can span several requests, while a job can have its own scope with an explicit end. Create an appropriate scope for background work and pass durable identifiers rather than retaining request-owned objects. Long-lived scopes also retain data and may create privacy or memory costs. A scope is an ownership arrangement; it is not automatically a database transaction or a guarantee about the user's current permissions.

    6.2.3 · Object creation vs object ownership

    A factory opens a connection and returns it. Who must close it? The caller might own it, or the factory might be returning a shared resource managed elsewhere. Holding a reference does not answer the ownership question.

    Specify ownership in the contract. Two components must not both assume they may close the same shared connection. Consider a repository that returns a lazy query result: reading it may still need the repository's connection. Closing the repository before consuming the result breaks that lifetime. Return bounded materialised data when appropriate, or return an explicit streaming resource whose owner is responsible for closing it.

    6.2.4 · Disposal, cleanup, and resource lifecycles

    A request borrows a connection, then fails while processing. Unless cleanup returns the connection, later healthy requests have less pool capacity. A small leak repeated over many failures can stop the application.

    Arrange cleanup for success, failure, and cancellation using structured scopes or finally-style code. Close streams, release permits, and roll back unfinished transactions. Memory garbage collection does not guarantee timely release of these external resources. If cleanup also fails, preserve the original problem and record the cleanup failure. Resource management is part of system capacity and correctness, rather than work that can be postponed until the process exits.

    6.2.5 · Lazy initialization

    A report generator may never be used during a particular run. Lazy initialisation waits until the first report request before constructing it, saving unused startup work. That first request now pays the construction cost and may encounter its failure.

    Two first callers can also arrive together. Coordinate initialisation and safe publication using the runtime's supported mechanism. Decide whether a failed initialisation is retried or remembered. For essential resources, starting them before advertising readiness may provide clearer behaviour than failing the first real user request. Lazy creation changes when work happens; it still needs lifetime, error, and concurrency rules.

    6.2.6 · Dependency cycles and captive dependencies

    Suppose A needs B to be constructed, while B needs A. This dependency cycle may reveal mixed responsibilities or a missing coordinator. Hiding a lookup in a global registry can postpone the problem without clarifying ownership.

    Another lifetime error is a captive dependency: a singleton stores a request-scoped unit of work and keeps using it after the request ends. Refactor the operation to receive a currently valid dependency or a narrow factory that creates an appropriate scope. Preserve the correct user and tenant context as well. Passing a container validation check is useful, but the real requirement is that every use occurs within the dependency's valid lifetime.

    Think further · How should resources be owned when a job outlives its request and user session?

    Give the job an explicit lifetime and scope, with durable identifiers rather than captured request objects. Create or borrow resources under a documented owner and close them at the appropriate boundary. Define whether current membership must be rechecked; a long-lived job must not silently inherit expired user authority.

    Remember: A reference remains valid only under its resource's ownership and lifetime contract.

    Try applying it: How should a job obtain resources if it must outlive the request that created it?

    PART 2 / UNIT 06 / CHAPTER 6.3

    Injection, locators & factories

    Prerequisites: 6.2 · Lifetimes, ownership & cleanup4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A service receives one container and resolves everything from it. Compare those hidden lookups with explicit collaborators and a narrow factory for legitimate runtime choices.

    6.3.1 · DI vs service locator

    A constructor that lists Sender and Repository tells us what the service needs. A method that silently calls global_registry.resolve(...) reveals that need only during execution. The latter is a service locator.

    Locators can have a deliberate role at an integration boundary, but using them throughout application code hides dependencies and makes isolated tests harder. Injecting the entire container into a service can preserve the same hidden lookups under a different name. Resolve collaborators near startup or the relevant scope boundary, then pass the specific contracts needed. This makes missing dependencies and ownership easier to review.

    6.3.2 · DI vs factory pattern

    A service may receive one sender chosen at startup. Alternatively, it may receive a sender factory because each notification chooses its channel at runtime. Injection supplies the collaborator; the factory performs a construction or selection operation when asked.

    The two techniques can work together. A factory also needs a lifetime contract: does it return a fresh caller-owned sender, a shared singleton, or a scoped object? A caller must not close a shared sender as if it had created a private one. Keep provider-specific construction inside the factory while making ownership and possible failure clear to its callers.

    Think further · How should resources be owned when a job outlives its request and user session?

    Give the job an explicit lifetime and scope, with durable identifiers rather than captured request objects. Create or borrow resources under a documented owner and close them at the appropriate boundary. Define whether current membership must be rechecked; a long-lived job must not silently inherit expired user authority.

    Remember: Use factories for creation decisions and explicit dependencies for work the caller already knows it needs.

    Try applying it: What must a sender factory say about whether its returned object may be closed by the caller?

    PART 2 / UNIT 06 / CHAPTER 6.4

    Creational patterns

    Prerequisites: 6.3 · Injection, locators & factories6 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Creating a notification can require choosing a writer, a compatible family, or a valid combination of fields. These are different construction problems with different useful patterns.

    6.4.1 · Factory Method, Abstract Factory, Builder, Prototype, Singleton

    Construction becomes a design problem when there are several valid ways to create something. Factory Method varies a creation operation. Abstract Factory produces a compatible family of objects. Builder assembles and validates a complex value in stages. Prototype copies a configured object. Singleton restricts access to an instance within a specified boundary.

    The individual examples below show what problem each solves. A direct constructor remains useful when it already expresses all required inputs. Extra construction machinery needs a reason: invalid partially built values, accidental sharing in copies, and global mutable state can introduce problems of their own. Choose the pattern by the variation that the application actually needs.

    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Factory Method

    A report exporter needs a writer, but different exporters may choose different formats. Its processing code can call make_writer(), then use the returned writer without choosing the concrete type itself. Factory Method makes that creation step a variation point.

    Use it when the creator has a meaningful construction choice to customise. A supplied function may be sufficient; inheritance is not always needed. Abstract Factory deals with a different scale of choice: a compatible family of products rather than one creation operation.

    export(rows):
    writer = make_writer()
    writer.write(rows)
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Abstract Factory

    An HTML notification needs a renderer and a compatible template. Selecting them independently could mix components that expect different content models. Abstract Factory creates the related objects as one family.

    The client asks the selected factory for each collaborator, keeping the family choice together. This helps when the application switches complete families. Adding a new kind of product can require changes to every factory, so there is a maintenance cost. If one stable set of objects is all that is needed, direct construction may be clearer.

    family = HtmlNotificationFactory()
renderer = family.renderer()
template = family.template()
renderer.render(template, data)
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Builder

    A notification requires a recipient and template, with optional locale and expiry. A builder collects these choices and checks them before creating the usable notification.

    The final build step should reject missing or incompatible fields. Until then, the partially assembled value should not be treated as ready to send. Builder is useful when staged construction improves clarity. For a small value, a constructor with named parameters may already express everything safely. Its purpose is controlled assembly, rather than creating a family of different products.

    builder.to(recipient).template(template_id)
notification = builder.expires_at(deadline).build()
# build rejects missing recipient or incompatible fields
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Prototype

    A report layout contains a carefully configured set of values. Prototype creates another layout by copying that configured instance rather than rebuilding every setting.

    Specify what the copy owns. A shallow copy can leave both layouts referring to the same mutable object; a deeper copy may duplicate more state. Copying a connection handle does not create an independently owned connection. Shared immutable font data can remain shared, while editable layout values need suitable ownership. Use copying when those rules are clearer than constructing fresh request state from immutable configuration.

    layout = prototype.clone_owned_values()
layout.title = "Monthly report"
# Shared immutable font data remains shared
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Singleton

    An application may load one immutable configuration object and share it with its services. A Singleton arrangement restricts access to an instance within a stated program or container boundary. Another process may still have its own instance.

    Keep that boundary and ownership explicit. Shared mutable request state can cause races and test interference. Container-managed singleton lifetime and a class offering hidden global access are related but different arrangements. Passing an application-owned instance to its users often makes dependencies easier to see and tests easier to isolate.

    configuration = load_immutable_configuration()
service = Service(configuration)
# One application-owned instance; no hidden global lookup
    Think further · How should resources be owned when a job outlives its request and user session?

    Give the job an explicit lifetime and scope, with durable identifiers rather than captured request objects. Create or borrow resources under a documented owner and close them at the appropriate boundary. Define whether current membership must be rechecked; a long-lived job must not silently inherit expired user authority.

    Remember: Choose construction machinery for a real variation, and define validity and ownership of the result.

    Try applying it: When would named constructor parameters be clearer than a builder?

    PART 2 / UNIT 06 / CHAPTER 6.5

    Structural patterns

    Prerequisites: 6.4 · Creational patterns8 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A wrapper can translate an interface, add metrics, control access, or simplify a subsystem. Follow the intent and contract of each structural pattern to tell them apart.

    6.5.1 · Adapter, Bridge, Composite, Decorator, Facade, Flyweight, Proxy

    Several patterns place objects between collaborators, but their purposes differ. Adapter translates an interface. Bridge separates two dimensions that vary independently. Composite gives leaves and groups a common way to be used. Decorator adds behaviour around an existing interface.

    Facade presents a focused entry to a subsystem. Flyweight shares suitable immutable data. Proxy controls access to a target. The examples below make these differences concrete. Preserve the intended contract when composing them: adding metrics can be straightforward, while adding retries to a payment sender changes the risk of repeated effects. A common diagram shape does not make these patterns interchangeable.

    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Adapter

    An SMS SDK returns provider-specific status codes. The application's Sender contract expects accepted, declined, or uncertain with a reference. An Adapter translates between these interfaces.

    The translation must preserve meaning. A provider timeout should not become a definite decline just because that is easier to encode. Keep SDK-specific types inside the adapter where practical, and test its mapping against the provider contract. Decorator usually adds behaviour around the same interface; Adapter's main job is to reconcile an interface or representation mismatch.

    send(message):
    raw = sdk.submit(encode(message))
    return map_provider_outcome(raw)
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Bridge

    Suppose notifications vary by content—alerts or receipts—and by transport—email or SMS. Subclassing every combination produces many similar classes. A Bridge lets each content object use a transport contract through composition.

    The two dimensions can then vary independently. This needs a well-chosen shared contract and some wiring. Adapter usually connects an existing mismatch; Bridge deliberately separates variations in the design. It is useful when those variations are real, rather than when one fixed sender would serve the application more simply.

    class Receipt:
    constructor(transport): self.transport = transport
    deliver(data): return self.transport.send(format_receipt(data))
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Composite

    A notification audience can be one user or a group containing other audiences. Composite gives leaves and groups a compatible interface so a caller can traverse the audience structure.

    Define duplicates, cycles, depth or size limits, and how failures are reported. A send to a group can partly succeed even if its method looks like a send to one user. The shared interface does not make the whole group atomic. Use a simple collection loop when the domain has no useful tree-shaped structure.

    recipients(node, seen):
    if node.id in seen: return []
    seen.add(node.id)
    return node.users_or_recursive_children(seen)
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Decorator

    A metrics wrapper records how long Sender.send takes, then returns its result. Decorator adds behaviour around a collaborator while retaining its interface.

    Order can change meaning: placing metrics inside a retry wrapper counts attempts, while placing it outside can measure one logical call. Retrying also changes the risk of duplicate effects, so it needs a safe repetition contract. Use decorators where composition makes such behaviour clear. Avoid burying essential business decisions in a long wrapper stack that callers cannot easily inspect.

    send(message):
    start = clock()
    try: return inner.send(message)
    finally: metrics.observe(clock() - start)
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Facade

    Submitting a notification may involve validation, template selection, and saving a delivery plan. A Facade offers one focused operation that coordinates this subsystem for its clients.

    The caller no longer needs to know every internal step. The response must still distinguish accepted work from completed delivery. Keep the facade focused; accumulating every unrelated operation turns it into a large coordinator that is difficult to change. A Proxy commonly stands in for the same target interface, while a Facade primarily offers a simpler entry to several cooperating parts.

    submit(command):
    validated = validate(command)
    return intents.persist(render_plan(validated))
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Flyweight

    Thousands of notifications may use one parsed template. Flyweight shares that reusable, immutable part while each rendering supplies its own recipient and variables.

    Separating shared content from per-use context reduces repeated storage. Mixing recipient state into the shared template could leak data between users. Measure whether memory pressure justifies extra pooling or caching; ordinary immutable reuse may be enough. Sharing also leaves version selection, cache expiry, and resource lifetime to be designed. The pattern identifies what can be shared, rather than solving every cache-management problem.

    template = parsed_templates.get(version)
output_a = render(template, context_a)
output_b = render(template, context_b)
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Proxy

    Before reading a document, a Proxy can check whether the actor currently has access, then forward the call to the target. It presents the target's interface while controlling access or another aspect of its use.

    Other proxies defer creation or represent a remote target. A remote call can fail or take substantial time, so its contract must expose the relevant uncertainty. Avoid interfaces that look cheap while hiding unbounded network retries or loads. A Facade simplifies subsystem operations; a Proxy usually represents the same conceptual target with controlled access.

    read(document_id, actor):
    authorize(actor, document_id)
    return target.read(document_id)
    Think further · How should resources be owned when a job outlives its request and user session?

    Give the job an explicit lifetime and scope, with durable identifiers rather than captured request objects. Create or borrow resources under a documented owner and close them at the appropriate boundary. Define whether current membership must be rechecked; a long-lived job must not silently inherit expired user authority.

    Remember: Similar object diagrams can hide different purposes and different changes to behaviour.

    Try applying it: Why does adding retries around a payment sender require more reasoning than adding timing metrics?

    PART 2 / UNIT 06 / CHAPTER 6.6

    Behavioral patterns

    Prerequisites: 6.5 · Structural patterns11 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A changing algorithm, a lifecycle transition, and a request pipeline each vary for different reasons. Use behavioural patterns to place the right decision where it can evolve clearly.

    6.6.1 · Strategy, Observer, Command, State, Chain of Responsibility, Template Method, Iterator, Mediator, Memento, Visitor

    Behavioural patterns make different kinds of decisions and coordination explicit. Strategy supplies an algorithm. Observer distributes notifications. Command represents a requested action. State organises behaviour by lifecycle. Chain of Responsibility chooses handlers, while Template Method fixes a process with selected extension points.

    Iterator controls traversal; Mediator coordinates collaborators; Memento captures a recoverable local state; Visitor adds operations over a known object structure. Read their individual examples as choices about where change should be easy. A pattern is useful when its extension point matches the application. A small conditional can remain clearer when no such variation is needed.

    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Strategy

    An order's price can be calculated under different pricing policies. Strategy supplies one calculation behind a contract, letting the caller use the selected policy without embedding every algorithm.

    Strategies must agree on amounts, units, errors, and effects. If there is only one stable formula, a function may be sufficient. Strategy varies a selected policy; State varies behaviour according to an entity's lifecycle and history. Choose the former when a policy is meant to be interchangeable, rather than letting a caller arbitrarily replace a payment's valid lifecycle state.

    price = pricing_strategy.calculate(order)
require(price.currency == order.currency)
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Observer

    A subject can notify several subscribed observers when something changes. Observer is useful for one-to-many reactions without making the subject call each concrete implementation directly.

    Decide whether callbacks run inline, in what order, and what happens if one throws or runs slowly. Remove subscriptions when their owners end so they do not retain unwanted objects. A local callback list exists only in process memory. When a required reaction must survive process loss, use an appropriate durable publication mechanism rather than treating local observation as a message broker.

    for observer in snapshot(subscribers):
    notify_under_defined_failure_policy(observer, event)
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Command

    SendReceipt(order_id, operation_id) records an intention that a handler can execute later. Command gives a requested action explicit data and identity. An event instead records a fact that has already been accepted.

    For durable work, prefer serialisable domain data over a closure holding a request's live connections. At execution time, the handler must check current validity and the chosen authorisation policy. Retries need duplicate handling. Representing an intention makes scheduling and audit easier, but storing a command alone does not establish safe repeated external execution.

    command = SendReceipt(order_id, operation_id)
handler.handle(command)
# Handler checks current authorization and state
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    State

    A pending payment and a captured payment accept different actions. State organises behaviour around that lifecycle. A guarded transition changes the state when the required evidence arrives.

    A small transition table can be clearer than a class for every state. Whichever representation is used, persist related state changes atomically and keep invalid transitions explicit. A caller cannot simply select “captured” as if choosing an interchangeable algorithm: the payment's history and evidence constrain it. This distinguishes lifecycle-dependent State from a selected Strategy.

    require((payment.state, event.kind) in allowed_transitions)
payment.state = next_state(payment.state, event)
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Chain of Responsibility

    A request passes through authentication, rate limiting, and parsing before reaching the application. A Chain of Responsibility gives each handler defined choices: reject, handle, transform, or continue.

    Specify the order and continuation rules. Forgetting to invoke the next handler can silently swallow work; placing expensive parsing before admission can change cost and exposure. A chain is a coordination structure, not a durable workflow protocol. If several stages must complete across crashes, they also need persistent progress and recovery rules.

    auth(rate_limit(parse(application)))(request)
# Each handler has explicit rejection and continuation rules
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Template Method

    Every import job must validate input, transform it, and commit the result in that order. Template Method fixes the overall sequence while allowing selected steps, such as format conversion, to vary.

    The base process must preserve its required checks when subclasses customise a step. Inheritance is a common implementation, but independent variations may be easier to express through composed strategies. Use the pattern when a stable process really has controlled extension points. Letting subclasses bypass validation or commit ordering undermines the very sequence the template was meant to protect.

    run(input):
    validate(input)
    result = transform(input)
    return commit(result)
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Iterator

    A caller asks an Iterator for the next item without needing to know whether it comes from an array, tree, or database cursor. The iterator keeps the traversal position.

    A lazy database iterator can also hold a connection. A slow reader may keep that resource open, while closing its owner too early can make the next read fail. Define closing, end-of-stream, ordering, and behaviour under mutation. For a small bounded result, materialising a list and releasing the connection before returning may provide a simpler contract.

    with open_bounded_cursor(query) as rows:
    for row in rows:
        consume(row)
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Mediator

    Inventory and payments need coordinated steps during checkout. A Mediator can receive their results and decide the next action, reducing direct knowledge between the collaborators.

    Give the coordinator a focused responsibility and explicit failure handling. Otherwise, it can become a large object that knows every detail of the application. In a distributed setting, a durable workflow orchestrator can carry this coordination across restarts, but the object pattern alone supplies no persistence. Separate the coordination idea from the mechanism needed to recover its progress.

    reservation = inventory.reserve(command)
outcome = payments.authorize(command.operation_id)
coordinate_outcomes(reservation, outcome)
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Memento

    Before an edit, a draft captures the values needed to restore its earlier local state. Memento provides such a supported snapshot without giving every caller access to arbitrary internals.

    Define which values are copied and what restoration means. References to shared mutable objects can make a supposed snapshot change later. Restoring the draft also cannot retract an email or reverse a payment already sent elsewhere. Use the pattern where local capture and restoration are well defined; external compensation, backups, and event histories address different recovery needs.

    before = draft.snapshot_owned_values()
draft.apply(edit)
draft.restore(before)
# No claim about undoing external effects
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Visitor

    A document tree contains known node types such as text and image. A Visitor supplies an operation, such as export or validation, that handles each supported node type.

    This makes adding operations easier without placing every operation on every node. Adding a new node kind can require updating all visitors, so the trade-off reverses for structural change. Pattern matching may be a simpler expression in some languages. Make unknown-node handling explicit so a new document version does not silently lose content during export.

    visit(node):
    match node.kind:
        case "text": return export_text(node)
        case "image": return export_image(node)
        case _: raise UnsupportedNode
    Think further · How should resources be owned when a job outlives its request and user session?

    Give the job an explicit lifetime and scope, with durable identifiers rather than captured request objects. Create or borrow resources under a documented owner and close them at the appropriate boundary. Define whether current membership must be rechecked; a long-lived job must not silently inherit expired user authority.

    Remember: Choose the extension point that matches the application's actual source of change.

    Try applying it: How does choosing a pricing strategy differ from moving a payment into its next valid state?
