    PART 3 / UNIT 10 / CHAPTER 10.3

    Races, anomalies & isolation

    Prerequisites: 10.2 · Commit, logging & versions5 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Two buyers want one seat, while two doctors can jointly leave nobody on call. Trace the different conflicts and choose protection for the whole invariant.

    10.3.1 · Locking and optimistic concurrency control

    Two buyers see seat version seven. Each tries UPDATE ... WHERE version=7, changing the owner and advancing the version. After one succeeds, the other's condition no longer matches, so it changes zero rows.

    This is optimistic concurrency control: validate the state assumption when applying the change. Zero rows means conflict, requiring a fresh read and business decision. Pessimistic locking coordinates before conflicting work instead. Locks can wait or deadlock; optimistic retries can waste effort under heavy contention. Choose according to conflict frequency and operation cost, and protect the whole invariant rather than treating every affected-row result as success.

    10.3.2 · Dirty reads, nonrepeatable reads, phantom reads

    A dirty read observes another transaction's uncommitted change. A nonrepeatable read sees a row change between two reads. A phantom changes the set of rows matching a repeated query—for example, a fourth reservation appears after a query first found three.

    These names describe histories worth distinguishing, but whether they occur depends on the chosen engine and isolation level. Write the problematic sequence in order and check the documented behaviour. Do not assume equal isolation names mean identical implementations. A test of one row read also cannot establish every predicate or write-conflict guarantee needed by the application.

    10.3.3 · Lost updates, write skew, serialization anomalies

    Two doctors are on call. Each transaction checks that the other doctor remains on call, then marks its own doctor off. If both see the original snapshot, they update different rows but leave nobody on call.

    This is write skew: individually plausible updates violate a shared rule. A lost update instead overwrites another writer's result. More generally, a serialization anomaly has no equivalent valid serial ordering. Protect the actual invariant with suitable serialization, coordinated locking, or a shared conflict point. Row-level protection alone does not necessarily cover a condition spanning several rows.

    10.3.4 · Isolation levels and implementation differences

    The selected engine's isolation implementation is part of the application contract. In PostgreSQL 18, ordinary Read Committed queries use statement snapshots. Repeatable Read gives a transaction snapshot but can still allow serialization anomalies. Serializable adds conflict handling that can reject a transaction.

    These rules are version- and statement-sensitive; other engines can differ. When a transaction must retry, restart the whole affected transaction using fresh reads, with bounded attempts. Repeating only its last statement can retain assumptions from a snapshot that is no longer valid. Keep externally visible effects safe under replay as well. An isolation name is a starting point for reading the actual guarantees.

    10.3.5 · Serializable execution and serializability

    Serializable transactions produce a committed result equivalent to some serial transaction order. That order need not be the same as wall-clock order between separate callers.

    Linearizability concerns operations respecting real-time precedence, as if each took effect at one point between its invocation and reply. Strict serializability combines real-time constraints with transaction serialization. Keep these properties separate when stating a requirement. A serializable transaction may abort and need retry, so protect external effects in any replayed code. Stronger concurrency guarantees help preserve a correctly expressed rule; they cannot correct a wrong fee calculation or supply every desired availability property.

    Think further · What changes when one local transaction is divided across independent databases?

    A former all-or-nothing invariant may no longer share one commit boundary. Identify which related changes require agreement, whether a distributed transaction is justified, or whether a workflow with explicit intermediate states and compensation fits. Local success at each store does not guarantee the combined business outcome.

    Remember: Concurrency control must match the rule being preserved, not just the individual row being updated.

    Try applying it: What does zero affected rows mean after an optimistic seat claim?

    PART 3 / UNIT 10 / CHAPTER 10.4

    Pools, recovery & ticket correctness

    Prerequisites: 10.3 · Races, anomalies & isolation4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A pool is full and the backup job says it succeeded. Examine connection ownership, multi-statement transactions, and actual restore evidence before making a reliability claim.

    10.4.1 · Database connection pooling

    Assume ten database connections, each held for an average of 100 ms. The simple fully busy service bound is 10/0.1 = 100 operations per second before other constraints and variability.

    A pool limits connections but also creates acquisition waits. Increasing its size can add contention instead of throughput. Measure hold time, lock waits, idle transactions, and queue age. If callers retain a connection while waiting for an unrelated HTTP service, shorten that ownership interval where the transaction allows it. Include acquisition in the request deadline. Pool capacity is useful only when the database can perform the work it admits.

    10.4.2 · Transactions across multiple operations

    Reserving a seat and inserting the corresponding local reservation must agree. If one commits without the other, the records no longer describe one valid outcome. Put both statements inside a deliberate transaction boundary.

    Check what the libraries actually do. An ORM save call does not establish that every related action shares the same transaction. Across stores or remote services, use an explicit coordination protocol and reconciliation where needed. Keep a local transaction short while covering the required invariant. Do not let a returned lazy result depend on resources already closed when the operation's scope ended.

    10.4.3 · Backup, recovery, and durability

    A backup job reports success. We still need to know whether its data can be decrypted, restored, and used by the application. Test restoration with the required schema, credentials, and business checks, and measure how long it takes.

    Replication maintains live copies and may repeat an accidental deletion. Backups preserve recoverable history under their retention policy. Point-in-time recovery also needs the appropriate log history. State which acknowledged writes can be recovered after each failure. Owning a backup file is useful evidence of a file, but the recovery promise requires a tested procedure and suitable independent storage.

    Try the mechanism in code

    Python · conditional seat claim

    from mechanisms import open_demo_store, claim_seat
db = open_demo_store()
db.execute("INSERT INTO seats VALUES (1,NULL)")
db.commit()
assert claim_seat(db, 1, "A")
assert not claim_seat(db, 1, "B")
db.close()

    A claims the available seat; B's later conditional claim fails. The affected-row result determines whether the change occurred. The executable checks also use two connections to the same store.

    This protects a local ownership rule. Payment, hold expiry, and stale callbacks need connected but separate workflow logic.

    PART 3 / UNIT 11 / CHAPTER 11.1

    Locality and cache placement

    Prerequisites: Networking Foundations for System Design, Data Models and Storage Technologies4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A product is read repeatedly between edits. Work out which cost a cache can avoid, how much active data fits, and which layer should hold the reusable representation.

    11.1.1 · Why caching works

    A product description is read thousands of times between edits. Reusing a stored response can avoid repeating the database lookup or calculation. This reuse is why caching can help.

    Assume a cache hit takes 1 ms, a miss takes 50 ms, and 90% of requests hit. The simple average service time is 0.9×1 + 0.1×50 = 5.9 ms, excluding queueing and other work. Compare this saving with memory, lookup, and maintenance costs. A result used only once may be a poor cache candidate. Hit ratio also does not establish tail latency: slow misses and queues can still dominate some users' waits.

    11.1.2 · Cache locality and the working set

    A user repeatedly opens the same product: that is temporal locality. Reading neighbouring records together illustrates spatial locality. A working set is the data actively needed during a relevant interval.

    A cache much smaller than that set may continually evict entries just before they are reused. A large scan can also displace useful entries under some policies. Measure bytes and object sizes as well as key counts, and distinguish frequently used data from the full historical collection. Preloading every object can fill memory with cold content. Admission rules decide what deserves a place before eviction decides what must leave.

    11.1.3 · In-process vs distributed caches

    Two application instances each keep a price in memory. One has price 10 and another price 12. Their in-process caches provide fast access but create separate copies whose freshness needs coordination.

    A distributed cache provides a shared network-accessible layer, adding encoding, connection, and failure costs. Choose by reuse patterns, duplicated memory, and required behaviour when a copy is stale or unavailable. Ordinary cached stock counts should not become the sole authority for exclusive allocation. Placing the cache elsewhere changes its access and failure boundaries; it does not by itself resolve the application's consistency rule.

    11.1.4 · Browser, CDN, application, and database caches

    A page can be answered by a browser cache, a CDN, an application cache, or a database buffer pool. Each stores a different kind of copy. Database pages and a rendered account response also have different keys and update rules.

    Draw the layers actually used and specify freshness at each. Invalidating an application object does not clear a browser's response. A public edge cache with a poorly scoped key can expose personal data. When diagnosing a stale result, identify which layer answered and which version it held. “The cache was cleared” is incomplete unless it names the particular copy involved.

    Think further · When should a product stop serving rather than return a stale cached result?

    Stop when the operation requires current authority or the permitted stale interval has ended. An old description may be allowed, while allocating scarce stock or deciding current access may not be. State which actions degrade and which wait or reject, with visible status and a recovery path.

    Remember: Cache value comes from useful reuse under a valid freshness and access policy.

    Try applying it: Why can a high hit ratio coexist with slow or incorrect user responses?

    PART 3 / UNIT 11 / CHAPTER 11.2

    Copies, freshness & eviction

    Prerequisites: 11.1 · Locality and cache placement4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A delayed reader inserts yesterday's price after a writer invalidates it. Follow cache population, expiry, versioning, and eviction as separate decisions.

    11.2.1 · Cache-aside, read-through, write-through, write-behind

    With cache-aside, application code loads from the source after a miss and populates the cache. Read-through places that loading behind the cache interface. Write-through includes backing-store work in the write path; write-behind delays it. Exact ordering varies by implementation.

    Trace failures explicitly. A volatile write-behind cache can lose acknowledged changes before backing persistence. Cache-aside also has a race: a reader fetches version one, a writer commits version two and invalidates, then the delayed reader inserts version one. Where freshness requires stronger behaviour, use an appropriate version or coordination protocol. A pattern name alone does not resolve these event sequences.

    11.2.2 · TTL and cache expiration

    A cache receives a value that was already five minutes old and gives it a one-minute TTL. The copy may then remain six minutes behind its source. TTL describes residence after insertion, rather than necessarily the age of the fact.

    Expiration also differs from eviction due to memory pressure. Choose lifetimes using tolerated staleness and refresh behaviour, and consider client-held copies. Adding jitter can spread expirations that would otherwise happen together. For a correctness-critical action, revalidate against the authority when required. A short display-cache TTL is useful only if it matches the promise made about that display.

    11.2.3 · Cache consistency and invalidation

    A writer updates the source and deletes a cache entry. A delayed reader can still repopulate it from an earlier read, leaving an old value after the invalidation. Simply deleting after writing does not prevent every race.

    Versioned entries, conditional population, or source-version checks can support a stronger protocol. Observe delayed or repeated invalidation events and their progress. Choose freshness per operation. Showing an older price may be acceptable if checkout verifies the actual price; allocating the last item from an old count can oversell it. Invalidation must serve the business rule, rather than merely keep copies approximately similar.

    11.2.4 · Eviction: LRU, LFU, FIFO, and alternatives

    At capacity three, access A,B,C,A,D. Ideal LRU treats the second access to A as recent and evicts B. FIFO preserves insertion order and evicts A. LFU favours frequently used entries but also needs a tie-breaking rule.

    Real cache policies may approximate these ideals. Test the actual policy with representative object sizes and request patterns. Eviction decides what leaves; admission decides what enters. Neither can make an arbitrarily large working set fit into memory. A policy that performs well on one tiny fixture may behave poorly during scans or changing popularity, so measure the workload it is meant to serve.

    Think further · When should a product stop serving rather than return a stale cached result?

    Stop when the operation requires current authority or the permitted stale interval has ended. An old description may be allowed, while allocating scarce stock or deciding current access may not be. State which actions degrade and which wait or reject, with visible status and a recovery path.

    Remember: Residence time and eviction policy do not by themselves establish current source data.

    Try applying it: How can a one-minute TTL serve a value that is more than one minute behind its source?

    PART 3 / UNIT 11 / CHAPTER 11.3

    Hot keys, stampedes & negative results

    Prerequisites: 11.2 · Copies, freshness & eviction5 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A cache restarts just as a product becomes popular. Control duplicate loading, absent lookups, warming, and permitted stale results before the origin becomes overwhelmed.

    11.3.1 · Hot keys

    A single product becomes extremely popular. Even a large cache cluster can overload the one owner serving that key. Adding nodes mainly gives other keys more capacity unless the design also distributes this key's traffic.

    For reads, local copies, replicas, or coalescing repeated work may help, with an explicit freshness policy. For writes, determine whether the value can be split or combined safely. An aggregate counter may allow distributed increments; exclusive stock allocation needs a stronger rule. Identify whether the pressure is transfer volume, recomputation, object size, or serialised updates before selecting a remedy.

    11.3.2 · Cache stampedes, penetration, and avalanche

    Many requests miss the same key and all recompute it: a cache stampede. Repeated requests for nonexistent keys are often called penetration. Broad expiry or cache loss can cause an avalanche of origin traffic.

    Use controls suited to the cause. Single-flight loading combines concurrent work for one key. Negative caching can remember a genuine absence. TTL jitter spreads expiry, while bounded refresh and origin admission protect the source. A refresh lock needs its own failure and expiry behaviour. Test cache loss: allowing every application instance to rebuild everything at once can overload the database that remains responsible for the real data.

    11.3.3 · Negative caching

    A client repeatedly asks for a product that does not exist. A short-lived “not found” entry can prevent repeated source lookups. This is negative caching.

    Distinguish absence from failure. A temporarily unreachable database has not established that the product is missing. Likewise, one user's denied access must not poison another user's cache entry. Scope keys correctly and use deliberate lifetimes. If the product is created just after its absence is cached, it may stay invisible until expiry or invalidation. The policy should state whether that delay is acceptable and how newly created records become visible.

    11.3.4 · Stale-while-revalidate

    A cached product description expires while its source is slow. Stale-while-revalidate can return an allowed older copy and refresh it in the background. The user avoids the immediate wait, and combined refresh work can protect the origin.

    Define separate ages for fresh data, permitted stale data, and unusable data. Repeated refresh failures should not silently extend stale serving forever. A description may tolerate this arrangement; an old payment reply cannot authorise a new charge. Make degradation visible where appropriate and preserve authoritative checks for operations whose correctness depends on current state. Faster responses have value only within the agreed freshness rule.

    11.3.5 · Cache warming and prefetching

    New application instances start with empty caches. Warming loads likely useful entries before normal demand; prefetching predicts what will be needed soon. Both spend bandwidth and memory before a user actually asks.

    Load a measured working set gradually rather than scanning the entire database from every new instance. Check whether prefetched values are used and whether they evict more valuable entries. Staggering a rollout, sharing a cache, or limiting admission may solve a cold-start problem more simply. Stop obsolete speculative work. The useful question is how much future work was avoided, rather than how many entries were loaded.

    Think further · When should a product stop serving rather than return a stale cached result?

    Stop when the operation requires current authority or the permitted stale interval has ended. An old description may be allowed, while allocating scarce stock or deciding current access may not be. State which actions degrade and which wait or reject, with visible status and a recovery path.

    Remember: Bound refresh and fallback work while keeping the accepted stale and absent meanings explicit.

    Try applying it: What should happen if background refresh keeps failing past the allowed stale age?

    PART 3 / UNIT 11 / CHAPTER 11.4

    Edges, partitions & the price of a cache

    Prerequisites: 11.3 · Hot keys, stampedes & negative results4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A cache cluster and CDN add more copies and another failure path. Compare their operations with source correctness and recovery capacity, including whether the cache should exist at all.

    11.4.1 · Redis-like data structures

    A set can track identifiers, a sorted set can organise scores or timestamps, and a hash can group fields. Redis-like systems expose such structures with operations suited to particular tasks.

    Choose by the operations needed, then examine their atomic scope. One atomic command does not make an arbitrary sequence of commands atomic. A script or transaction may protect the local sequence, subject to the selected system's rules and key placement. Expiry, persistence, and replica behaviour remain separate decisions. A convenient list or stream is not automatically a durable queue with the required acknowledgment and recovery semantics.

    11.4.2 · CDN architecture and origin shielding

    An origin shield collects edge misses before they reach the source, reducing duplicate origin work. A CDN places permitted representations near users. Both depend on correct keys and sharing rules.

    Decide how query parameters, headers, identities, and content versions affect the representation. A signed URL is a capability with a scope and lifetime, not permission to ignore private-data policy. Purge propagation follows the provider contract and may not remove copies already kept by clients. Immutable versioned URLs can simplify public asset updates. Trace every remaining copy when immediate revocation matters; proximity and bandwidth savings do not establish access correctness.

    11.4.3 · Cache partitioning and replication

    Partitioning assigns different keys to different owners. Replication makes additional copies under a protocol. A distributed cache may use both, but failover can still lose, evict, or expose delayed entries.

    Specify whether the application falls back, serves permitted stale data, or rejects when the cache fails. Stable hashing can reduce key remapping during membership changes, while leaving hot-key traffic uneven. Keep source and cache recovery capacity explicit. The real peak may arrive when a cache cluster restarts and every missing value needs reconstruction. Test that scenario rather than sizing the origin only for a warm-cache hit ratio.

    11.4.4 · When caching is harmful

    A cache adds a lookup, encoding, memory use, and copy-maintenance work. If results are rarely reused, those costs can exceed the work saved. If its key omits authorisation scope, the cache can also serve the wrong user's result.

    Test with the cache empty and unavailable. A warm cache can hide insufficient source capacity until the day it disappears. Sometimes a better query or index removes the bottleneck with fewer freshness and recovery obligations. Keep caching where measured reuse and the agreed correctness policy justify it. Removing an unhelpful cache can simplify both performance and reasoning.

    Try the mechanism in code

    Python · ideal LRU

    from mechanisms import LRU
cache = LRU(3)
for key in "ABC": cache.put(key, key)
cache.get("A")
assert cache.put("D", "D") == ("B", "B")

    After A,B,C,A, ideal LRU considers B the least recently used. Adding D evicts B, as the assertion checks.

    The fixture models entry count and exact recency. Actual caches can approximate the policy and use byte or expiry limits. Eviction alone says nothing about whether a loaded value is current.

    Download the executable mechanism collection ↓ · Follow the connected complete design →

    THE WORKBENCH · TRY CHANGING THE INPUTS

    Follow which cache entry is used least recently

    The cache holds a fixed number of entries. Each access loads a missing key or moves an existing key to the most recently used end. Real caches may use approximate eviction, byte limits, and expiry. Choosing an entry to evict does not tell us whether its value is fresh.

    Think further · When should a product stop serving rather than return a stale cached result?

    Stop when the operation requires current authority or the permitted stale interval has ended. An old description may be allowed, while allocating scarce stock or deciding current access may not be. State which actions degrade and which wait or reject, with visible status and a recovery path.

    Remember: Evaluate each cache by saved work, maintained semantics, and the cost of losing it.

    Try applying it: Which workload would show that removing a cache improves the whole system?

    PART 3 / UNIT 12 / CHAPTER 12.1

    Scale compute & route requests

    Prerequisites: Requirements, Estimation, and Engineering Trade-offs, Networking Foundations for System Design, Data Models and Storage Technologies, Database Internals, Transactions, and Concurrency Control, Caching and Content Delivery6 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Adding application instances changes traffic distribution and often connection demand. Find which work is independent, where required state lives, and which signal should drive growth.

    12.1.1 · Vertical vs horizontal scaling

    A busy application can run on a larger machine or on more machines. Vertical scaling increases one node's resources. Horizontal scaling adds nodes and distributes suitable work.

    Neither guarantees proportional throughput. A larger database machine can postpone distribution work, while extra application instances can share independent computation. A common lock or downstream database may remain the limit. Compare startup delay, failure impact, cost, and the work needed to operate the result. Profile the bottleneck first, make the smallest justified change, then measure again. The limiting resource can move after a successful improvement.

    12.1.2 · Stateless vs stateful services

    A request reaches a replacement web instance. Can that instance handle it using the same authenticated identity and stored state? A stateless application avoids keeping required per-client conversation state only in a particular instance between requests.

    It still uses state elsewhere. Local sessions or accepted memory-only jobs can prevent transparent replacement. Move required state to a suitable owner or specify affinity and recovery. Check compatible configuration, state access, and duplicate effects across instances. Distributing requests freely works only when these conditions hold; labelling a service “stateless” does not establish them by itself.

    12.1.3 · Load distribution algorithms

    Round-robin distributes backend selections in turn. Least-connections uses active connections as a load clue. Weights can represent different capacities, and hashing can keep related traffic together.

    The best clue depends on the workload. One expensive request can occupy an instance longer than many cheap requests, while a long-lived connection can carry changing traffic. Inspect per-instance saturation and waiting instead of only counting requests. Client-side and server-side balancing also place discovery and retry decisions in different components. Choose a policy that reflects useful load, and remember that routing cannot add capacity to a shared downstream bottleneck.

    12.1.4 · Health checks and failover

    A process responds to a simple ping, but cannot serve real traffic. Another process can serve a reduced response even though a shared optional dependency is down. Health checks need to reflect the routing decision they control.

    Liveness concerns whether a process should be restarted. Readiness concerns whether it should receive traffic under the chosen policy. Requiring every dependency in every readiness check can remove all instances during one shared outage. Use bounded, meaningful checks and deliberate degradation. A traffic switch also needs valid state and connection behaviour; routing to a new instance does not recover work that existed only in the old one's memory.

    12.1.5 · Sticky sessions

    Sticky sessions send a client's requests to the same instance. This can support local session state or improve cache reuse, but also creates an affinity that affects balancing and recovery.

    If that instance fails, decide how the client reconnects and how required state is recovered. Heavy users may create uneven load. For replaceable web instances, externally owned sessions can remove some affinity needs. Where sticking is deliberate, document the consequences rather than relying on it invisibly. Affinity can be an optimisation or a constraint; the authoritative location and lifetime of session state still need a clear design.

    12.1.6 · Autoscaling metrics

    A worker queue's oldest job is getting older even while CPU looks moderate. Scaling solely on CPU might miss the delay users care about. The signal should reflect the constrained work: CPU for computation, queue age for job delay, or connections for some waiting workloads.

    Autoscaling also has startup time, minimums, and maximums. Use stabilisation to avoid repeatedly adding and removing instances, and cap spending and downstream pressure. Request-count scaling assumes comparable request costs. Keep existing headroom and admission controls for bursts that arrive before new capacity is ready. Automation reacts to a limit; it does not remove the reaction interval.

    Think further · Can more partitions scale one globally hot exclusive ownership decision?

    Cold partitions do not divide the authority required for one exclusive key. Read copies or batching can help suitable work, while changing the invariant or allocation model needs a valid protocol. Measure the hot owner and explain how any proposed partition changes its actual work without permitting conflicting winners.

    Remember: Scale the constrained work while bounding shared downstream demand.

    Try applying it: What must remain true before any healthy instance can serve the next request?

    PART 3 / UNIT 12 / CHAPTER 12.2

    Replicate and partition data

    Prerequisites: 12.1 · Scale compute & route requests6 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A dataset no longer fits its original owner. Compare copies, partitions, stable key placement, and ownership movement without assuming that evenly stored bytes imply evenly distributed traffic.

    12.2.1 · Replication

    A primary can copy writes to a replica before or after replying. In asynchronous replication, a reply may precede receipt on the replica. If that replica is promoted after losing the primary, recent acknowledged writes may be absent.

    Synchronous arrangements wait for a defined replica milestone and can increase delay or block during communication failure. State exactly which copies and milestones acknowledgment requires. Replication can improve reading or continuity while adding lag and recovery rules. Independent failure placement also matters: two copies on one lost disk provide little protection. A copy count is useful only alongside its protocol and failure assumptions.

    12.2.2 · Partitioning and sharding

    A dataset can be divided into partitions. When separate storage owners hold those portions, this is commonly called sharding. The key determines where data lives and which queries need several owners.

    Tenant-based placement may keep each tenant's data together while leaving one large tenant hot. Cross-shard uniqueness, joins, transactions, and movement need additional design. Keep a routing and relocation procedure, and name where invariants are enforced. Add this complexity when a measured storage or write problem justifies it. A large user count alone does not identify a partition key or establish that one database has reached its limit.

    12.2.3 · Range partitioning vs hash partitioning

    Range partitioning keeps ordered keys together, which can help scans and expiration by time. But if every new event goes into today's range, that owner receives most writes. Hash partitioning spreads keys while making ordered range reads less local.

    A time bucket plus a spread dimension can distribute ingestion, at the cost of reading several partitions for one time range. State that fan-out explicitly. Neither technique automatically splits one extremely popular key. Choose by the writes, reads, retention, and skew the application actually has, rather than using “balanced storage” as a substitute for measuring traffic.

    12.2.4 · Consistent hashing and rendezvous hashing

    Modulo routing can move many keys when the owner count changes. Consistent hashing uses a stable placement, often a ring with virtual positions, to limit reassignment. Rendezvous hashing instead scores each key-owner pair and selects the highest eligible score.

    Both aim to keep much of the old assignment while membership changes. Neither guarantees equal request traffic: one key can be far more popular than others. Clients must agree about membership and hash behaviour, and data still needs safe movement and replication. Changing the hash function also changes placement, so treat it as a migration rather than a harmless implementation detail.

    12.2.5 · Rebalancing

    Moving a partition while requests continue is a coordination operation. Copy its data from a defined starting point, capture changes made during the copy, validate the destination, and establish when it becomes the owner.

    Readers and writers need a consistent way to discover that transition, such as a routing epoch. Throttle copying so it leaves capacity for users. Keep the old copy until the new ownership and recovery conditions permit removal. Plan rollback and reconciliation too. A move that deletes the source before proving the destination current can turn a capacity improvement into data loss.

    12.2.6 · Hot partitions and skew

    Fleet averages look healthy, but one partition handles 70% of writes. More cold partitions do little for that owner. Inspect requests, bytes, and delays by partition to find the actual skew.

    A range split helps only if the traffic can divide. One hot entity may require read copies, batching, or a redesigned ownership rule. Randomising writes can spread append pressure but force reads to combine more partitions. Determine whether the issue is volume, size, or a serialised invariant. Choose a remedy that changes that pressure, rather than repeatedly buying capacity elsewhere in the cluster.

    Think further · Can more partitions scale one globally hot exclusive ownership decision?

    Cold partitions do not divide the authority required for one exclusive key. Read copies or batching can help suitable work, while changing the invariant or allocation model needs a valid protocol. Measure the hot owner and explain how any proposed partition changes its actual work without permitting conflicting winners.

    Remember: Data distribution needs query, invariant, routing, and migration rules as well as a key function.

    Try applying it: Why does a new hash owner not automatically solve one extremely popular key?

    PART 3 / UNIT 12 / CHAPTER 12.3

    Lag, proxies & saturated pools

    Prerequisites: 12.2 · Replicate and partition data5 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A replica receives a write but has not applied it, while applications wait for connections. Follow actual progress and ownership before changing routing or increasing pool sizes.

    12.3.1 · Read replicas and read/write splitting

    A user updates a profile on the primary, then reads from a replica that has not applied the change. The next response shows the old value. Read/write splitting needs a freshness policy.

    Route critical reads to a sufficiently current owner, track session progress where supported, or explicitly allow delayed results. Classifying by SQL verb alone is unsafe: a SELECT may acquire a lock or participate in a transaction requiring current state. Read replicas can distribute appropriate reads while writes remain elsewhere. Make the operation's required observations part of the routing decision, rather than assuming every read can go to any replica.

    12.3.2 · Replication lag

    A source has accepted changes through position 100, but a replica has applied only through 90. This position difference describes part of its replication lag. The transport may have received newer records that still wait to be applied.

    Measure source, receipt, and apply progress where the system supports them. A small average can hide one stalled replica. Time-based lag estimates also need interpretation when traffic varies. Promotion must respect the acknowledgment and possible-loss contract, not just happen quickly. For a user needing read-your-writes, route according to the required version or another supported mechanism rather than relying on the fleet's average freshness.

    12.3.3 · Database proxying

    A database proxy can route clients or reuse backend connections. Some implementations multiplex several client sessions onto fewer database connections. This can change assumptions about session variables, temporary tables, or long transactions.

    Check which state must stay attached to a particular backend. Document where identity, failover, and routing decisions occur, and size the proxy itself. It can become another constrained or failed component. Pooling does not remove transaction limits, and a failed call cannot always be transparently repeated after a connection switch. Choose proxy features against the application's actual session and operation contract.

    12.3.4 · Connection pool saturation

    Ten application instances each open a pool of twenty database connections. Adding ten more instances can double connection demand even if the database has no more capacity. Waiting callers may then accumulate both in application pools and inside the database.

    Bound the aggregate, reserve recovery capacity, and include acquisition waits in deadlines. A request waiting on a database lock may hold a connection while using little CPU. Measure hold time and contention before increasing pool sizes. Scaling the admission points can worsen an outage when it increases pressure on the shared resource already causing the wait.

    12.3.5 · Bottleneck identification

    A request spends most of its time waiting for one database query. Adding web instances is unlikely to fix that path; a query or index change may help more. Another service may instead be limited by independent CPU work and benefit from workers.

    Trace useful completions and waiting through the system. Compare CPU, memory, disk, network, connections, and lock contention with offered load and queues. High utilisation is a clue, not proof of the business bottleneck. Change one material factor and measure again. This links an intervention to evidence and shows whether the limit moved elsewhere.

    Think further · Can more partitions scale one globally hot exclusive ownership decision?

    Cold partitions do not divide the authority required for one exclusive key. Read copies or batching can help suitable work, while changing the invariant or allocation model needs a valid protocol. Measure the hot owner and explain how any proposed partition changes its actual work without permitting conflicting winners.

    Remember: Read freshness and capacity diagnosis depend on the real progress and wait boundaries.

    Try applying it: How can doubling application replicas overload the same database?

    PART 3 / UNIT 12 / CHAPTER 12.4

    Regions, write paths & scale economics

    Prerequisites: 12.3 · Lag, proxies & saturated pools5 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    The service needs more capacity and perhaps another region. Compare queues, failure placement, read and write rules, and total operating cost under equal requirements.

    12.4.1 · Queueing and overload

    A queue can absorb a brief burst when workers later catch up. If arrival stays above completion, the backlog keeps growing. Longer waiting can make a request useless even before memory runs out.

    Bound both queue length and age, prioritise required work, and reject or shed work that cannot meet its deadline. A request with a two-second deadline should not be accepted silently behind ten seconds of work. Explain the overload result so callers do not immediately create a retry storm. A queue is a place for controlled waiting, not a way to turn insufficient sustained capacity into sufficient capacity.

    12.4.2 · Single points of failure

    Two application containers run on one host. They survive a single process failure but not the host's failure. A single point of failure is a dependency whose loss defeats the required service, which may be a machine, router, credential source, or operator-controlled procedure.

    Inspect independent failure domains rather than counting process boxes. Redundancy also needs detection, valid state, surviving capacity, and failover. Check recovery dependencies: a data path may be replicated while every replacement instance needs one unavailable configuration service to start. Trace what must work during a failure, not only what runs during normal operation.

    12.4.3 · Multi-region strategies

    A second region can help locality or continuity, but it changes where writes are accepted and how copies agree. Active-passive keeps one current authority and needs promotion and recovery rules. Active-active needs a precise coordination or conflict policy for concurrent activity.

    Waiting across regions adds propagation time. Copying asynchronously reduces that wait but may lose recent acknowledged changes during failover. Begin with tolerated interruption, data loss, and locality requirements. Choose write authority and read freshness per operation. A single “multi-region” label cannot establish which work continues during a partition or which state survives it.

    12.4.4 · Scaling writes vs scaling reads

    A product description can be copied to many readers with an allowed freshness delay. Allocating the last seat needs exclusive ownership of that seat. These operations have different scaling options.

    Read scaling often uses suitable replicas or caches. Write scaling must divide, reduce, or batch ownership work while preserving its invariants. One hot account or global sequential allocator can remain serialised despite many shards. First remove unnecessary coordination or indexes where justified. Commutative counters may support independent updates; exclusive reservations need a protocol that prevents incompatible winners. Scale the actual rule, rather than assuming reads and writes benefit from the same arrangement.

    12.4.5 · Scale-out economics

    Ten small nodes introduce repeated baseline memory, extra connections, transfer, monitoring, and operating work. They may or may not cost less than one larger node for the required workload.

    Compare candidates with equal service targets and spare capacity for the same failures. Include startup, cache warming, migration, and recovery. Managed services can exchange provider charges for some staffing work, but the application still owns its correctness. Cost per successful business outcome is more useful than cost per attempted request when retries differ. Identify the bottleneck before purchasing capacity that cannot increase useful completions.

    Try the mechanism in code

    Python · stable rendezvous mapping

    from mechanisms import rendezvous
for key in range(1000):
    old = rendezvous(key, ["A","B","C"])
    new = rendezvous(key, ["A","B","C","D"])
    assert old == new or new == "D"

    For each key, adding D either preserves the old owner or assigns the key to D. The assertion checks that stable-mapping property across the fixture.

    It does not move stored data or synchronise client membership. A popular key still has one selected owner in this model, regardless of how balanced the key counts look.

    Download the executable mechanism collection ↓ · Follow the connected complete design →

    THE WORKBENCH · TRY CHANGING THE INPUTS

    Compare owners before and after adding D

    Change the key and compare its owner before and after D joins. The same key always receives the same scores in this example. Choosing a new owner does not copy data, agree on membership, or spread the traffic of a single popular key.

    Think further · Can more partitions scale one globally hot exclusive ownership decision?

    Cold partitions do not divide the authority required for one exclusive key. Read copies or batching can help suitable work, while changing the invariant or allocation model needs a valid protocol. Measure the hot owner and explain how any proposed partition changes its actual work without permitting conflicting winners.

    Remember: A bigger topology helps only when its capacity, authority, and failure behaviour match the need.

    Try applying it: Which write invariant would remain concentrated despite adding many cold shards?

    PART 3 / UNIT 13 / CHAPTER 13.1

    Upload bytes without losing identity

    Prerequisites: API Design and Communication Contracts, Data Models and Storage Technologies, Database Internals, Transactions, and Concurrency Control5 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A client uploads bytes while the application records metadata. Make both identities and their handoff explicit so an interrupted transfer cannot become verified processing input.

    13.1.1 · Binary/object storage

    A processing job needs both a PDF's bytes and information about its owner and progress. Store immutable binary content separately when its access and lifecycle differ from the mutable job record.

    The record should identify a particular object version, its size or checksum, and ownership. A row pointing to a missing or incomplete object is a broken workflow even if both storage services individually operated correctly. Track upload state and clean up abandoned bytes. Verify the chosen object store's guarantees; “object storage” names an interface category rather than a universal consistency or durability contract.

    13.1.2 · Large-file upload architecture

    Instead of sending a large upload through application workers, the service can issue a narrowly scoped authorisation for the client to stream directly to storage. The application still owns permission, quotas, metadata, and the decision that a file is ready.

    A client may abandon the upload or send different bytes than expected. Validate completion, size, and ownership before starting processing. Expire unused upload intents and reconcile unreferenced objects. A signed upload URL is a capability: its scope and lifetime determine what its holder may do. Grant only the intended object operation, rather than broad access to the storage collection.

    13.1.3 · Multipart and resumable uploads

    An interrupted large upload should not always restart from byte zero. Multipart upload divides it into named parts and has a separate completion step. Resumable upload remembers confirmed offsets or parts so the client can continue.

    Specify how retries identify a part and what happens if the client's source file changes. Acknowledging every part does not by itself establish that the assembled object is the right complete file. Verify the final content under the chosen protocol. Provider entity tags are not universally content hashes. Remove expired incomplete sessions, or abandoned parts can create storage growth that no visible completed file explains.

    13.1.4 · Checksums and content addressing

    A downloaded file differs from the uploaded bytes. A checksum can help detect corruption according to its algorithm's properties. A suitable cryptographic digest can also identify content under stated collision assumptions.

    Content addressing derives an identity from that digest, supporting immutable references or deduplication. Verify the actual stored or received bytes rather than hashing only a client's claim. Matching content does not establish permission to access it or that the content is safe. Cross-tenant deduplication can reveal information through existence checks, so design its scope carefully. Integrity, identity, authorisation, and content safety are related but separate decisions.

    13.1.5 · Metadata vs binary data

    A user replaces a document after an extraction completed. If the same input identifier silently refers to new bytes, we can no longer explain which file produced the earlier result.

    Give binary versions stable identities. Keep annotations, classifications, attempts, and review status in metadata that names those versions. When the input changes, create a new version and decide which derived results must be recomputed. Retain or remove historical artifacts according to policy. This separation lets the application explain an output without treating mutable processing state as part of the immutable original file.

    Think further · How would you investigate an extracted field after both source and model have changed?

    Use stable references to the exact source version, region, transform/model version, parameters, and review evidence. Keep the disputed output version identifiable. Re-running a changed or nondeterministic model is not proof of the old result. Retain appropriate evidence under the lifecycle policy and distinguish reproducibility limits from missing provenance.

    Remember: Immutable content identity and a tracked lifecycle connect stored bytes to application progress.

    Try applying it: What cleanup is needed if the object exists but its metadata transaction fails?

    PART 3 / UNIT 13 / CHAPTER 13.2

    Build and rebuild a search index

    Prerequisites: 13.1 · Upload bytes without losing identity4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Search needs its own representation of source content. Follow term indexing, stage progress, and a generation switch while updates and deletions continue.

    13.2.1 · Search engines and inverted indexes

    Consider D1 = “blue car” and D2 = “blue bike.” An inverted index records that blue occurs in D1 and D2, while car occurs only in D1. A query can use these postings to find candidates without scanning every document's text.

    Tokenisation and normalisation affect which terms are recorded. Updates also need document identity and version: an older extraction must not overwrite a newer representation. Keep recoverable sources and transformation information so the index can be rebuilt. Its retrieval structure has its own freshness and access obligations, even when the original document is stored correctly elsewhere.

    13.2.2 · Indexing pipelines

    A document can be uploaded successfully while indexing fails. Treat extraction, validation, enrichment, indexing, and publication as distinguishable stages so the application can report where progress stopped.

    Each retry should name its input version and intended output, rather than create another searchable document blindly. Give malformed or repeatedly failing files a bounded retry and review path. Publication must also respect current access policy; an old “public” flag copied into an artifact may no longer be valid. A useful completed state names the source and index version whose required work actually finished.

    13.2.3 · Search ingestion and reindexing

    A new analyser needs a fresh search index while users continue searching. Build a new generation from a defined snapshot or source position, then apply changes that occurred during the build.

    Include deletions as well as inserts and edits. Validate results before switching a serving alias or routing version. Keep the old usable generation until rollback and compatibility conditions permit removal. Equal document counts do not establish equal versions, permissions, or contents. The transition is safe only when readers know which representation is authoritative and new writes are not lost between the initial copy and the switch.

    Think further · How would you investigate an extracted field after both source and model have changed?

    Use stable references to the exact source version, region, transform/model version, parameters, and review evidence. Keep the disputed output version identifiable. Re-running a changed or nondeterministic model is not proof of the old result. Retain appropriate evidence under the lifecycle policy and distinguish reproducibility limits from missing provenance.

    Remember: A derived index needs versions, access rules, and a rebuild protocol.

    Try applying it: Why do matching document counts fail to prove that a reindex is ready to serve?

    PART 3 / UNIT 13 / CHAPTER 13.3

    Move data through batch and streams

    Prerequisites: 13.2 · Build and rebuild a search index5 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A nightly report and an immediate event alert need different freshness. Compare batch, continuous processing, transformation placement, and change capture using the progress each can establish.

    13.3.1 · Batch vs streaming pipelines

    A nightly batch can recompute yesterday's report from a bounded input. A streaming processor handles continuing input and records progress as it arrives. Choose by the required freshness and recomputation behaviour.

    Streaming can reduce delay, but adds late arrivals, partitioned state, and checkpoint recovery. Batch processing has failure and resource costs too. State whether a result is provisional: later input may change a total. A simple scheduled batch is appropriate when hours of delay are acceptable. A low-latency requirement may justify streaming, provided its recovery and state rules are designed as carefully as the normal path.

    13.3.2 · ETL vs ELT

    An ETL pipeline extracts data, transforms it, then loads the target. ELT loads first and transforms in the target environment. The difference changes where raw data exists and where computation occurs.

    Transforming early can minimise sensitive fields before they reach analytics. Loading raw data can support later transformations but adds storage and governance work. In either arrangement, version transformations, validate input and output, and keep ownership and lineage. Neither acronym establishes data quality or repeatability. Choose where each step belongs by its privacy, compute, and query needs rather than treating either sequence as inherently superior.

    13.3.3 · Change Data Capture (CDC)

    A source row changes, and a supported Change Data Capture mechanism records that committed change for downstream consumers. CDC can keep search or analytics current without repeatedly scanning the whole source.

    An initial snapshot and later change stream need a consistent handoff position. Otherwise, changes made during copying can be missed or applied wrongly. Preserve source identifiers, positions, and schema information, handle repetition, and monitor lag. A destination may expose a different or delayed view of the source's transactions. CDC transports changes; the destination still needs a clear rule for applying them and serving consistent results.

    13.3.4 · Data lakes and warehouses

    A data lake can keep flexible datasets, often in object storage, while a warehouse provides curated analytical structures and serving facilities. Actual product boundaries overlap, so compare their supported operations.

    Raw inputs can make replay possible but also accumulate poorly understood and sensitive data. Identify immutable source versions, curated outputs, catalog information, owners, and access policies. Choose file formats and partitions for the scans and recovery work that need to run. Without schema, lineage, and lifecycle management, storing more bytes can make the data harder to trust. Retaining raw data needs a purpose, not just available space.

    13.3.5 · Stream processing fundamentals

    An event occurred at noon but reaches a processor three minutes later. Its event time describes the source occurrence; processing time describes when the system handles it. A time-windowed result needs a rule for this late event.

    Stream processors maintain keyed state and progress. A watermark estimates how far event-time processing has advanced under lateness assumptions; it is not proof that no earlier event can arrive. Define accepted lateness, corrections, and when a result is final. Checkpoint and external-effect boundaries also matter. Consumers need to know whether a count can change after its first publication.

    Think further · How would you investigate an extracted field after both source and model have changed?

    Use stable references to the exact source version, region, transform/model version, parameters, and review evidence. Keep the disputed output version identifiable. Re-running a changed or nondeterministic model is not proof of the old result. Retain appropriate evidence under the lifecycle policy and distinguish reproducibility limits from missing provenance.

    Remember: Data movement needs a defined handoff, time meaning, and recovery position.

    Try applying it: How should a late event change a result already published for a closed time window?

    PART 3 / UNIT 13 / CHAPTER 13.4

    Quality, provenance & replay

    Prerequisites: 13.3 · Move data through batch and streams4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    An extracted value is disputed after a pipeline update. Trace exact inputs, transformations, checks, and retained copies so the result can be investigated and corrected.

    13.4.1 · Data provenance and lineage

    An extracted amount is disputed. To investigate it, we need the exact file version, page or region, extractor version, parameters, and any review decision that produced it. Provenance records origins; lineage connects artifacts through transformations.

    Store stable references that can actually be checked. An explanatory label alone is weak if the underlying evidence cannot be located. These records support correction and reproducibility without proving every extraction right. They also have their own retention needs: copying raw personal data into a permanent audit record can defeat deletion of the original. Keep useful evidence with an explicit lifecycle.

    13.4.2 · Data quality, schema validation, and replay

    A record contains both amount and currency, so it passes a structural schema check. If the amount is interpreted in the wrong units, the record is still wrong. Quality checks need semantic rules as well as field presence.

    Check identity, ranges, relationships, completeness, and source versions. Quarantine invalid inputs with actionable reasons and enough evidence for repair. Replaying corrected transformations must not repeat external side effects or create duplicate records. Compare source and destination business invariants alongside counts and versions. An empty error queue establishes little if a processor consistently accepts and publishes the wrong meaning.

    13.4.3 · Lifecycle policies and retention

    Deleting a PDF leaves its extracted text, thumbnail, and search entry behind. A retention policy on original bytes alone has not completed the document's lifecycle.

    Track every relevant copy, including logs and recoverable snapshots. A durable deletion workflow can record progress and retry unfinished steps. Minimal deletion markers may be needed to stop old workers or replay from recreating removed results; minimise the personal information retained in them. Maintain indexes that can find a user's objects efficiently. Test restoring older state against the deletion history, so recovery does not silently republish content that should remain removed.

    13.4.4 · Designing data-intensive applications

    Follow one document from upload to extraction, review, and search. Every step takes an identified input, applies a transformation, and produces state used by the next step. The complete design is this connected set of operations.

    For each connection, define the source owner, version, order, retry identity, validation, and recovery. Keep inputs recoverable where rebuilding is required, within the retention policy. Observe progress across stages rather than only queue throughput. A fast broker cannot repair missing provenance or an index serving the wrong tenant's documents. End-to-end correctness depends on how these contracts work together.

    Try the mechanism in code

    Python · source and attempt fencing

    from mechanisms import Workflow
run = Workflow("file-version-2", epoch=8)
assert not run.complete(7, "file-version-2", "old")
assert not run.complete(8, "file-version-1", "wrong-input")
assert run.complete(8, "file-version-2", "current")

    The workflow rejects an old epoch and the wrong input version, then accepts the current combination. These local conditions make the attempt's authority explicit.

    A real store must check and apply them atomically and validate the output. Provenance also needs the transform version and relevant source evidence, not just a result filename.

    Download the executable mechanism collection ↓ · Follow the connected complete design →

    THE WORKBENCH · TRY CHANGING THE INPUTS

    Should this worker be allowed to finish?

    Choose an attempt and check its ownership epoch, input version, and document state. A real database must check these conditions and save the result atomically. This step does not include an external model call or an object-store write.

    Think further · How would you investigate an extracted field after both source and model have changed?

    Use stable references to the exact source version, region, transform/model version, parameters, and review evidence. Keep the disputed output version identifiable. Re-running a changed or nondeterministic model is not proof of the old result. Retain appropriate evidence under the lifecycle policy and distinguish reproducibility limits from missing provenance.

    Remember: Quality and provenance belong to the output contract and every copy's lifecycle.

    Try applying it: What would let an old worker recreate personal data after the source was deleted?

    PART 4 / UNIT 14 / CHAPTER 14.1

    Partial failure & the meaning of time

    Prerequisites: Networking Foundations for System Design, Runtime, Processes, Threads, and Concurrency, Database Internals, Transactions, and Concurrency Control7 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    One service commits while its caller loses the reply. Begin with partial failures and the limits of time observations before trying to order events across machines.

    14.1.1 · What makes a distributed system difficult?

    An order service calls a payment provider. The provider may succeed while the order service cannot receive its reply. Different machines can keep working, stop, or lose communication independently, so there is no single local observation that explains everything.

    Distributed design specifies what outcomes are allowed despite this uncertainty. Begin with clear state owners and operations, then introduce additional copies or coordination for a real requirement. More nodes add possible failure combinations alongside capacity. The design therefore needs a protocol: rules for messages, state changes, acknowledgments, and recovery. A diagram showing connected machines does not supply those rules on its own.

    14.1.2 · Partial failures

    The provider charges a card, but the order service loses the reply. The local order may still be pending while the remote effect already exists. This is a partial failure: some of the overall operation happened and another part did not complete as observed.

    Keep “not attempted” separate from “attempted, outcome unknown.” Record an operation or provider reference and reconcile the status. A local rollback cannot erase the remote charge. Compensation is possible only where the business and provider support a suitable further action. Treating every exception as a definite clean failure can lead to resubmitting an effect that already succeeded.

    14.1.3 · Network uncertainty

    A heartbeat does not arrive. The other machine might have failed, or its message might simply be delayed. For a time, these cases can look identical to the observer.

    A timeout is a practical suspicion and a limit on waiting, not proof that the old process stopped. A retry can overlap the delayed original request. Bound waiting to protect resources, while using a protocol to prevent incompatible owners or duplicate effects. State which operations must wait or reject when authority is uncertain. A short timer can improve responsiveness, but correctness must also hold when its suspicion is wrong.

    14.1.4 · Fault models

    Suppose a protocol assumes machines either follow its rules or crash. A participant that lies about its stored history is outside that assumption. A fault model states the failures the design claims to tolerate.

    Common models include crash-stop, crash-recovery, message loss, partitions, and arbitrary Byzantine behaviour. Recovery also depends on whether required persistent state survives a restart. State these conditions before calculating a replica count. Three copies on one failed device have a different failure exposure from independently placed durable copies. Correctness reasoning is meaningful only for the failure cases and resource assumptions it actually covers.

    14.1.5 · Time, clocks, and event ordering

    Two machines stamp events using their own clocks. Clock drift or adjustment can make the later causal event appear earlier by timestamp. A wall-clock comparison therefore does not necessarily establish what caused what.

    Use an appropriate monotonic clock for elapsed durations where available. For expiry, identify the authority for time and the uncertainty the rule permits. An ordering requirement may need a sequence or protocol log rather than client timestamps. Recording source time and observed time separately helps explain delayed events. The design must distinguish user-facing dates, measured durations, and causal relationships instead of asking one timestamp to establish all three.

    14.1.6 · Physical vs logical clocks

    A physical clock estimates real time. A logical clock records ordering information and need not count seconds. A logical counter can tell us something about event relationships without saying what time of day they occurred.

    Use the kind of time appropriate to the question. Displaying a date and ordering protocol actions are different tasks. Even subtracting timestamps from two machines can be misleading if their clock errors are unknown. A combined physical/logical scheme needs its own specified rules. Name which meaning each stored field has so later code does not interpret an ordering counter as a duration or a timestamp as proof of causality.

    14.1.7 · Lamport clocks and vector clocks

    A process with Lamport counter 5 receives a message carrying 9. It advances to max(5,9)+1 = 10. Local increments and these receive rules ensure that a causal predecessor has a smaller counter. A smaller counter alone does not prove causation.

    Vector clocks keep progress for several participants. Vectors [1,0] and [0,1] each contain progress absent from the other, so they represent concurrent versions under the model. This can reveal conflicts but costs metadata. Neither clock decides how to merge two account changes or independently provides a global real-time commit order. The clock describes a relation; the application still needs a valid resolution rule.

    Think further · Which operations may continue during a partition while exclusive allocation must wait?

    Operations with explicitly permitted stale or independent results may continue. Exclusive allocation needs valid authority and may have to wait or reject when agreement is unavailable. State per-operation observations rather than weaken the entire system silently. Recovery must reconcile progress without introducing another owner.

    Remember: A local observation may leave remote outcomes unknown; clocks describe different kinds of order.

    Try applying it: Why does a missing heartbeat fail to prove that the old owner has stopped?

    PART 4 / UNIT 14 / CHAPTER 14.2

    Consistency as a reader-visible contract

    Prerequisites: 14.1 · Partial failure & the meaning of time6 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A user reads a value, writes another, and switches replicas. Describe the allowed observations before choosing a consistency model or relying on a product's “strong” label.

    14.2.1 · Consistency models

    A user writes a post, reads it, then switches replicas. What may the next read show? A consistency model specifies which observation histories the system permits.

    Write examples before choosing a setting: can a read return an older value, can two readers see different orders, and must a reply appear after its parent post? Different objects can need different rules. A feed count may tolerate delay while an allocation requires one winner. Stronger observations can require more coordination or fewer available serving paths during a partition. Name the model and its operation scope; a bare word such as “strong” leaves important assumptions unstated.

    14.2.2 · Strong consistency and eventual consistency

    Replicas may briefly disagree after an update, then converge once updates stop and communication and repair succeed. Eventual consistency expresses convergence under such assumptions. It does not by itself specify a maximum delay or decide how conflicts are merged.

    “Strong consistency” is often used for linearizable behaviour, but check what the speaker means. A social feed may allow propagation delay while the author still needs to read their own post immediately. State these per-operation contracts. Delayed convergence does not excuse losing an acknowledged update outside the agreed failure policy. Freshness, conflict handling, and durability need their own precise rules.

    14.2.3 · Linearizability

    A write of 2 finishes before another client begins a read. For a linearizable register, that read cannot return the superseded value 1 unless an intervening write permits it. Each operation behaves as if it took effect at one point between invocation and response, respecting real-time precedence.

    Overlapping operations can have more than one valid ordering. A timed-out operation can still take effect because the client never obtained a definite completed result. Achieving linearizability requires a suitable protocol for writes and reads. Majority arithmetic and timestamps alone leave version choice, concurrency, and recovery rules unresolved.

    14.2.4 · Serializability vs linearizability

    Two database transactions can be equivalent to a serial order without that order necessarily following the real-time order observed by separate clients. Serializability concerns whole transactions and their equivalent serial execution.

    Linearizability concerns real-time ordering of operations. Strict serializability combines transaction serialization with real-time precedence. Distinguish these when combining transactions and replica reads. Also identify the actual atomic boundary: a serializable local transaction does not bring an external payment provider into the same transaction. The property helps reason about work within its scope; messages and remote effects still need their own ordering and recovery design.

    14.2.5 · Sequential and causal consistency

    Sequential consistency allows one common ordering that preserves each participant's program order, without necessarily preserving real-time order across participants. Causal consistency preserves dependencies while permitting unrelated concurrent events to appear in different orders.

    Consider a reply written only after its author read a post. A causally consistent view should not expose that dependent reply without the parent information it depends on. The system needs dependency tracking or a supported protocol to provide this observation. Ordinary delayed replication alone does not establish it. Use a concrete event history to decide which order matters, rather than requiring a total order for every unrelated action.

    14.2.6 · Read-your-writes and monotonic reads

    After editing a profile, a user expects the next read to include that edit. Read-your-writes provides this session guarantee. After seeing version ten, the user also may expect not to see version nine later; that is monotonic reads.

    Routing, replication-position tracking, or another suitable protocol can support these rules. They do not necessarily provide global linearizability. Decide how progress follows a session when the user changes devices or an instance fails. Sticky routing alone may lose the guarantee at failover. A read might need to wait, use a current owner, or return an explicit unavailability result rather than silently go backward.

    Think further · Which operations may continue during a partition while exclusive allocation must wait?

    Operations with explicitly permitted stale or independent results may continue. Exclusive allocation needs valid authority and may have to wait or reject when agreement is unavailable. State per-operation observations rather than weaken the entire system silently. Recovery must reconcile progress without introducing another owner.

    Remember: Choose consistency by legal histories and their scope.

    Try applying it: Which history distinguishes a session moving backward from a permitted delayed read by another user?
