    PART 4 / UNIT 14 / CHAPTER 14.3

    Partitions, CAP, PACELC & quorums

    Prerequisites: 14.2 · Consistency as a reader-visible contract4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A partition separates machines that all remain alive. Use CAP, ordinary coordination costs, and quorum intersection to identify what each side may safely do.

    14.3.1 · CAP theorem, with its actual assumptions

    Two groups of replicas cannot communicate during a partition. If both must answer every request, they cannot always preserve CAP's formal atomic-consistency requirement for the shared read/write object. The impossibility concerns those defined properties under the specified partition model.

    CAP is therefore not a permanent menu of any two desirable features. Decide what each operation does when coordination is unavailable. Exclusive allocation may reject or wait; a different operation may serve an explicitly weaker view. State the exact property rather than equating formal availability with an ordinary uptime percentage. When the network is functioning, latency and coordination still require separate analysis.

    14.3.2 · PACELC as a useful extension

    A write can wait for a distant replica even when the network is healthy. That improves some coordination possibilities but adds travel time. PACELC draws attention to this ordinary latency/consistency trade-off as well as CAP's partition case.

    The mnemonic asks: during a partition, what availability/consistency choice is made; else, what latency/consistency trade-off is made? Use it as a review lens rather than a substitute for the protocol. Different operations and configurations can take different paths. Quantify the distances and waits with stated assumptions instead of assigning one permanent letter label to a product.

    14.3.3 · Quorums and read/write trade-offs

    With three fixed replicas, a two-member read set and a two-member write set must overlap. More generally, R+W>N gives read/write intersection, and W>N/2 gives intersection between write quorums.

    That is a statement about sets. A reader still needs a correct way to interpret the versions it receives, and writers need ordering, persistence, and concurrency rules. Membership changes or substitute nodes can invalidate a naive fixed-set argument. In N=3,R=2,W=2, at least one queried participant belongs to the completed write set, but that observation alone is not a linearizability proof. Keep the arithmetic and protocol claims separate.

    14.3.4 · Split-brain situations

    An old leader pauses. Another leader is elected, but the old process later resumes and tries to write. If both are treated as authorities, the system has split brain.

    A missing heartbeat cannot physically stop the earlier owner. An ownership protocol must be paired with enforcement where effects are accepted. For example, a storage receiver can reject requests carrying an older fencing epoch after it has accepted a newer one. Expiring only a local lock variable leaves the paused process able to act elsewhere. Test delayed messages and resumed workers as well as clean crashes, because these histories expose the stale-owner problem.

    Think further · Which operations may continue during a partition while exclusive allocation must wait?

    Operations with explicitly permitted stale or independent results may continue. Exclusive allocation needs valid authority and may have to wait or reject when agreement is unavailable. State per-operation observations rather than weaken the entire system silently. Recovery must reconcile progress without introducing another owner.

    Remember: Set intersection supplies a protocol ingredient; authority and version rules supply the rest.

    Try applying it: Which additional rules would a two-of-three read/write design need before claiming linearizability?

    PART 4 / UNIT 14 / CHAPTER 14.4

    Coordination, safety & liveness

    Prerequisites: 14.3 · Partitions, CAP, PACELC & quorums4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Some shared decisions need agreement; other work can proceed independently. State both forbidden outcomes and required progress, including the conditions under which progress can pause.

    14.4.1 · Distributed coordination

    Some decisions need agreement: who owns a partition, which configuration is current, or what order metadata changes follow. Distributed coordination establishes such shared decisions under a failure protocol.

    Use it where the invariant needs it. Independent updates that safely commute may not require a shared round on every operation. The coordinator also needs recovery and failure rules; a service name does not make it reliable. Decide how clients behave when it is unavailable. Reusing safe cached configuration can differ from issuing new exclusive ownership. Separating these activities helps preserve useful service without granting incompatible authority.

    14.4.2 · The fallacies of distributed computing

    A design may quietly assume every network call succeeds, arrives instantly, costs nothing, and reaches an unchanged destination. The fallacies of distributed computing collect warnings about such assumptions, including bandwidth, security, infrastructure diversity, and multiple administrators.

    Turn each warning into a concrete review question. What is the deadline? Who controls the other endpoint? How is the message versioned and authorised? How much data does fifty-way fan-out transfer? These questions uncover hidden requirements. The list is an engineering aid rather than a protocol guarantee. Its value comes from applying the concerns to real paths and failure histories.

    14.4.3 · Safety vs liveness

    “No seat is sold to two buyers” excludes a bad outcome: it is a safety property. “Every accepted booking eventually resolves” asks for progress, a liveness obligation that needs stated environmental assumptions.

    Rejecting every request can preserve the first property while providing no useful progress. Conversely, replying immediately can appear responsive while breaking exclusive ownership. Write both requirements and identify which failures may delay completion. Some network and failure models prevent unconditional progress guarantees. Expose stuck work so operators can restore progress without inventing a second winner or losing an already accepted operation.

    Try the mechanism in code

    Python · ordering models

    from mechanisms import vector_relation, lamport_receive
assert vector_relation([1,0], [0,1]) == "concurrent"
assert vector_relation([1,0], [1,2]) == "before"
assert lamport_receive(5, 9) == 10

    Neither [1,0] nor [0,1] dominates the other, so the model reports concurrency. [1,0] precedes [1,2], and receiving 9 at Lamport value 5 advances it to 10.

    These are ordering calculations. A smaller Lamport number alone does not prove causation, and neither clock decides a business merge or consensus outcome.

    Download the executable mechanism collection ↓ · Follow the connected complete design →

    THE WORKBENCH · TRY CHANGING THE INPUTS

    When must a read set meet a write set?

    Keep the same N replicas, then vary the number read and written. The calculation shows whether the sets must share a member. To decide which value a read can return, we also need rules for versions, concurrent writes, persistence, repair, and membership changes. Intersection alone does not prove linearizability.

    Think further · Which operations may continue during a partition while exclusive allocation must wait?

    Operations with explicitly permitted stale or independent results may continue. Exclusive allocation needs valid authority and may have to wait or reject when agreement is unavailable. State per-operation observations rather than weaken the entire system silently. Recovery must reconcile progress without introducing another owner.

    Remember: Safety and liveness are separate obligations under an explicit failure model.

    Try applying it: How could a system preserve exclusive ownership while still failing every user's useful request?

    PART 4 / UNIT 15 / CHAPTER 15.1

    Choose a replication model

    Prerequisites: Distributed Systems Fundamentals6 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A primary replies before a replica catches up. Compare replication models by write authority, acknowledgment milestones, conflicts, and the history available after failure.

    15.1.1 · Primary/replica architectures

    A primary accepts the writes for a dataset and replicas keep copies. One current authority can simplify conflict handling, but the topology needs rules for replacing that authority and preventing an old primary from returning as a competing writer.

    State when a write is acknowledged and which failures preserve it. Replica reads may show earlier data. “One primary, two replicas” describes placement, not a complete consensus protocol. Persistence, election eligibility, membership, and recovery determine the actual guarantee. Ask what happens to an acknowledged write if the primary disappears before its newest changes reach another eligible owner.

    15.1.2 · Leader/follower replication

    A leader sends an ordered stream of updates to followers. A follower may receive bytes, persist them, and later apply them to its local state. These milestones are not necessarily simultaneous.

    Track the positions relevant to the implementation. Receipt in memory may not provide crash-recovery protection. A follower serving reads may still be behind even after receiving recent records. Synchronous and asynchronous arrangements choose different acknowledgment points and waits. Promotion needs a rule about which history is safe to continue. Understanding these stages makes lag and durability claims more precise than saying that a follower “has the data.”

    15.1.3 · Multi-leader replication

    Two regions accept writes locally while their connection is interrupted. On reconnection, both may have changed the same record. Multi-leader replication needs a resolution rule for those concurrent updates.

    Last-writer-wins can converge by choosing a timestamp, but clock differences or overwriting can discard meaningful work. Convergence alone does not establish a correct business merge. Use multiple writers where conflict semantics fit the domain, or add coordination for rules requiring one winner. Include deletes, prolonged disconnection, and replication-loop prevention in the design. Local write latency is a benefit only when the resulting observations and conflicts remain acceptable.

    15.1.4 · Leaderless replication

    A client contacts several replicas and compares their versions instead of sending every write through one permanent leader. Leaderless designs use protocols of this kind, with choices about read repair, hinted handoff, and background anti-entropy.

    Each mechanism solves part of the problem. Quorum counts still need correct version interpretation, membership, and concurrency rules. Test two concurrent writes and a stale replica returning after a long failure. Choose the arrangement for its actual availability and conflict contract. Removing a permanent leader does not remove every need for coordination, nor does two replies out of three automatically establish linearizability.

    15.1.5 · Synchronous vs asynchronous replication

    A primary can reply immediately and copy later, or wait for specified replica evidence. Asynchronous replication chooses the earlier reply. If the only current copy is then lost, a promoted replica may lack recent acknowledged writes.

    Synchronous replication waits, but the word needs detail: does a replica acknowledge receipt, durable storage, or application? Waiting for independent durable copies can strengthen protection within the failure model, while adding latency and possible blocking. State which milestone success promises and test it during failover. The configuration is part of the application's data-loss contract, rather than an operating detail detached from users.

    15.1.6 · Quorum-based systems

    In a fixed three-node group, any two-member majority overlaps another two-member majority. This can carry evidence from one decision into a later one, provided the shared participant follows the protocol.

    A quorum is an allowed decision set, not simply a vote count. Members may need to persist a vote or accepted record before replying and obey later restrictions based on it. Election eligibility and membership transitions also matter. Without these rules, intersecting sets can still acknowledge incompatible histories. Use quorum arithmetic to understand a reviewed protocol, rather than treating it as a complete algorithm for consistent storage.

    Think further · What must a repaired region establish before it accepts authoritative writes again?

    It needs current authority, compatible committed history, required durable copies, valid routing, and sufficient capacity. An old leader may require rebuilding and fencing. Apply the supported rejoin protocol and reconcile uncertain external effects. A repaired machine being reachable is not evidence that its old state is safe to resume.

    Remember: Replica count matters only with persistence, ownership, and recovery rules.

    Try applying it: What must a synchronous acknowledgment mean if it is meant to survive process loss?

    PART 4 / UNIT 15 / CHAPTER 15.2

    Raft and replicated state machines

    Prerequisites: 15.1 · Choose a replication model5 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A new leader must preserve accepted history. Study deterministic command application and the election, log, commit, and membership rules that make replicated decisions safe.

    15.2.1 · Consensus and replicated state machines

    Suppose replicas agree on the sequence “create task 7, then complete task 7.” If each applies the same commands deterministically from the same state, they can maintain equivalent task state. This is the replicated state-machine approach.

    Consensus supplies agreement under its stated fault and progress assumptions. Values such as random identifiers or current time must be part of an agreed command or otherwise handled consistently; recomputing them independently can make replicas differ. Also separate state-machine application from external effects. Applying one command on several replicas must not send several unprotected charges. External delivery needs explicit ownership, duplicate handling, and recovery outside the agreed log boundary.

    15.2.2 · Raft: terms, elections, log replication, commit

    Raft organises agreement around a leader and a replicated log. A term identifies an election generation. A candidate needs a majority of votes and a sufficiently up-to-date log under Raft's comparison rules. Votes and required log state are persisted as specified by the protocol.

    The leader replicates entries and advances its commit position. It can directly use majority replication to commit a current-term entry; earlier entries become committed through the protocol's ordering rules. Counting copies of an arbitrary older entry is insufficient. This distinction preserves history across leadership changes. Reads also need a supported freshness mechanism. The paper's rules work together; this explanation is not a replacement implementation.

    15.2.3 · Paxos: conceptual foundations

    Paxos uses numbered proposals and intersecting groups to preserve an agreed choice. During preparation, a proposer gathers promises and any relevant earlier accepted value. It must carry the required value forward when it asks for acceptance.

    The key idea is preserving prior evidence, rather than allowing each new leader to choose freely. Multi-Paxos uses related decisions to build an ordered sequence, often reducing repeated preparation around a stable leader. This is a conceptual introduction. Persistence, changing membership, retries, and progress under contention need precise rules. Use a reviewed implementation for real coordination instead of turning the introductory voting picture into production lock code.

    15.2.4 · Log ordering and durability

    A record can appear in one replica's log without being committed. A node can also have committed records it has not applied yet. Ordering, commitment, durable storage, and application describe different progress.

    Recovery must retain the committed history while handling incompatible uncommitted suffixes. Reply according to the protocol's actual acceptance rule, rather than because bytes reached some follower. Monitor commit and apply progress, and ensure snapshot installation represents a compatible history. These distinctions explain why a local log inspection alone may not establish what the application is entitled to expose as an accepted result.

    15.2.5 · Membership changes

    Suppose an old cluster and a new cluster have disjoint decision majorities. Replacing membership abruptly can let both make incompatible decisions. A supported membership transition prevents that gap.

    Raft's joint-consensus approach temporarily requires the relevant majorities from both configurations. New nodes can first catch up without voting. Use the implementation's reconfiguration procedure, preserving persistent identities and testing interruption during the change. Increasing a cluster-size setting is not merely adding capacity: it changes which groups have authority. The safety argument must remain valid at the transition, not only before and after it.

    Think further · What must a repaired region establish before it accepts authoritative writes again?

    It needs current authority, compatible committed history, required durable copies, valid routing, and sufficient capacity. An old leader may require rebuilding and fencing. Apply the supported rejoin protocol and reconcile uncertain external effects. A repaired machine being reachable is not evidence that its old state is safe to resume.

    Remember: Consensus rules work together to preserve a decision history; a copy count is insufficient.

    Try applying it: Why can an arbitrary old log entry on a majority still need more reasoning before commitment?

    PART 4 / UNIT 15 / CHAPTER 15.3

    Fences, leases & failure detection

    Prerequisites: 15.2 · Raft and replicated state machines4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A paused worker wakes after its lease expired. Separate suspicion, ownership transfer, and resource-side enforcement to see where stale actions must be rejected.

    15.3.1 · Split-brain prevention and fencing tokens

    Worker A has token 7 and pauses. Its lease expires; B obtains token 8. A later resumes and sends an old write. The receiving resource must reject that stale authority.

    A fencing token is an ordered ownership epoch checked at the effect boundary. The receiver must compare the token and apply the protected action atomically under its rule. Issuing a token that storage never checks does not fence a worker. Also account for effects already accepted before the newer owner took over. Fencing blocks later stale actions; it does not undo earlier accepted ones or automatically protect an unrelated external API.

    15.3.2 · Failure detection

    Missing heartbeats suggest failure, but a long pause or congested network can produce the same observation. Failure detectors trade responsiveness against false suspicions according to timing assumptions.

    Shorter intervals can begin recovery sooner while increasing unnecessary suspicion. Keep this tuning separate from the protocol that transfers authority and fences stale owners. Safety should hold even if a suspicion is wrong. A received heartbeat also does not establish that every request can meet its deadline, so readiness and load signals can still be useful. Detection provides evidence; ownership rules determine which participant may act on it.

    15.3.3 · Strongly consistent metadata services

    A metadata service can maintain current ownership epochs or configuration through a strongly consistent protocol. These are usually small control decisions, rather than the full high-volume application payload.

    Identify which actions need a fresh decision and which can use safe cached information. During a metadata outage, existing traffic might continue while new leases or deployments must wait. Drawing this control/data distinction makes the failure policy clearer. Avoid placing every request behind a synchronous control-plane lookup without a reason. The control service's own capacity, fault assumptions, and recovery are still dependencies of the decisions it owns.

    15.3.4 · Distributed locks and leases

    A lock grants permission to a named owner. A lease makes that permission time-bounded under particular timing rules. The holder can pause past expiry and later continue unless the protected resource recognises that its authority is stale.

    Use resource-side fencing where that history threatens correctness. Release operations must check ownership, so an old holder cannot delete a newer owner's lock. Acquisition and the later protected action are separate events with a gap between them. For an invariant entirely inside one database, a local transaction may avoid unnecessary distributed locking. Choose coordination for the actual shared resource and failure history.

    Think further · What must a repaired region establish before it accepts authoritative writes again?

    It needs current authority, compatible committed history, required durable copies, valid routing, and sufficient capacity. An old leader may require rebuilding and fencing. Apply the supported rejoin protocol and reconcile uncertain external effects. A repaired machine being reachable is not evidence that its old state is safe to resume.

    Remember: Failure detection does not stop a process; the protected effect needs valid authority enforcement.

    Try applying it: Where must token 7 be rejected after token 8 has become current?

    PART 4 / UNIT 15 / CHAPTER 15.4

    Conflicts, CRDTs & regional trade-offs

    Prerequisites: 15.3 · Fences, leases & failure detection4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Replicas must merge concurrent changes or choose which authority may proceed across regions. Evaluate convergence and recovery against the business invariant rather than as ends in themselves.

    15.4.1 · Conflict resolution and CRDT introduction

    A grow-only set can merge copies by union: each addition remains present, and merging in different orders converges. CRDTs design types around update and merge rules with suitable algebraic and delivery assumptions.

    More complex types need metadata. An observed-remove set distinguishes additions known at removal from concurrent additions. Convergence does not enforce an arbitrary rule such as nonnegative stock. Choose semantics that match the domain, and preserve the metadata needed for safe merge and cleanup. Some business edits are better handled by explicit conflict review. An automatic convergent answer is useful only if that answer means the right thing.

    15.4.2 · Multi-region replication trade-offs

    A local asynchronous reply and a cross-region durable quorum expose different latency and possible-loss behaviour. Regional replication must state where writes are authoritative, which copies acknowledgment requires, and how conflicts or promotion work.

    During a partition, some operations may reject while permitted stale reads continue. On reconnection, an old primary must catch up or reconcile before it is trusted to write again. Test failback as well as failover. Restoring traffic quickly can conceal a second failure if stale authority or history returns after the visible outage. The regional design includes that return path, not merely the initial switch.

    Try the mechanism in code

    Pseudocode · three replicas, one partition

    A,B,C contain committed index 8
partition isolates old leader A
B and C elect eligible B in term 5
B appends index 9, term 5
B and C durably replicate index 9
Raft commit rule establishes committed prefix
A cannot acknowledge a new quorum-committed write alone
rejoin: A follows term 5 and repairs uncommitted suffix

    The example assumes correct non-Byzantine participants, durable protocol state, and three fixed voters. B's current-term entry reaches a valid majority while A is isolated.

    Follow the full Raft rules for election, log repair, commitment, reads, and membership. This trace explains one history and is not an executable replacement protocol.

    Download the executable mechanism collection ↓ · Follow the connected complete design →

    Think further · What must a repaired region establish before it accepts authoritative writes again?

    It needs current authority, compatible committed history, required durable copies, valid routing, and sufficient capacity. An old leader may require rebuilding and fencing. Apply the supported rejoin protocol and reconcile uncertain external effects. A repaired machine being reachable is not evidence that its old state is safe to resume.

    Remember: A deterministic merge is useful only when its meaning and failure assumptions fit the domain.

    Try applying it: Why can a convergent counter still be unsuitable for allocating the last item?

    PART 4 / UNIT 16 / CHAPTER 16.1

    Queues, logs & delivery boundaries

    Prerequisites: API Design and Communication Contracts, Database Internals, Transactions, and Concurrency Control, Distributed Systems Fundamentals, Replication, Leader Election, and Consensus9 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A message is accepted, delivered, executed, and acknowledged at different times. Trace those boundaries to understand queues, logs, repetition, and the scope of delivery guarantees.

    16.1.1 · Synchronous vs asynchronous communication

    Checkout can save an order and let receipt delivery happen later. Synchronous communication makes the caller wait for a result; asynchronous communication separates submission from observing completion.

    The delayed work still needs an owner. If accepting an order promises a receipt workflow, record the required intent durably instead of leaving it only in the request's memory. A queue can absorb a burst, but continued arrivals above worker capacity still build a backlog. State what the initial response means and where clients or operators can see progress after the initiating request ends.

    16.1.2 · Queues vs logs vs pub/sub

    A queue commonly distributes jobs among consumers. A retained log keeps an append history that consumers can replay. Pub/sub delivers publications to subscribers according to a particular retention and acknowledgment policy.

    Products combine these behaviours, so read their actual contract. A subscriber absent during an ephemeral publication may never receive it. A consumer that must recover after a long outage needs enough retention and a stored progress position. Choose by recovery and ordering requirements, rather than assuming that every broker is a durable history. The important question is which records remain and how a returning consumer finds its next work.

    16.1.3 · Producers, consumers, brokers

    A producer submits a message, the broker stores or routes it, and a consumer performs work. “Acknowledged” can refer to several points: broker receipt, durable replication, consumer receipt, or completion of the business effect.

    Name the point that matters. Include stable message identity, schema version, ownership, and correlation information. A broker may be healthy while every consumer rejects the payload. Observe end-to-end age and outcomes as well as enqueue rate and broker uptime. Following one message through these stages reveals which component has actually accepted responsibility at each step.

    16.1.4 · Partitions, consumer groups, offsets

    Kafka-style partitions provide ordered lanes. An offset identifies progress in one lane, and a consumer group distributes partition work among members. Order within a partition does not establish order across all partitions.

    When group membership changes, a partition can move to another consumer. Work near the progress-commit boundary may repeat. Choose keys for the ordering the domain needs and commit progress according to the effect contract. One very popular partition can limit the group while other consumers are idle. Adding workers does not divide that lane automatically. Separate lane ownership, processing concurrency, and completed effects when reasoning about throughput.

    16.1.5 · Delivery guarantees

    A broker delivers the same record twice. A consumer can still make one local database change if it recognises the event identity and commits that recognition with the change. A later external call may have different repetition behaviour.

    Delivery guarantees need a boundary: are we counting broker deliveries, execution starts, or committed effects? Trace source acceptance, retained records, retries, effect commit, and progress acknowledgment. A guarantee at one link does not automatically extend across the whole path. This vocabulary becomes useful when each stage states exactly what survives a crash and what can be repeated.

    16.1.6 · At-most-once and at-least-once processing

    A consumer acknowledges before applying an effect, then crashes. The broker may not redeliver, so the effect is missing. This placement can support at-most-once handling at the chosen boundary: zero outcomes remain possible.

    If the consumer applies the effect before acknowledging, a crash in between can cause redelivery. This supports at-least-once handling under the retention and recovery assumptions, but repetition must be safe. For one local database effect, store the processed event identifier and effect in the same transaction. Doing those steps separately creates another failure gap. Neither placement alone makes an unrelated external call atomic with broker progress.

    16.1.7 · Exactly-once processing within defined boundaries

    A stream-processing transaction can couple consumed progress and produced records inside a system that supports that operation. An exactly-once claim can be meaningful within that stated boundary and fault model.

    Now substitute an external email or payment provider for the produced record. Unless another protocol covers it, the transaction cannot establish one external effect. Idempotency may make repeated attempts have one relevant outcome under a key and retention policy, while executions can still start more than once. Name the records, effects, failures, and recovery covered by the guarantee. Avoid treating “exactly once” as a property that automatically crosses every connected service.

    16.1.8 · Ordering guarantees

    Messages can be published in order and still commit effects out of order when consumers process them in parallel. Distinguish log order, delivery order, start order, and effect-completion order.

    If account changes require sequential application, coordinate by account or an equivalent ordering boundary. A later message should not be treated as applied while an earlier required change remains unresolved. Poison records need a deliberate policy: skipping restores movement but may break the sequence. Sequence numbers and gap detection can help expose that choice. State the business ordering requirement before selecting a partitioning and concurrency arrangement.

    16.1.9 · Consumer acknowledgements

    A consumer finishes its local update, but its acknowledgment is lost. The broker can redeliver the record. If acknowledgment were earlier, a crash could instead lose the update.

    The acknowledgment tells the broker what progress it may record under its protocol. No placement makes it automatically atomic with a separate external system. Use appropriate local transactions, inbox/outbox records, provider keys, and reconciliation. Also match acknowledgment deadlines or lease extensions to expected processing time. Otherwise, healthy long-running work may be reassigned repeatedly. Identify the effect boundary first, then choose where progress can safely advance.

    Think further · How could one broker transaction be exactly-once while two emails are sent?

    The broker may atomically couple consumed progress and produced records while email lies outside that transaction. A consumer can send, lose its completion reply, and send again on recovery. Use the provider contract, stable identity where supported, and reconciliation; do not extend the broker guarantee to an unrelated effect.

    Remember: Name the accepted record or effect before claiming at-most-once, at-least-once, or exactly-once behaviour.

    Try applying it: What changes if the consumer replaces its local counter update with an external email call?

    PART 4 / UNIT 16 / CHAPTER 16.2

    Retries, consumers & event history

    Prerequisites: 16.1 · Queues, logs & delivery boundaries4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A consumer crashes after applying an event, while another record fails on every retry. Design repeat-safe effects and a repair path, then distinguish delivery history from authoritative domain history.

    16.2.1 · Retries and dead-letter queues

    A temporary provider outage may deserve a delayed retry. A permanently invalid address will not improve because the same payload is sent a thousand times. Classify failures and bound the attempts and waiting time.

    A dead-letter queue holds work needing another path, such as repair or review. It does not mean the business task is complete. Retain original identity, source version, attempt information, and a safe error reason. Give important unresolved work an owner and alerting. Replay must preserve duplicate and ordering rules. A repair process should restore valid progress rather than turn rejected records into uncontrolled new operations.

    16.2.2 · Poison messages

    A particular message fails every time while neighbouring messages work. It may have malformed data, an unsupported schema, or a rule violation. Such a poison message needs a different response from a transient network fault.

    Quarantine enough evidence to diagnose it and decide whether dependent records must wait. Avoid retaining unnecessary sensitive payloads. A software bug can also reject an entire legitimate historical version, so inspect failure patterns and samples before discarding data. Bounded retries protect resources while a review path protects the business work. Both are needed when skipping a record could leave an important operation unresolved.

    16.2.3 · Idempotent consumers

    The first delivery inserts processed(event_id) and increments a counter in one transaction. A second delivery encounters the same unique identity and does not repeat the increment. This is an idempotent consumer for that local effect.

    Keep the identity long enough for the supported replay and delivery window. If recognition is only in memory, restart loses it. If recognition commits separately from the effect, a crash can either lose or repeat the work. External providers remain outside this local transaction, so they need their own stable key or reconciliation. State what outcome is protected rather than assuming the consumer's name establishes it.

    16.2.4 · Event sourcing

    Instead of storing only the latest order state, event sourcing keeps the accepted domain events as its authoritative history. Applying them in order reconstructs the current state. A snapshot can speed this work if it records the event position it represents.

    The history must remain interpretable as schemas change. Define corrections, replay, privacy, and retention. Rebuilding a projection must not resend real charges or emails merely because their events are read again. Auditability also depends on domain and access rules; append-only storage is not automatically a sufficient financial ledger. Choose the approach for a real need to preserve and interpret that history.

    Think further · How could one broker transaction be exactly-once while two emails are sent?

    The broker may atomically couple consumed progress and produced records while email lies outside that transaction. A consumer can send, lose its completion reply, and send again on recovery. Use the provider contract, stable identity where supported, and reconciliation; do not extend the broker guarantee to an unrelated effect.

    Remember: Retrying, deduplicating, and preserving events serve different recovery needs.

    Try applying it: How should a repaired poison record be replayed without duplicating its established effects?

    PART 4 / UNIT 16 / CHAPTER 16.3

    Read models, the outbox & sagas

    Prerequisites: 16.2 · Retries, consumers & event history4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    An order commits but still needs publication and later compensation. Connect read models, outbox delivery, and sagas to make the obligations between local owners explicit.

    16.3.1 · CQRS

    An order command model checks legal transitions. A customer-history view arranges the same accepted information for convenient reading. CQRS separates these responsibilities or models when their requirements differ.

    A projection may update the read model later, so define what a user sees immediately after a command. It may need a current-owner read, a progress indicator, or an accepted delay. CQRS can use one database and process. Event sourcing and separate services are additional choices. The extra models and synchronisation are worthwhile when they simplify actual workloads, not merely because reads and writes have different names.

    16.3.2 · Transactional outbox

    An order commits, then the process dies before publishing OrderPlaced. A transactional outbox closes this local gap by writing the order change and publication intent in the same database transaction.

    A relay later publishes the intent and records its progress. If it crashes after publication but before recording progress, publication can repeat. Use stable event identities and consumer duplicate handling. Monitor old pending intents and retain an appropriate recovery history. The pattern coordinates local state with the obligation to publish; it does not make every subscriber part of the original transaction or guarantee one external effect everywhere.

    16.3.3 · Sagas and compensating transactions

    Checkout reserves stock, authorises payment, and arranges shipment across separate owners. A saga records these local steps and the actions needed if the overall workflow cannot continue.

    Compensation might release a reservation or request a refund. It may itself fail and need retries, and it is not always a perfect inverse: a refund can occur after costs or user-visible effects. Persist both forward and compensating progress. Distinguish uncertain, recoverable intermediate states from final outcomes. When replies are lost, reconcile with the relevant authority before assuming a step did not happen or starting it again.

    Think further · How could one broker transaction be exactly-once while two emails are sent?

    The broker may atomically couple consumed progress and produced records while email lies outside that transaction. A consumer can send, lose its completion reply, and send again on recovery. Use the provider contract, stable identity where supported, and reconciliation; do not extend the broker guarantee to an unrelated effect.

    Remember: Local atomic progress closes specific gaps while external steps retain their own failure and recovery rules.

    Try applying it: Why can an outbox relay still publish one event twice?

    PART 4 / UNIT 16 / CHAPTER 16.4

    Coordinate durable workflows

    Prerequisites: 16.3 · Read models, the outbox & sagas6 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A durable job outlives its request, scheduler, and first worker. Give each occurrence and attempt an identity, limit replay, and reconcile outcomes that remain uncertain.

    16.4.1 · Choreography vs orchestration

    With choreography, participants react to each other's events. With orchestration, an explicit coordinator records workflow progress and chooses the next action. Both can implement the same business sequence with different ownership and visibility.

    Choreography can avoid one central controller but make end-to-end state harder to see. Orchestration makes retries and compensation explicit while adding a coordinator and evolving workflow definition. Neither removes participant failure. Choose according to the complexity, audit needs, and teams changing the process. Carry a shared correlation identity through either design so an operator can follow one business operation across its steps.

    16.4.2 · Workflow engines

    A workflow pauses for human approval, then resumes after a process restart. A workflow engine can persist progress, timers, and retry decisions under its supported programming model.

    Activities still call outside systems. If an activity's effect succeeds but its completion record is lost, it may run again. Understand the engine's replay, determinism, versioning, activity identity, and cancellation rules. Use stable effect identities and reconciliation where necessary. The engine makes durable coordination easier; the application must still define correct transitions and safe external actions. Persistent orchestration is a useful mechanism with a scope, rather than a universal exactly-once guarantee.

    16.4.3 · Durable job execution

    A durable job has an identity, input reference, progress state, attempt history, and an owner that can be replaced. A worker completes only if its current attempt or fencing epoch is still valid.

    Store large inputs separately and verify their version before processing. An old worker must not overwrite a newer attempt's output. Bound retries and expose terminal or review states when work cannot finish automatically. A process-local background task has none of these recovery properties merely because the request returned 202. The response and durable acceptance contract must agree about who will continue the work after a crash.

    16.4.4 · Scheduling, leases, and worker coordination

    A schedule says a report is due at noon. The scheduler needs a stable occurrence identity, such as (schedule_id,occurrence), and an atomic way to claim or create that run.

    Define missed periods, clock changes, overlap, and failover. A lease can expire while its worker still runs, so protect effects with an appropriate idempotency or fencing protocol. A single scheduler process does not by itself make runs recoverable or unique across restarts. Separate deciding that an occurrence is due from safely executing its external effect. Both stages need durable identity and recovery rules.

    16.4.5 · Backpressure and replay

    A consumer falls behind and later replays retained input. Replaying as fast as possible can overwhelm the same live dependencies currently serving users. Backpressure and replay need coordinated capacity limits.

    Give catch-up work its own rate budget, preserve source identities, and suppress unintended repeated side effects. Retention must cover the required recovery interval. Monitor oldest age and per-key blockage as well as queue length and throughput. A processor can be busy while one important operation remains stuck. Useful progress means business work reaching its defined outcome, rather than merely reading many historical messages.

    16.4.6 · Reconciliation after partial failure

    A local payment remains pending while the provider shows it charged. Reconciliation compares these intended and observed states and repairs the mismatch using the stable operation identity.

    Query and update safely instead of blindly submitting another charge. The reconciler must also be authorised, idempotent, and observable. Run it periodically and during recovery, and track unresolved discrepancies by age and owner. It is part of the normal protocol for partial failures. It supplements correct persistence and validation on the main path rather than excusing missing records that make later investigation impossible.

    Try the mechanism in code

    Python · duplicate delivery, one local effect

    from mechanisms import open_demo_store, consume_local_event
db = open_demo_store()
assert consume_local_event(db, "E1", "orders")
assert not consume_local_event(db, "E1", "orders")
assert db.execute("SELECT value FROM counters").fetchone()[0] == 1
db.close()

    The first transaction records E1 and increments the counter. The second finds E1 already processed and leaves the counter at one.

    Event recognition and the local effect share a transaction. Replacing the counter update with an external email or payment call requires another protocol; it changes the boundary this example protects.

    Think further · How could one broker transaction be exactly-once while two emails are sent?

    The broker may atomically couple consumed progress and produced records while email lies outside that transaction. A consumer can send, lose its completion reply, and send again on recovery. Use the provider contract, stable identity where supported, and reconciliation; do not extend the broker guarantee to an unrelated effect.

    Remember: Persistent ownership and safe effect identity let accepted work recover without inventing new intentions.

    Try applying it: What should recovery do when a provider shows success but the local workflow remains pending?

    PART 4 / UNIT 17 / CHAPTER 17.1

    Failure domains & redundancy

    Prerequisites: Requirements, Estimation, and Engineering Trade-offs, Scalability, Load Balancing, and Data Distribution, Replication, Leader Election, and Consensus, Message Queues, Events, and Distributed Workflows4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Several replicas share a hidden dependency and fail together. Review the serving and data goals, then calculate what independent capacity really remains after a failure.

    17.1.1 · Failure domains and fault isolation

    Two workers use the same disk and credential source. Their processes are separate, but one disk failure or credential change can stop both. A failure domain groups parts exposed to a common cause.

    Map process, host, zone, dependency, and administrative correlations. Fault isolation limits how one failure spreads, for example by separating critical resource pools. The separation costs capacity and operating work, so choose it according to the harm and recovery objective. Test the shared dependencies as well as individual processes. Counting replicas without their common causes can greatly overstate the protection the design provides.

    17.1.2 · Availability vs durability

    A database refuses requests during recovery but keeps all committed rows. This is a period of unavailability without demonstrated committed-data loss. A web application can show the opposite problem: it keeps replying successfully but drops writes stored only in memory.

    Define availability and durability independently. Specify useful eligible responses, data-loss tolerance, and the failures being covered. Timeouts, traffic failover, backups, and replication influence different parts of that contract. A general promise of reliability needs these details before it can be measured. Choose checks that establish serving behaviour and retained state rather than treating either one as evidence of both.

    17.1.3 · Redundancy

    Two instances each operate at 70% of their individual capacity. If one fails, the remaining instance cannot absorb both workloads at the same rate. Redundancy needs enough surviving capacity or an explicit reduced-service policy.

    It also needs independent failure placement, usable state, detection, and traffic movement. Shared bad configuration can disable every replica at once. Test takeover and restoration under the actual load instead of treating the second box as automatic protection. Spare resources are useful when the system can find them, direct work to them, and preserve the required state during the transition.

    17.1.4 · Active-active vs active-passive

    In active-active operation, several locations or owners serve the selected function. Active-passive keeps a standby ready for takeover. The choice can differ by layer: application instances may all serve while one database leader owns writes.

    A passive standby can have drift or warmup problems that appear only during takeover. Multiple active owners need routing and suitable coordination or conflict rules. For either arrangement, define detection, promotion, fencing, surviving capacity, and the return after repair. A standby that has never reconstructed usable state is an untested assumption. The operating model is a complete transition procedure, not just a traffic label.

    Think further · How can a disaster drill restore infrastructure yet fail the business recovery requirement?

    Machines can restart while the recovered data is too old, encrypted backups are unreadable, active authority conflicts, or accepted jobs are missing. Check the complete business journey and its RTO/RPO, including keys, state, identity, validation, and useful traffic return. A drill proves only the scenarios it actually exercises.

    Remember: Redundancy requires independence, valid state, and sufficient surviving capacity.

    Try applying it: Can two instances each at 70% load absorb the loss of either one?

    PART 4 / UNIT 17 / CHAPTER 17.2

    Retries, circuit breakers & isolation

    Prerequisites: 17.1 · Failure domains & redundancy6 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A slow provider consumes every connection and triggers retries. Use deadlines, budgets, breakers, and resource isolation to limit the pressure rather than merely repeat the same work faster.

    17.2.1 · Timeouts

    A client permits two seconds for an operation. It would be wasteful to spend three seconds waiting for a database connection before starting the query. An overall deadline bounds the useful lifetime of the request.

    Stage limits can cover connection setup, pool acquisition, and execution, but should fit the remaining overall time. Propagate that remaining time downstream and clean up work when possible. A timeout means the caller stopped waiting; an external write may already have occurred. Record which stage timed out so diagnosis distinguishes waiting from computation. Independent full timeouts at every layer can keep useless work alive far beyond the caller's limit.

    17.2.2 · Retries, exponential backoff, jitter

    A dropped connection before a safe lookup may justify another attempt. An invalid payment amount will not improve if the same request is repeated. Classify the error before retrying.

    Use bounded attempts, increasing backoff, jitter, and a deadline. Repeated effects need a stable operation identity. Respect relevant retry guidance while keeping the whole business operation within its intended lifetime. Retry ownership should be clear across layers; several independently aggressive policies can multiply load. Retries are additional work spent to recover from a particular failure, so include that work in capacity and recovery planning.

    17.2.3 · Retry storms

    Four nested layers each allow three attempts. One logical request can then create up to 3⁴ = 81 downstream attempts. During a dependency outage, this amplification can turn partial capacity into a complete collapse.

    Jitter spreads attempts in time but does not reduce their total by itself. Use an overall attempt budget, admission controls, and suppression of redundant work. Measure original intents separately from attempts and useful completions. An outage-related rise in requests may come from retries rather than new users. Protect capacity for successful work and recovery instead of letting repeated failures consume it all.

    17.2.4 · Circuit breakers

    A dependency repeatedly fails. A circuit breaker can temporarily reject new calls rather than making every caller wait for another likely failure. Common states are closed, open, and half-open, where limited probes test recovery.

    Define which failures count and how probes are bounded. Avoid all instances probing simultaneously after a shared timer. The breaker does not repair the dependency or decide a safe business fallback. It must not turn a failed authorisation call into a fabricated payment approval. Its useful role is controlling further resource expenditure while the application returns or performs a deliberately chosen degraded behaviour.

    17.2.5 · Bulkheads

    Receipt email stalls and occupies every worker. Payment authorisation now cannot obtain resources even though its provider is healthy. Bulkheads reserve or separate resources for work with different failure priorities.

    Dedicated pools can keep optional delivery from consuming checkout's whole allowance. Check shared limits as well: two pools may still exhaust one database or host memory. Too much partitioning can leave spare resources unused, so choose boundaries by harm and workload. Observe saturation and rejection in each pool. Isolation is effective when it covers the resource through which failure would spread, not merely when two thread-pool names exist.

    17.2.6 · Rate limiting

    A token bucket accumulates tokens at a configured rate up to a capacity. Each admitted request spends tokens. It permits a bounded burst while controlling continuing admission. A shaper may instead delay work to change its pace.

    For several tenants, combine fairness with protection of total service capacity. Define the identity, cost unit, burst, and failure policy. A limiter whose remote state is unavailable must reject, allow, or use a previously allocated local budget according to an explicit contract. These choices change both availability and abuse exposure. Test that path rather than assuming the limiter always has a healthy backing store.

    Think further · How can a disaster drill restore infrastructure yet fail the business recovery requirement?

    Machines can restart while the recovered data is too old, encrypted backups are unreadable, active authority conflicts, or accepted jobs are missing. Check the complete business journey and its RTO/RPO, including keys, state, identity, validation, and useful traffic return. A drill proves only the scenarios it actually exercises.

    Remember: Bound both useful work and recovery attempts at the resource boundaries that can saturate.

    Try applying it: Why can jitter reduce synchronisation while leaving total retry work excessive?

    PART 4 / UNIT 17 / CHAPTER 17.3

    Shed load and degrade deliberately

    Prerequisites: 17.2 · Retries, circuit breakers & isolation4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Some features can continue with reduced data; others must stop when their authority is unavailable. Define shedding, degradation, fallbacks, and probes from those meanings.

    17.3.1 · Load shedding

    Under overload, the service may stop generating recommendations while preserving order status and reconciliation. Load shedding rejects selected work early enough to keep resources available for higher-priority outcomes.

    Choose priorities from product and correctness requirements. Rejecting after expensive computation saves little. Return a clear overload result and bound subsequent retries. Shedding can improve useful completions while demand exceeds capacity; it cannot sustain an impossible workload forever. More capacity, less work, or a changed target may still be needed. Measure useful accepted outcomes so a drop in raw throughput is not mistaken for failure when deliberate shedding protects essential work.

    17.3.2 · Graceful degradation

    A product page can remain useful without recommendations. A sale cannot safely proceed merely because an old cached count says stock exists. Graceful degradation preserves an agreed subset of useful behaviour while respecting the rules that still matter.

    Specify which data may be stale, which actions pause, and what the user sees. Test rarely exercised degraded paths before relying on them during an incident. Catching every error and returning a default does not establish safety. The alternative outcome needs the same clarity about permissions, freshness, and meaning as the ordinary one.

    17.3.3 · Fallbacks

    A cached help page may substitute for an unavailable content service. A default account balance cannot substitute for an unavailable ledger. A fallback is another behaviour whose meaning must be acceptable for this operation.

    Check its freshness, duration, access scope, and extra load. A fallback can itself overload another dependency or hide a long incident. Switching providers also changes operation identity and recovery unless their semantics are deliberately aligned. Make degraded operation visible where needed. Evaluate the substituted result as a business outcome rather than treating any returned response as successful recovery.

    17.3.4 · Health checking

    A process keeps restarting because its liveness check calls an unavailable shared provider. Restarting cannot repair that provider and may make recovery harder. Keep probes focused on the decision they control.

    Liveness asks whether the process needs restarting. Readiness can stop new traffic while ongoing work finishes. Startup probes or allowances can cover warmup. Bound checks and avoid coupling every process restart to independent external failures. A probe response is evidence about that probe, not proof that every critical operation meets its objective. Monitor real useful operations alongside these local signals.

    Think further · How can a disaster drill restore infrastructure yet fail the business recovery requirement?

    Machines can restart while the recovered data is too old, encrypted backups are unreadable, active authority conflicts, or accepted jobs are missing. Check the complete business journey and its RTO/RPO, including keys, state, identity, validation, and useful traffic return. A drill proves only the scenarios it actually exercises.

    Remember: A degraded result must remain a permitted business outcome.

    Try applying it: Why is a cached help page a different fallback from a guessed account balance?

    PART 4 / UNIT 17 / CHAPTER 17.4

    Recover, test & learn from failure

    Prerequisites: 17.3 · Shed load and degrade deliberately8 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    The outage ends when useful service and required state recover. Set recovery objectives, test restores and authority changes, and learn from correlated failure rather than only process restarts.

    17.4.1 · RTO and RPO

    An incident begins at noon. Service returns at 12:20, so the interruption lasted twenty minutes. If recovery restores data only through 11:55, there is five minutes of data-loss exposure relative to the incident point.

    RTO is the recovery time objective. RPO is the recovery point objective, expressing acceptable loss exposure in time. Set them for the business function, then check the whole procedure: detection, decision, restoration, validation, and traffic return. Timing only a file copy misses much of the outage. A faster restore may also use older data, so evaluate the two objectives separately.

    17.4.2 · Backups and restore testing

    A backup survives the lost host, but its only decryption key was on that host. The bytes exist, yet the application cannot recover them. A useful backup needs the surrounding restoration resources too.

    Document credentials, keys, schema versions, retained logs, and the usable recovery environment. Restore actual backups and check business invariants, rather than relying only on job status or checksums. Keep copies separate from the failure they protect against. Live replication can repeat corruption or deletion, while historical backups can support a different recovery point. Specify which role each copy serves and test the corresponding procedure.

    17.4.3 · Failover and failback

    Failover moves service or write authority to a replacement. Failback returns it after repair. Both transitions need valid history, sufficient capacity, routing, and protection from conflicting owners.

    An old primary may need rebuilding from the new history before rejoining. Promote according to the promised data-loss policy, and fence stale writers. Client connections, DNS caches, and retries can continue using old paths after a database promotion succeeds. Test the full user-visible sequence, including return after repair. Recovery is incomplete if traffic looks restored but a later old owner can reintroduce incompatible writes.

    17.4.4 · Multi-zone and multi-region deployments

    Copies in separate zones can survive some local incidents. Separate regions cover other failures but add propagation delay, transfer cost, data-placement concerns, and recovery work.

    Check dependencies that remain shared. A global credential change or configuration fault can still affect all regions. Plan capacity for surviving traffic and catch-up work, not just the normal split. Select placement according to named failure and recovery goals. Geographic distance is one part of independence; the authority protocol and operational dependencies determine whether the locations can actually provide the promised protection.

    17.4.5 · Chaos engineering

    Begin a fault exercise with a question: if a worker pauses past its lease, can its old completion overwrite a new result? Then choose a controlled pause and observe the specified outcome.

    Chaos engineering tests such hypotheses under bounded faults. Define the affected scope, stop conditions, observations, recovery owner, and environment appropriate to the risk. Random process killing without a hypothesis can cause harm without clarifying a mechanism. Increase scope only when justified. A passing drill provides evidence for that scenario and configuration; it does not prove every future failure harmless.

    17.4.6 · SLO-based reliability decisions

    Suppose optional calls consume most of a request's deadline and cause most failures. Removing them from the critical path may improve users' experience more directly than adding another region.

    Use SLO and error-budget evidence to choose reliability work. Keep important low-volume operations visible: their failures can disappear inside a large denominator dominated by cheap successful reads. Segment indicators where the harm differs. More redundancy has both cost and complexity, so evaluate the mechanism it improves. An error budget is a decision aid, rather than permission to ignore a severe failure merely because it affects few events.

    17.4.7 · Cascading failures

    A slow provider holds connections. Waiting requests accumulate, callers retry, and the extra work overloads previously healthy components. This feedback creates a cascading failure.

    Break the actual resource path with deadlines, bounded admission, retry budgets, isolation, and meaningful degradation. Keep capacity for recovery. A breaker that sends every failed request to one fallback can start another cascade. Trace both the original path and the recovery path under correlated failure. Testing each dependency in isolation can miss the interaction that makes a modest initial slowdown become a system-wide outage.

    17.4.8 · Incident analysis and prevention

    After an incident, reconstruct what happened, which conditions allowed it, how it was detected, and what helped or delayed recovery. Stopping at “human error” leaves unanswered why one action could affect every replica.

    A useful analysis connects corrective work to observed mechanisms. Scoped credentials can reduce exposure; tested restores can improve recovery; bounded retries can limit amplification. Give each action an owner and evidence of completion. Avoid adding alerts without a useful response. The aim is to reduce recurrence or harm by changing the system and its operating conditions, rather than attaching blame to the person closest to the trigger.

    Try the mechanism in code

    Python · retry amplification

    attempts_per_layer = 3
independent_retry_layers = 4
assert attempts_per_layer ** independent_retry_layers == 81

    The arithmetic gives 81 permitted downstream attempts in the nested worst case. Actual execution can stop sooner, but failures may activate many layers at once.

    Use an overall retry budget and deadline, protect useful work, and keep operation identity stable. Jitter spreads attempt timing without reducing the configured total by itself.

    Machines can restart while the recovered data is too old, encrypted backups are unreadable, active authority conflicts, or accepted jobs are missing. Check the complete business journey and its RTO/RPO, including keys, state, identity, validation, and useful traffic return. A drill proves only the scenarios it actually exercises.

    Remember: Recovery evidence covers the tested journey and must account for unresolved business effects.

    Try applying it: What could make a fast infrastructure recovery fail the original data-loss requirement?

    PART 5 / UNIT 18 / CHAPTER 18.1

    Threats, identity & authorization

    Prerequisites: Networking Foundations for System Design, Application Architecture and Domain-Driven Design, API Design and Communication Contracts, Data Models and Storage Technologies7 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A tenant administrator guesses another tenant's document ID. Follow identity, permissions, roles, and the trust boundaries the request crosses before deciding which controls are needed.

    18.1.1 · Threat modeling

    Begin with a document service's valuable assets: private files, credentials, processing capacity, and trustworthy audit records. Identify users, workers, administrators, and possible attackers, then ask how each asset could be misused.

    For example, could one tenant guess another's file identifier, forge a processing callback, or submit files that exhaust extraction workers? Threat modelling connects such paths to their impact, controls, and tests. Draw data flows and trust boundaries, but also record the actors' real privileges. Prioritise plausible harmful paths. A diagram alone is incomplete if it leaves unclear what must be protected and who may reach it.

    18.1.2 · Trust boundaries

    A browser submits a document, a worker reads it from storage, and an operator changes production settings. Each crosses a boundary with different expectations about identity, data, and authority.

    A trust boundary marks where those expectations change. Validate the relevant evidence at the boundary rather than assuming a request is legitimate because it came from an internal network. Forwarded identity headers need a configured trusted source. Stored uploads remain untrusted content and may require restricted execution and resource budgets when parsed. Saving bytes does not make their instructions or structure safe for a privileged worker.

    18.1.3 · Authentication vs authorization

    An administrator of tenant A may manage A's documents while having no permission to tenant B's files. Authentication establishes who the actor is. Authorisation checks what that actor may do to the particular resource in context.

    Derive tenant membership from trusted identity evidence and enforce it on reads, edits, exports, and background work. Deny access unless the policy allows it. Difficult-to-guess identifiers can reduce enumeration but cannot replace ownership checks. Test permitted and forbidden paths with two tenants, including overlapping local identifiers. A correct login system does not establish that every later resource lookup is correctly authorised.

    18.1.4 · Sessions, cookies, tokens

    A browser can send a session credential in a cookie. The server may use it to find session state. Another design may verify claims in a token. Cookies describe a browser storage and transport mechanism; they do not alone define the authentication scheme.

    Protect credentials using the appropriate secure transport, cookie attributes, validation, and CSRF controls. Decide how logout, expiry, and revocation work. A signed token may still be expired, intended for another audience, or no longer sufficient for a resource action. Choose a reviewed protocol and library, and validate the fields required by that protocol rather than treating a valid signature as the whole decision.

    18.1.5 · OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect

    An application may ask another service for delegated access using OAuth 2.0. To establish a login identity, OpenID Connect adds an identity layer with its own assertions and validation rules.

    Do not treat an arbitrary access token as proof of identity. Use the appropriate reviewed flow and maintained library, following current guidance such as authorisation code with PKCE where applicable. Validate the issuer, audience, token type, redirects, and required state or nonce evidence for that flow. These requirements differ by role and protocol. Keeping identity and delegated permission distinct prevents a convenient login shortcut from becoming permission to call the wrong API.

    18.1.6 · Role-based and attribute-based access control

    Role-based access control assigns permissions through roles. Attribute-based access control evaluates trusted facts such as tenant, owner, classification, and request context. A service can use both.

    For example, “tenant administrator” must be tied to a tenant. Treating that role as global grants far too much. Roles can become broad, while detailed attribute rules can be harder to explain and test. Keep policy inputs trustworthy and check revocation and queued work. A central policy engine helps only when every required enforcement point calls it correctly. Evaluate the whole path rather than merely choosing a policy language.

    18.1.7 · Least privilege

    An extraction worker needs to read one input and write its output. It does not ordinarily need to list every tenant's files or alter deployment settings. Least privilege gives it the operations and scope required for that job.

    Use separate runtime, deployment, and administrative identities where appropriate. Short-lived scoped credentials can reduce exposure, but need workable refresh and failure behaviour. Review effective inherited permissions as well as the intended role. Emergency access needs its own limits and audit. The useful question is what this identity can actually do now, not only what its description says it should do.

    Think further · What should revocation mean for an issued object capability and a queued export?

    Specify both boundaries. An already issued capability may remain valid until expiry unless the delivery system supports revocation. A queued export may need a current policy check before execution or publication. Keep users informed about the chosen lifetime and ensure workers cannot bypass it using an old submission snapshot.

    Remember: Authenticated identity is an input to resource-specific permission, not permission by itself.

    Try applying it: Which paths must reject a tenant A administrator requesting tenant B data?
