    PART 5 / UNIT 18 / CHAPTER 18.2

    Secrets, encryption & trust boundaries

    Prerequisites: 18.1 · Threats, identity & authorization7 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A stored file is encrypted, but the processing worker can read every file and every key. Examine credentials, cryptography, segmentation, and control placement against the actual threat.

    18.2.1 · Defense in depth

    Tenant-scoped queries, storage permissions, limited object capabilities, worker isolation, and audit records can provide complementary protection for a private document. Defense in depth makes a single control failure less likely to cause the full harm.

    Check independence. If every layer trusts the same client-supplied tenant field without validation, repeating the check adds little. Also examine failure behaviour: a broken policy dependency should not silently disable access controls. Trace which control stops each misuse path and how its result is enforced. Several control names do not necessarily provide several effective barriers.

    18.2.2 · Secrets management

    A secret has a lifecycle: creation, distribution, use, rotation, and revocation. Assign an owner and limit who can read or replace it. Keep credentials out of source, logs, client bundles, and command history.

    Managed identities or short-lived credentials may reduce stored secrets, while still needing bootstrap and outage plans. Rotation can require a period when both old and new versions work, followed by verified retirement. Encrypting a secret file offers little separation if every reader also has its key. The relevant protection comes from actual identity, access, key custody, and operating boundaries.

    18.2.3 · Encryption in transit and at rest

    TLS protects traffic while it travels under its protocol. Encryption at rest protects stored bytes under particular key and access assumptions. Trace where each protection begins and ends.

    A compromised application with legitimate decryption rights may still read the data it is allowed to access. Backups, logs, extracted text, and exports also need appropriate protection; encrypting the original storage does not automatically protect a CSV sent elsewhere. Choose controls for the identified threat and use reviewed cryptographic protocols and libraries. Encryption is one part of access and key design, rather than a replacement for it.

    18.2.4 · Password hashing

    A stolen password database should make each guess expensive. Purpose-built password-hashing algorithms use salts and configurable work, unlike fast general-purpose hashes. Reversible encryption creates a different risk because someone holding the key can recover the passwords.

    Use a maintained implementation and current OWASP guidance. Select parameters for the deployment's hardware and capacity rather than copying one universal textbook value. Store algorithm and parameter information so hashes can be upgraded, and rehash when appropriate. Protect verification and recovery against abuse as well. Password hashing addresses offline guessing; the login and account-recovery paths still need their own controls.

    18.2.5 · Key management and rotation

    Data encrypted with key version one may still be needed after version two becomes active. Key rotation therefore needs a mapping from data to the key version that can decrypt it.

    Key management covers generation, storage, access, rotation, backup, and destruction. Envelope encryption can separate data keys from a key-encryption authority. Verify historical recovery before deleting old versions; retaining every key indefinitely can also conflict with deletion goals. Record the services and datasets depending on each version and test rotation and restore together. Changing the active key is only one step in the lifecycle.

    18.2.6 · Network segmentation

    An upload worker may need storage access but no route to the production administration interface. Network segmentation limits reachable paths and can reduce lateral movement after compromise.

    Outbound rules matter too. A service fetching a user-provided URL might otherwise reach private internal endpoints. Restrict and validate the relevant destinations and behaviours. An allowed network connection still needs appropriate authentication and operation-level permission. Test actual reachability, name resolution, and return paths rather than only reading a firewall-rule description. Network placement supplies one barrier in a wider access design.

    18.2.7 · Zero-trust principles

    A request from an internal address is not automatically trustworthy. Zero-trust principles make identity, resource, action, and context explicit rather than granting implicit access solely from network location.

    Apply limited privileges and inspectable policy at appropriate boundaries. The approach is not one product, and it does not require a new central lookup for every packet. Cached credentials and policy need clear expiry and revocation behaviour. A mesh or VPN can provide useful transport and identity mechanisms while leaving business authorisation to be designed. State what evidence permits each action so the trust assumptions can be reviewed.

    Think further · What should revocation mean for an issued object capability and a queued export?

    Specify both boundaries. An already issued capability may remain valid until expiry unless the delivery system supports revocation. A queued export may need a current policy check before execution or publication. Keep users informed about the chosen lifetime and ensure workers cannot bypass it using an old submission snapshot.

    Remember: Security depends on real access and key boundaries, including how they fail and rotate.

    Try applying it: Which recovery assets become useless if their only decryption key is lost?

    PART 5 / UNIT 18 / CHAPTER 18.3

    Tenant isolation, audit & deletion

    Prerequisites: 18.2 · Secrets, encryption & trust boundaries5 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A correct API query is followed by a badly scoped cache or export. Carry tenant policy and minimal data through every copy, audit event, and deletion stage.

    18.3.1 · API security and common vulnerabilities

    A parameterised query can prevent a value from becoming SQL syntax. It does not establish whether the actor may read the selected row. Input safety and object authorisation address different risks.

    Review excessive data exposure, unsafe resource use, injection, and server-side requests alongside ownership checks. Bound expensive exports and validate destinations used for callbacks or fetches. Test attempts to change protected properties, cross tenant boundaries, bypass quotas, or call privileged operations. A syntactically valid request can still be harmful. Follow how accepted input is used, rather than stopping the review after parsing.

    18.3.2 · Multi-tenant isolation

    A document lookup checks tenant membership correctly, but a shared cache uses only document_id as its key. A result saved for tenant A can now be returned on tenant B's path. Isolation failed outside the database query.

    Carry trusted tenant context through caches, queues, object URLs, search, exports, telemetry, and administration. Recheck resource relationships instead of trusting arbitrary tenant values in job messages. Composite keys and database policies can add enforcement when configured correctly. Test two tenants and every route by which their data travels. Isolation is an end-to-end property of those paths, not a single filter.

    18.3.3 · Data minimization

    A diagnostic event may need an operation identifier and error class, but not the full document or access token. Data minimisation asks which information is necessary for a defined purpose.

    Collecting less sensitive data reduces exposure and makes retention and deletion easier. Avoid storing fields just because they might be interesting later. Record the intended use, permitted readers, retention, and derived uses. This is an architectural choice made when designing messages, logs, and storage—not merely a later policy document. Retain enough to operate the service while deliberately excluding unnecessary private content.

    18.3.4 · Audit trails

    An administrator exports a private dataset. An audit trail should identify the actor, scope, target, action, and outcome, with useful time or sequence information. It should also resist inappropriate alteration by the people whose actions it records.

    Store necessary identifiers and context rather than complete sensitive payloads. A “request received” record does not prove the export completed or a change committed. Record the relevant outcome boundary and reconcile interrupted privileged operations. Protect access and retention of audit data itself. Trustworthy evidence requires clear event meanings as well as an append path.

    18.3.5 · Privacy, retention, and deletion

    Deleting a record can require work in objects, indexes, caches, and recoverable copies. If the API reports completion, specify whether all required work finished or whether a durable deletion request has merely been accepted.

    Track multi-store deletion progress and recovery. Test that old snapshots and replay do not recreate removed content without applying the deletion history. Privacy requirements vary by organisation and jurisdiction and need the appropriate review; this architecture lesson does not supply legal rules. It explains how collection, access, correction, retention, and deletion become concrete state transitions across the system's copies.

    Think further · What should revocation mean for an issued object capability and a queued export?

    Specify both boundaries. An already issued capability may remain valid until expiry unless the delivery system supports revocation. A queued export may need a current policy check before execution or publication. Keep users informed about the chosen lifetime and ensure workers cannot bypass it using an old submission snapshot.

    Remember: Isolation and privacy are lifecycle properties across the whole data path.

    Try applying it: Which derived records could survive a delete that removes only the original file?

    PART 5 / UNIT 18 / CHAPTER 18.4

    Supply chains and security reviews

    Prerequisites: 18.3 · Tenant isolation, audit & deletion4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A trusted artifact still needs a controlled route to production, and users need workable safe recovery. Review the complete sensitive journey and the assumptions its controls depend on.

    18.4.1 · Supply-chain security

    A trusted release depends on more than application source. Build tools, dependencies, artifacts, deployment credentials, and update mechanisms form its supply chain.

    Control dependency resolution, verify artifact identity, and limit build and runtime privileges. A signature proves a signing relationship, not that the signed code is harmless. Keep provenance and a way to respond to vulnerable or compromised releases. Untrusted contribution builds should not gain deployment secrets merely because trusted branch builds use them. Trace how code becomes a running artifact, identifying who can change each step and what evidence the next step checks.

    18.4.2 · Security vs usability trade-offs

    An account-recovery rule can be so difficult that legitimate users invent unsafe workarounds. Conversely, a convenient shortcut granting every administrator global access can break tenant isolation. Evaluate the actual user journey and threat.

    Safe defaults, scoped administration, understandable recovery, and proportionate extra verification can improve both protection and usability. Keep mandatory constraints explicit: convenience scores cannot justify cross-tenant disclosure. Examine fallback behaviour as carefully as normal login. A security control succeeds when people can use the supported safe path and the system continues to enforce the required boundaries.

    18.4.3 · Secure-by-design reviews

    Follow a sensitive export from request to download. Check the caller and tenant, filtered resources, queued context, worker permissions, output object, download capability lifetime, and audit result.

    Then change the conditions: membership is revoked after enqueue, a worker retries after cancellation, or deletion starts before publication. The chosen policy must determine what happens at each later boundary. Record who owns each control and how it is checked. A review checklist aids coverage, while tests and configurations provide evidence. “Secure by design” should describe this reasoning and enforcement, rather than an unsupported label attached to the architecture.

    Try the mechanism in code

    Python · synthetic tenant policy

    from mechanisms import permit_demo
actor = {"tenant":"A", "active":True, "actions":["read"]}
assert permit_demo(actor, {"tenant":"A"}, "read")
assert not permit_demo(actor, {"tenant":"B"}, "read")

    The predicate permits the same-tenant read and rejects tenant A reading tenant B. It assumes the supplied actor and resource attributes are already trustworthy.

    This is authorisation logic, not credential validation. Every object, queue, cache, and export path must enforce the relevant rule with valid context.

    Download the executable mechanism collection ↓ · Follow the connected complete design →

    Think further · What should revocation mean for an issued object capability and a queued export?

    Specify both boundaries. An already issued capability may remain valid until expiry unless the delivery system supports revocation. A queued export may need a current policy check before execution or publication. Keep users informed about the chosen lifetime and ensure workers cannot bypass it using an old submission snapshot.

    Remember: Secure design joins threat-specific controls with actual enforcement and testable outcomes.

    Try applying it: What must happen if membership is revoked after a private export is queued?

    PART 5 / UNIT 19 / CHAPTER 19.1

    Observe behavior with three signals

    Prerequisites: Requirements, Estimation, and Engineering Trade-offs, Networking Foundations for System Design, Runtime, Processes, Threads, and Concurrency, Database Internals, Transactions, and Concurrency Control6 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A user waits while CPU looks normal. Combine population measurements, individual timelines, and structured events to find the work or wait the dashboard missed.

    19.1.1 · Monitoring vs observability

    A user waits five seconds for a payment request while the CPU dashboard looks normal. Monitoring the CPU told us about one known signal; it did not explain the user's wait.

    Monitoring tracks selected conditions. Observability emphasises being able to explain behaviour using the system's outputs and instrumentation. These are useful emphases rather than universal product boundaries. Start from an operation and connect its work, waiting, dependencies, and state changes. Collect evidence that supports questions and actions. More telemetry is not automatically more understanding, particularly when it is uncorrelated or hides the business outcome.

    19.1.2 · Logs, metrics, and traces

    A latency histogram shows that many requests are slow. A trace reveals where one of them waited. A structured log explains the error returned by a particular attempt. Metrics, traces, and logs answer complementary questions.

    Logs record events; metrics aggregate measurements; traces connect work along an execution path. Sampling, dropped records, clock differences, and privacy limits affect what each can establish. Use stable operation identities where appropriate to connect detailed evidence. Avoid turning every unique identifier into a metric label. Combine population-level measurements with individual histories rather than expecting one trace or log line to describe every user.

    19.1.3 · Structured logging

    Instead of a free-form line such as “payment failed,” record named fields: event type, operation identity, outcome class, and relevant duration or safe scope. Structured logging makes their meanings easier to query consistently.

    A start event and a committed outcome are different observations. If a finish event is missing, the process might have stopped, but that absence does not identify the payment's remote result. Keep credentials and raw private documents out of routine logs. Bound message sizes and volume so an error burst cannot turn logging itself into the next outage. Record enough to investigate with a clear purpose and retention policy.

    19.1.4 · Distributed tracing

    A five-second trace shows 4.6 seconds acquiring a database connection. Optimising SQL execution is unlikely to remove most of that wait. Instrument the acquisition and queue intervals so the trace exposes them separately.

    Distributed tracing connects spans for work and waits across components. Asynchronous jobs may need links rather than a parent relationship implying they finished within the original request. A trace is one execution, possibly sampled. Compare it with normal traces, errors, and distributions before concluding that the same explanation covers the population. The useful result is a supported location for delay, not just a coloured timeline.

    19.1.5 · Trace IDs, span IDs, context propagation

    A trace identifier connects related spans; each span identifier names a particular piece of work. Context propagation carries the needed relationships over calls and messages.

    Incoming context can be untrusted. Validate or replace it according to policy, and never treat a trace identifier as permission to access a resource. For queued work, preserve appropriate correlation or links across the request and later attempts. Standard formats aid interoperability but do not instrument every library automatically. Check that each transport actually carries the context and that sensitive user data is not smuggled into it as a convenient correlation field.

    19.1.6 · Golden signals

    Traffic rises, queues grow, and responses become slower while errors initially remain low. Looking only at failure counts would miss the developing problem. Golden signals commonly combine latency, traffic, errors, and saturation.

    Define useful responses and eligible work, rather than counting every HTTP 200 as business success. Break down important operations where high-volume cheap calls could hide low-volume critical failures. Interpret resource pressure alongside user outcomes. These signals organise investigation, while workload-specific measures such as oldest unresolved payment age can reveal harm outside the ordinary request-response path.

    Think further · What evidence would support a latency explanation beyond correlation with a release?

    Locate the extra wait or execution on affected paths, compare normal and slow populations, inspect resource saturation and changed behaviour, and test a focused intervention. A release marker is a clue. Evidence is stronger when the mechanism predicts the symptom and the correction changes that mechanism under comparable conditions.

    Remember: Useful telemetry connects a user-visible outcome to its resource and state path.

    Try applying it: What can a trace show that a latency histogram cannot, and what can the histogram show that one trace cannot?

    PART 5 / UNIT 19 / CHAPTER 19.2

    Choose indicators, budgets & alerts

    Prerequisites: 19.1 · Observe behavior with three signals5 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A full pool creates long waits, but paging on every CPU fluctuation overwhelms responders. Choose bounded evidence, indicators, and alerts that support a particular operating decision.

    19.2.1 · RED and USE methods

    RED examines rate, errors, and duration for request-serving components. USE examines utilisation, saturation, and errors for resources. Apply the perspective that fits the question being asked.

    A full connection pool can delay requests while CPU stays low. USE points attention to the saturated pool; RED shows the resulting duration and error behaviour. Use sufficient time detail and per-owner views to find bursts or hot shards hidden by averages. Neither method replaces domain indicators. A queue of uncertain charges can need action even while the general web service looks healthy.

    19.2.2 · SLIs, SLOs, error budgets

    For a 99.9% success target, the allowed bad-event rate is 0.1%. If 1% of eligible events fail during an interval, the service spends that budget at ten times the allowed rate. This is tenfold error-budget burn.

    An SLI measures the behaviour; an SLO sets its target and window; the error budget expresses the allowed shortfall. Define both good and eligible events, including relevant failures. Segment critical operations when one denominator hides their harm. Handle low-volume indicators thoughtfully. The objective guides service decisions over its population and window; it is not a promise that every individual request succeeds.

    19.2.3 · Alert design and alert fatigue

    An alert should lead someone to a useful action. Repeated pages about isolated CPU spikes can distract responders, while sustained rapid budget consumption may indicate immediate user harm.

    Choose windows and thresholds suited to the response time and objective. Assign an owner, include context, and provide a runbook for urgent cases. Avoid a series of alerts that all demand the same action during known degradation. Review missed incidents and unnecessary pages, not just the number configured. Alerting is an operating workload, so its value includes helping people recognise and mitigate the right problem promptly.

    19.2.4 · Sampling and telemetry cost

    Keeping every trace forever may cost too much. Head sampling chooses early; tail sampling can use later observations such as duration or failure, but needs buffering and processing capacity.

    Sampling and retention change which questions can be answered. Unique request IDs as ordinary metric labels can create unbounded numbers of series. Put detailed identities in suitable logs or traces and use bounded metric dimensions. Protect telemetry ingestion during failure bursts, when both volume and need can rise. Select a strategy according to diagnostic purpose, cost, and privacy instead of treating either maximum collection or maximum reduction as the default goal.

    19.2.5 · Dashboards

    Begin a dashboard with a decision: is the service meeting its objective, what changed, or which resource needs capacity? Show the relevant user outcomes before unrelated infrastructure measurements.

    Include units, denominators, windows, deployment markers, and data gaps. A line without a stable definition can mislead during an incident. Provide useful drill-downs and ownership rather than hundreds of equal-priority panels. Check the dashboard against known examples or earlier incidents. The purpose is to shorten a reasoning path from symptom to action, not simply display all available measurements on one screen.

    Think further · What evidence would support a latency explanation beyond correlation with a release?

    Locate the extra wait or execution on affected paths, compare normal and slow populations, inspect resource saturation and changed behaviour, and test a focused intervention. A release marker is a clue. Evidence is stronger when the mechanism predicts the symptom and the correction changes that mechanism under comparable conditions.

    Remember: Measure the relevant denominator and make each urgent signal actionable.

    Try applying it: Why should a unique request ID usually stay out of a general metric label?

    PART 5 / UNIT 19 / CHAPTER 19.3

    Profile and investigate production

    Prerequisites: 19.2 · Choose indicators, budgets & alerts5 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A deployment precedes a slowdown, but correlation is only a clue. Use profiles, traces, query evidence, and a coordinated response to test explanations and restore useful service.

    19.3.1 · Profiling

    A profiler can show where CPU samples occur, where allocations grow, or where threads block. Under a representative workload, this can reveal repeated parsing or lock contention missed by coarse request metrics.

    Choose a method with acceptable overhead and privacy behaviour. A function consuming most CPU is not necessarily responsible for most response time if requests spend longer waiting on I/O. Compare profiles with traces and completion rates. Make a focused change, then measure again. Profiling is most useful when it tests an explanation about an actual bottleneck rather than producing a ranking to optimise blindly.

    19.3.2 · Query and application performance diagnosis

    Split a slow request into queue wait, connection acquisition, lock wait, query execution, network transfer, and encoding. This gives plausible causes a place in the path.

    If p99 grows from 200 ms to five seconds with modest CPU, a full pool or lock may be responsible, but evidence must distinguish them. Compare slow and normal requests and recent changes. Preserve useful evidence before restarting components, and assess whether a restart would add load or erase diagnostic state. Diagnosis narrows a hypothesis with observations; a familiar symptom alone does not establish its cause.

    19.3.3 · Incident response

    During a complex incident, coordinate mitigation, communication, evidence, and decision ownership. Keep a timeline and limit unrelated changes so the situation remains understandable.

    Choose an intervention that restores useful service while protecting state. Code rollback may be unsafe after an incompatible data migration. Track pending business outcomes after infrastructure recovers: unresolved provider charges still require reconciliation. A stopped alert does not by itself close those outcomes. Scale incident leadership and communication to the event's complexity, keeping a clear owner for decisions and follow-up work.

    19.3.4 · On-call and runbooks

    A runbook saying only “restart the service” leaves diagnosis, risk, and verification to the responder. A useful runbook explains what to inspect, which actions are supported, when to stop, and how to confirm recovery.

    On-call also needs access, escalation, rehearsal, and sustainable ownership. Audit emergency access. Let service owners reduce recurring failure mechanisms instead of merely extending instructions for repeated manual repair. If nightly reconciliation or cache rebuilding is constantly needed, that operating burden is evidence about the architecture. Good instructions help people operate it; persistent toil may require changing the system itself.

    19.3.5 · Root-cause investigation

    A failure follows a deployment, but the deployment may only be the trigger. An unbounded queue or incompatible schema can explain why that change caused widespread harm.

    Test explanations against the timeline and affected requests. Ask which resource or state transition connects the suspected cause to the observation, and whether the proposed fix changes that mechanism. Correlation starts an investigation; it does not complete it. Several contributing conditions are common. Keeping them visible leads to stronger prevention than choosing one short label that hides why detection, isolation, or recovery also failed.

    Think further · What evidence would support a latency explanation beyond correlation with a release?

    Locate the extra wait or execution on affected paths, compare normal and slow populations, inspect resource saturation and changed behaviour, and test a focused intervention. A release marker is a clue. Evidence is stronger when the mechanism predicts the symptom and the correction changes that mechanism under comparable conditions.

    Remember: Separate triggers from mechanisms and preserve correctness while mitigating harm.

    Try applying it: Which evidence would distinguish a slow query from a long wait to acquire its connection?

    PART 5 / UNIT 19 / CHAPTER 19.4

    Learn from incidents and trace async work

    Prerequisites: 19.3 · Profile and investigate production4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    An asynchronous job remains unresolved after HTTP serving recovers. Follow the accepted operation through its later attempts, and use incident evidence to improve the system that owns it.

    19.4.1 · Blameless postmortems

    A blameless postmortem records impact, timeline, detection, mitigation, and contributing conditions using what people knew at the time. Include the measures that helped as well as the gaps.

    “Be more careful” supplies no change to the failure mechanism. Assign specific corrective work with an owner and evidence that it changes future behaviour. Explain why safeguards failed to prevent or limit harm, and avoid exposing unnecessary customer or employee information. The document should help the team reason about recurrence and recovery, rather than turn hindsight into a judgment of the nearest individual.

    19.4.2 · Capacity monitoring

    A fleet's average CPU is low while one shard fills its disk and a connection pool stays saturated. Capacity monitoring needs the resources and owners that can actually limit service.

    Track rates, queue age, growth, and surviving capacity under failure. Include background costs such as compaction, backup, and migration. Alert early enough for the available response: a disk growing faster than procurement is a different risk from a short CPU burst. Keep uncertainty in forecasts and revise them when traffic patterns or releases change. A useful forecast includes both the approaching limit and the time needed to act.

    19.4.3 · Observability across asynchronous workflows

    An HTTP request returns 202 in a few milliseconds, but its extraction job waits for hours. Measuring acceptance latency alone misses the service the user actually requested.

    Follow the stable operation identity through submission, delivery, attempts, stage commits, retries, and final outcome. Separate queue delay from processing duration and record stale or duplicate attempt rejection. Define completion age and success at the business boundary. Provide a way to locate stuck work across brokers, workers, stores, and providers. Asynchronous observability extends the history beyond the original connection so accepted work does not disappear from view.

    Try the mechanism in code

    Python · one trace accounting model

    stages_ms = {"other":300, "pool_wait":4600, "query":100}
assert sum(stages_ms.values()) == 5000
assert stages_ms["pool_wait"] / sum(stages_ms.values()) == .92

    Pool acquisition takes 4,600 of 5,000 ms, or 92% of this request's elapsed time. The query itself accounts for only 100 ms.

    Investigate hold times, locks, and the wider population before attributing the whole incident to one trace. The arithmetic locates the wait but does not establish why the pool is full.

    Download the executable mechanism collection ↓ · Follow the connected complete design →

    Think further · What evidence would support a latency explanation beyond correlation with a release?

    Locate the extra wait or execution on affected paths, compare normal and slow populations, inspect resource saturation and changed behaviour, and test a focused intervention. A release marker is a clue. Evidence is stronger when the mechanism predicts the symptom and the correction changes that mechanism under comparable conditions.

    Remember: Operation age, outcomes, and recovery conditions extend beyond the original request.

    Try applying it: What should an on-call engineer inspect when acceptance is healthy but document completion has stopped?

    PART 5 / UNIT 20 / CHAPTER 20.1

    Environments, VMs & containers

    Prerequisites: Networking Foundations for System Design, Application Architecture and Domain-Driven Design, Reliability, Fault Tolerance, and Disaster Recovery, Security Architecture and Privacy, Observability, Monitoring, and Incident Engineering4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    The same image works locally and fails in production. Compare environments and runtime isolation, keeping persistent state, resources, and platform duties explicit.

    20.1.1 · Development vs staging vs production

    A service passes development tests but fails in production because its network permissions and connection limits differ. Development, staging, and production have different purposes, yet the relevant behaviours need deliberate compatibility.

    Use staging to exercise protocols, identity, migrations, and failure paths with appropriate test data and secrets. Exact production scale may be impractical, so record what staging cannot establish. Separate environment values from business meaning. A local pass is evidence for that environment; it does not prove storage, network, or load behaviour elsewhere. Make the differences visible enough that release checks can address the important ones.

    20.1.2 · Virtual machines vs containers

    A virtual machine presents virtualised hardware and a guest operating system. A container commonly isolates processes while sharing the host kernel. Both provide useful boundaries, but their isolation and operating responsibilities differ.

    Choose using workload, expertise, startup behaviour, and required separation. Images, identity, networking, storage, and resource limits need design in either case. Several containers on one host still share its failure and capacity. VM boundaries also sit on shared physical and administrative infrastructure. Identify the actual threat and failure model rather than treating either packaging label as complete isolation.

    20.1.3 · Container fundamentals

    A container packages an executable environment. Runtime settings then restrict its CPU, memory, files, and network access. Packaging helps repeatability when image and configuration are controlled.

    Required persistent data should not live only in an ephemeral writable layer that disappears on replacement. Resource limits can also throttle or terminate work, so preserve necessary progress and handle shutdown. Broad host mounts or privileged execution can weaken the intended isolation. Inspect the actual runtime permissions and persistence path. A reproducible image is one input to a predictable service, alongside configuration, state, and operating policy.

    20.1.4 · Kubernetes fundamentals

    Kubernetes controllers compare declared objects with observed cluster state and work to reconcile differences. Pods, scheduling, services, and node agents provide primitives for running and locating workloads.

    The platform does not infer an application's transaction invariants or create its tested backups and access model automatically. Identify which cluster responsibilities the team operates and which a provider manages. An orchestrator adds a control plane and a substantial configuration surface. If simpler deployment machinery meets the requirements, that can be a reasonable choice. Adopt platform facilities for their concrete benefits while retaining ownership of application behaviour and recovery.

    Think further · How can rollback restore old code while leaving incompatible data or effects?

    Old code can return while new schemas, values, provider calls, and published messages remain. Maintain compatibility during overlap and identify the point where contraction ends safe rollback. Some outcomes need forward repair or compensation. Restoring an artifact cannot reverse every state transition it previously performed.

    Remember: Packaging improves repeatability only with controlled configuration and appropriate state ownership.

    Try applying it: Which data would disappear if a container's writable layer were replaced?

    PART 5 / UNIT 20 / CHAPTER 20.2

    Control planes, scheduling & configuration

    Prerequisites: 20.1 · Environments, VMs & containers5 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    The scheduler cannot place new work, but existing requests still succeed. Separate control and serving paths, then examine startup, scaling, configuration, and replacement dependencies.

    20.2.1 · Control plane vs data plane

    The control plane decides placement and configuration. The data plane carries the running application's traffic. Under some conditions, a control-plane outage stops new scheduling while already running workloads continue.

    Draw both paths. A request that unnecessarily performs a synchronous configuration lookup can turn a control-plane problem into a serving outage. Cached values need validity and update rules, particularly for permission changes. Recovery also may need a configuration or credential service before replacements can start. A redundant data path is useful only when its required startup and authority dependencies are understood.

    20.2.2 · Scheduling and service discovery

    A scheduler assigns a workload to eligible resources. Its decisions can consider capacity, affinity, anti-affinity, and failure domains. Service discovery later helps callers locate the running endpoints.

    A scheduled process may still be starting and not ready for traffic. Discovery can lag both startup and termination, so clients need bounded handling of stale endpoints. Placement also says nothing about shared-data correctness: two healthy replicas can each point to an unrelated local database. State the storage and readiness contracts alongside the scheduling rule. Successful placement establishes where work runs, rather than that the whole application state is coordinated.

    20.2.3 · Autoscaling

    Scaling up creates more workers, but each may open additional database connections. If the database is already saturated, the extra concurrency can worsen the queue. Scale useful capacity while respecting downstream limits.

    Choose signals appropriate to the workload and include warmup, minimum capacity, and maximum spend. Scaling down needs draining: stop accepting new work, finish or transfer durable jobs, and release resources. Killing an unrecorded background task loses it. Autoscaling during retries also needs care, because attempt traffic can rise while useful demand is unchanged. The platform and application admission rules should act together.

    20.2.4 · Configuration and secret delivery

    A bad configuration can disable every otherwise healthy replica without changing application code. Treat configuration delivery as a versioned, validated operation with a recovery path.

    Roll out risky changes in a controlled way and record the effective version in telemetry. Some settings can reload safely; others require replacing connections or processes. Secrets need stricter access and logging controls than ordinary values. Verify that the application actually uses the intended version. This gives an incident investigation something concrete to compare with the time the behaviour changed.

    20.2.5 · Immutable infrastructure

    Instead of manually changing a server until it works, immutable infrastructure replaces it from a defined artifact and configuration. Repeatability improves when provisioning and inputs are controlled.

    Runtime data still changes, and rollback still depends on compatible state. Keep persistence and migrations explicit. If an emergency edit is needed, capture it in the maintained configuration so replacement does not lose it or recreate drift. Check the running artifact and values as well as the deployment's intention. Rebuilding the same machine definition does not automatically restore its lost data or reverse an external effect.

    Think further · How can rollback restore old code while leaving incompatible data or effects?

    Old code can return while new schemas, values, provider calls, and published messages remain. Maintain compatibility during overlap and identify the point where contraction ends safe rollback. Some outcomes need forward repair or compensation. Restoring an artifact cannot reverse every state transition it previously performed.

    Remember: Running traffic and creating replacement capacity can depend on different paths.

    Try applying it: Which dependency could let current instances serve while preventing every replacement from starting?

    PART 5 / UNIT 20 / CHAPTER 20.3

    Releases, flags & schema migrations

    Prerequisites: 20.2 · Control planes, scheduling & configuration6 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A release writes a new field, then a rollback restores a reader that cannot understand it. Keep artifacts, flags, configuration, and migration stages compatible while versions overlap.

    20.3.1 · Infrastructure as Code

    Infrastructure as Code makes resource definitions and policies reviewable and repeatable. A change plan can reveal proposed replacements, but the real effect depends on provider behaviour, stored state, privileges, and drift.

    A resource replacement can be destructive for a stateful service. Understand lifecycle and recovery before applying it. Coordinate concurrent updates and protect secrets outside ordinary tracked values. Verify the resulting state. Also preserve the state information and credentials needed to recover the infrastructure definition itself. Code is a useful source of desired configuration, while restoration remains an operating procedure with dependencies.

    20.3.2 · CI/CD

    Continuous integration checks changes. Delivery prepares a releasable artifact, and deployment places that artifact into an environment. Preserve identity from the source through the built artifact to the version actually running.

    Use scoped pipeline permissions and meaningful checks for the release risks. A test in one environment may miss mixed-version traffic during a database migration. Keep untrusted build input away from release secrets. Automation reduces manual variation, but its own partial failures need a supported recovery path. A green pipeline is evidence of its defined checks, rather than proof of every production assumption.

    20.3.3 · Rolling, blue-green, and canary deployments

    Rolling deployment replaces instances gradually. Blue-green prepares another environment before switching traffic. Canary sends a controlled traffic subset to the new version before wider exposure.

    Each needs compatible state, draining, spare capacity, and verification. A canary receiving only cheap requests can miss an expensive-path regression. Choose cohorts and stop conditions using the meaningful outcomes. Blue-green can duplicate application capacity while both versions still share one mutable database; switching traffic back does not reverse its changes. Select the release arrangement according to the risk and operating cost, including the data transition.

    20.3.4 · Feature flags

    A feature flag can release code separately from exposing a behaviour. Give the flag an owner, scope, safe default, observable state, and removal plan. Combinations of flags also create combinations to test.

    The flag is not authorisation. A browser-controlled setting must not grant a privileged server operation. Consider disabling after the feature has written a new data format: older code may still need to understand it. Keep state compatibility and migration separate from the exposure switch. Flags offer control over some transitions, while stale flags and hidden configuration can accumulate their own complexity.

    20.3.5 · Rollbacks and database migrations

    A release removes a database column. Rolling back its code now restores a reader that needs the missing column. The old artifact exists, but the state is no longer compatible with it.

    Expand-and-contract avoids this abrupt transition. Add compatible structures, deploy code that tolerates the overlap, backfill with bounded resumable work, and verify. Remove old structures only after old readers are gone. Mark when rollback stops being supported. Code, configuration, schema, and external effects have different reversal rules, so a rollback procedure must name the assumptions it relies on.

    20.3.6 · Multi-environment configuration

    Production uses different endpoints and credentials from staging. Those are environment values. The meaning of a payment amount should remain the same unless a deliberate business policy says otherwise.

    Validate required fields and types at startup or controlled reload. Use explicit versions and careful defaults for security and retention. An absent value should fail clearly when guessing could route data to the wrong region or tenant. Avoid scattered environment-specific conditionals that no test setup reproduces. Keep the effective configuration understandable so differences between environments are intentional rather than accidental business semantics.

    Think further · How can rollback restore old code while leaving incompatible data or effects?

    Old code can return while new schemas, values, provider calls, and published messages remain. Maintain compatibility during overlap and identify the point where contraction ends safe rollback. Some outcomes need forward repair or compensation. Restoring an artifact cannot reverse every state transition it previously performed.

    Remember: Release safety includes data and protocol transitions, not only selecting an old executable.

    Try applying it: At what point in expand-and-contract does rollback to the old reader become unsafe?

    PART 5 / UNIT 20 / CHAPTER 20.4

    Platforms, serverless & ownership

    Prerequisites: 20.3 · Releases, flags & schema migrations6 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A managed platform offers useful capabilities while leaving application choices in your hands. Compare delegated work, limits, topologies, and internal developer needs under the same service requirements.

    20.4.1 · Twelve-Factor App principles

    The Twelve-Factor App describes operational practices such as explicit dependencies and configuration, backing-service treatment, process discipline, and logs as event streams. These ideas can improve repeatability for suitable service applications.

    They are methodology rather than a universal proof of quality. Stateful work and current platforms still need explicit persistence, identity, limits, and recovery. Apply each practice's purpose to the actual workload. Checking twelve labels does not establish authorisation, transaction correctness, or usable backups. A design remains accountable to its requirements and observed behaviour, even when it follows a well-known set of conventions.

    20.4.2 · Serverless compute

    A function platform manages some provisioning and invocation work. An activity can still time out, restart, or be invoked again. Rapid scaling may also create too many concurrent calls to one database.

    Externalise required state, bound downstream concurrency, and use operation identities for effects. Compare startup delay, sustained cost, portability, and remaining operating work with container or VM alternatives. The application still needs monitoring and secure access. “Serverless” describes a delegation arrangement, not unlimited capacity or absence of failures. Use it where its execution model suits the work and its recovery requirements.

    20.4.3 · Cloud vs on-premises trade-offs

    Cloud and on-premises operation place responsibilities in different hands. Compare procurement delay, expertise, networking, data placement, managed capabilities, recovery, and exit costs for the same workload.

    Cloud capacity remains subject to quotas and provisioning time. Predictable owned capacity can be efficient in some circumstances but requires equipment and disaster management. Avoid generic cheapest-provider claims without current rates and full assumptions. The atlas uses hypothetical cost units for arithmetic; a procurement choice needs actual quotations and organisational requirements. The useful comparison is the complete operating arrangement rather than one machine price.

    20.4.4 · Infrastructure ownership and managed services

    A provider manages database patching and replication. The application team still chooses data access, schema, acknowledgment settings, retention, and how recovery is validated. Managed service means selected responsibilities have moved, not that business responsibility has disappeared.

    Read the actual contract and failure boundaries. Self-management offers control while requiring expertise and on-call work. In either arrangement, test client behaviour during maintenance, throttling, failover, and credential changes. List what the team still owns. That makes cost and staffing comparisons more accurate than describing an entire system as simply managed or self-hosted.

    20.4.5 · Deployment topologies and networking

    A module diagram shows application responsibilities. A deployment topology shows their processes, machines, zones, networks, data, and trust boundaries. It reveals whether two replicas share the same host or storage dependency.

    Include relevant ingress, egress, encryption termination, private routes, and operating access. Follow the loss of one placement: how does a replacement obtain its configuration and state? Label whether arrows represent traffic, control, or another dependency. The purpose is to explain actual communication and failure relationships, rather than redraw logical boxes with infrastructure logos.

    20.4.6 · Platform engineering basics

    A platform team can offer a reusable way to build artifacts, obtain identity, emit telemetry, and deploy with tested defaults. Platform engineering treats development teams as users of those capabilities.

    Provide understandable limits, ownership, and supported escape paths for different workloads. An opaque mandatory framework can hide decisions that application teams still need to make. Measure useful adoption, reliability, and operating burden rather than only the number of internal tools created. A platform abstraction earns its place when it reduces repeated work while exposing the failure and resource behaviour relevant to its users.

    Try the mechanism in code

    Pseudocode · safe release progression

    add_compatible_schema_field()
deploy_mixed_version_safe_code()
backfill_with_bounded_progress()
verify_old_and_new_readers()
retire_old_readers()
remove_obsolete_schema_only_when_safe()

    Old and new readers coexist during compatible expansion and backfill. Retire old readers before removing the structures they need.

    Rollback is safe only while its state and protocol assumptions still hold. Destructive contraction or external effects may require forward repair. Verify the actual running artifact and configuration too.

    Old code can return while new schemas, values, provider calls, and published messages remain. Maintain compatibility during overlap and identify the point where contraction ends safe rollback. Some outcomes need forward repair or compensation. Restoring an artifact cannot reverse every state transition it previously performed.

    Remember: A platform abstraction should simplify repeated work while exposing the limits its users must manage.

    Try applying it: Which correctness and recovery responsibilities remain with a team using a managed database?

    PART 5 / UNIT 21 / CHAPTER 21.1

    Budgets, bottlenecks & honest benchmarks

    Prerequisites: Requirements, Estimation, and Engineering Trade-offs, Runtime, Processes, Threads, and Concurrency, Database Internals, Transactions, and Concurrency Control, Scalability, Load Balancing, and Data Distribution, Reliability, Fault Tolerance, and Disaster Recovery, Observability, Monitoring, and Incident Engineering, Deployment, Cloud Infrastructure, and Platform Architecture6 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A service misses its response-time goal. Budget the path, locate the limit, and design a benchmark that can test the proposed explanation without hiding waiting or errors.

    21.1.1 · Performance budgets

    Assume a request has a 200 ms budget: 30 ms for edge and network, 20 ms for queues, 100 ms for data access, and 50 ms for computation and response. These allocations add to the end-to-end target.

    A performance budget makes the expected costs visible before implementation. Validate the assumed allocations with measurements under the stated workload. Include connection waits, encoding, tails, and failure paths, rather than budgeting only the main query. Work that exhausts the budget before reaching the query still matters to the user. A proposed allocation is an objective to check, not a measured result.

    21.1.2 · CPU, memory, disk, network, and database bottlenecks

    A slow request may compute heavily, wait on disk, wait for a lock, or queue for a database connection. High CPU suggests one set of hypotheses; low CPU does not rule out a severe delay.

    Trace the critical path and resource queues. Memory pressure can cause allocation stalls or termination, while transfer volume can saturate a network. A bottleneck tree organises possible explanations so measurements can distinguish them. Change the component implicated by the evidence rather than adjusting everything at once. An improvement can reveal another limit, so repeat the observation after the change.

    21.1.3 · Profiling and benchmarking

    A profile shows where runtime work occurs. A benchmark compares behaviour under chosen conditions. To make a result useful, record the workload, data distribution, capacity, versions, warmup, concurrency, duration, and success criteria.

    A fast isolated function does not establish application throughput. Include variability, failures, and resource cost, and compare equivalent service promises. Preserve enough setup to reproduce a change in behaviour after a dependency or schema update. The value of a benchmark is the question it answers under its conditions, rather than the size of its most impressive number.

    21.1.4 · Load, stress, spike, and soak testing

    A load test checks expected demand. A stress test explores limits. A spike test examines abrupt changes, while a soak test looks for long-duration effects such as leaks or compaction backlog.

    Choose the test for the uncertainty. Also inspect the generator: one that waits for each slow reply may stop issuing traffic that real users would continue to send. Check its own capacity and record errors, abandonment, waiting, and correct business results. High request throughput with lost reservations is a failed correctness test. Each measurement needs a workload and an outcome definition that match the claim being investigated.

    21.1.5 · Benchmark methodology and statistical pitfalls

    A generator waits for a slow response before sending the next request, although real arrivals would continue independently. The test omits some waiting that users would experience. This is a common form of coordinated omission.

    Other pitfalls include tiny samples, unrealistic data, undisclosed warm caches, omitted failures, and incompatible versions. Report the method and distributions with appropriate precision. Change one factor or use a justified experimental design. A result supports the tested conditions; a different traffic mix, failure state, or data distribution may produce another outcome. Preserve the context rather than presenting the number as a general property of the system.

    21.1.6 · Tail latency analysis

    A service's p99 rises from 200 ms to five seconds. First ask whether a rare expensive operation changed or whether many operations slowed. Split queueing, execution, network, and required fan-out.

    Use population distributions and representative traces together. Averaging individual machines' percentiles does not reconstruct a fleet percentile, and very high percentiles need enough observations to estimate usefully. One slow trace suggests a path to investigate, not a universal explanation. Compare normal and slow cases under the same workload. Tail analysis connects the distribution to its causes instead of assuming the mean describes all users.

    Think further · When could a more expensive architecture be simpler to operate overall?

    Compare total work for people as well as the invoice. A managed service may reduce patching, backup, or recovery burden while adding charges and leaving application responsibilities. Evaluate the same correctness and service goals with explicit staffing assumptions. Choose the design the team can understand, change, and recover reliably.

    Remember: Performance evidence is meaningful only with its workload, conditions, and outcome definition.

    Try applying it: How could a load generator accidentally omit the very delays users would experience?

    PART 5 / UNIT 21 / CHAPTER 21.2

    Capacity, architecture & cost per outcome

    Prerequisites: 21.1 · Budgets, bottlenecks & honest benchmarks6 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Extra nodes, caches, and transfer can change both capacity and cost. Compare complete architectures using explicit inputs and useful outcomes rather than one attractive infrastructure rate.

    21.2.1 · Queue saturation and throughput ceilings

    As offered traffic rises, useful completions eventually stop increasing. Extra work then waits or is rejected. A queue stores that mismatch; it supplies no additional service capacity.

    Observe successful outcomes, latency, and saturation to locate the throughput knee, where additional demand sharply worsens experience. Reserve margin for variability, background work, maintenance, and the failures the system promises to tolerate. A short benchmark maximum is not automatically a safe production target. State which amount of useful traffic remains supportable after a node or zone is lost, rather than sizing only the healthy fleet.

    21.2.2 · Performance tuning vs architecture changes

    A query spends most of its time scanning rows. An index may solve the problem without changing data ownership. Sharding that database would introduce routing and migration while possibly leaving the expensive query design intact.

    Performance tuning changes an implementation within its arrangement; an architecture change alters major placement, ownership, or interaction. Either may be justified. Measure before and after, and include correctness, operating work, and migration risk. Some central invariants really require a different model to scale. Choose the intervention by the demonstrated limit, rather than assuming the larger architectural change is the more effective one.

    21.2.3 · Horizontal scaling economics

    Compare one larger deployment, replicated application instances sharing a data owner, and partitioned storage. More nodes add baseline memory, discovery, coordination, and network work. Their advantage depends on which load can actually be divided.

    Use equal requirements and failure headroom. A partitioned design may cost more at small scale while extending a later ceiling, but that is a hypothesis to test. Keep price, operating labour, and traffic assumptions explicit. Hypothetical rates can teach arithmetic; actual spending decisions need current prices. Node count alone cannot establish useful capacity or a lower cost per successful outcome.

    21.2.4 · Compute, storage, networking, and telemetry costs

    A cheap computation can produce a large response sent millions of times. Transfer may dominate its total cost. Follow the cost path through compute, requests, storage, indexes, replicas, backups, networking, and telemetry.

    Include operational work where relevant. A cache can save source computation while adding memory and invalidation cost. Compression can save transfer while adding CPU. The worked prices in this atlas are fictional inputs, not current provider quotations. Keep the units and accounting period visible so the reader can replace the inputs and understand which part of the cost changes.

    21.2.5 · Cost per request or transaction

    Assume monthly cost is 3,000 units and the system completes 150,000 useful business outcomes. The unit cost is 3,000/150,000 = 0.02 units per outcome.

    Dividing by every attempt can conceal waste if many attempts fail or repeat. Choose a meaningful denominator such as completed orders or delivered documents, while retaining technical breakdowns for diagnosis. State the period and included expenses. Compare successful work under equivalent requirements; an operation that returns quickly but loses its result is not the same outcome. This keeps cost optimisation tied to the service users actually receive.

    21.2.6 · Capacity reservation vs elastic capacity

    A steady baseline can suit committed capacity, while occasional bursts may favour capacity added when needed. Reservations trade commitment and idle-risk for particular commercial terms. Elastic resources still need provisioning time and may have different rates.

    Compare baseline utilisation, burst duration, growth uncertainty, and failure needs. Buying for a rare peak can leave resources idle; waiting to scale after a short burst begins can arrive too late. A mixed approach may fit, but the balance needs measured traffic and current terms. Keep these commercial assumptions separate from the technical proof that surviving capacity meets the workload.

    A complete cost worksheet with fictional inputs

    Monthly rates below are invented teaching inputs, not provider quotations. Capacity, p99, and availability are evaluation dimensions whose results must be measured; this cost table cannot establish them.

    Fictional monthly cost units; compare only after checking requirements
    ArchitectureComputeDataCacheStorageTransferTelemetryTotal
    Single deployment40300012010371
    Replicated application1603005012020551
    Partitioned design320900100240401402

    Compare latency, availability, and operating work under stated assumptions

    Construct a 100-request trace for each option: single deployment has 98 observations at 190 ms, one at 900 ms, and one at 1,400 ms; replicated application has 98 at 140 ms, one at 450 ms, and one at 800 ms; partitioned design has 98 at 110 ms, one at 600 ms, and one at 1,600 ms. Nearest-rank p99 is observation 99 after sorting. These synthetic traces deliberately show that lower common-case latency can coexist with worse tail latency. They predict no real deployment.

    For a separate steady-state availability model, assume independent app-instance availability of 0.99 and data-owner availability of 0.999. An interchangeable pool of k apps is available with probability 1 − 0.01^k. The single and replicated options require one data owner. The partitioned operation in this example requires all three independent owners, so multiply by 0.999³. Shared outages, overload, failover time, repair, and correlated failures are omitted; these probabilities are not SLO commitments.

    Illustrative comparison; latency traces, availability probabilities, and operating judgments are assumptions
    ArchitectureMonthly cost unitsConstructed p99Modeled availabilityOperational complexity judgment
    Single: 1 app, 1 data owner371900 ms98.901%Lower: one app release and one data owner
    Replicated: 4 apps, 1 data owner551450 ms99.899999%Medium: rolling releases, shared cache, pool capacity and failover
    Partitioned: 8 apps, 3 required data owners1,402600 ms99.700300%Higher: routing, rebalancing, multiple owners and partial recovery

    For a per-key request touching only one shard, the all-three-owners availability expression does not apply. Replication with an actual quorum or failover protocol also needs a different model. The calculation is executable as architecture_comparison() in the mechanism collection. Choose a candidate against the workload and targets, then test tail latency, degraded capacity, restoration, and operating burden. Cost arithmetic alone cannot establish those properties.

    Think further · When could a more expensive architecture be simpler to operate overall?

    Compare total work for people as well as the invoice. A managed service may reduce patching, backup, or recovery burden while adding charges and leaving application responsibilities. Evaluate the same correctness and service goals with explicit staffing assumptions. Choose the design the team can understand, change, and recover reliably.

    Remember: Filter by required behaviour before ranking cost, and keep modelled quantities distinct from measured results.

    Try applying it: Why can a lower cost per attempt coexist with a higher cost per completed order?

    PART 5 / UNIT 21 / CHAPTER 21.3

    Efficiency and a useful test portfolio

    Prerequisites: 21.2 · Capacity, architecture & cost per outcome4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    An optimisation saves CPU while adding transfer, or a test suite adds checks without covering failures. Evaluate the whole effect and choose evidence for the particular risk.

    21.3.1 · Cost-performance optimization

    A smaller instance is cheaper but misses the latency target under the same traffic. It is not a comparable successful design. Cost-performance optimisation first requires feasible correctness, service, security, and maintenance behaviour.

    Then vary factors such as cache size, batching, compression, placement, or capacity shape with measurements. Check downstream effects: saving write bytes may add repeated expensive decompression on reads. Record the workload and objective that make the choice useful. An optimisation can become unsuitable after the traffic mix changes, so retain the conditions and a way to reconsider it.

    21.3.2 · Sustainability and resource efficiency

    Removing unused retained data saves storage work. Bounding retries avoids repeated computation and transfer. Resource efficiency begins by finding work the service does not need to perform.

    Right-size capacity and batch suitable background operations without breaking deadlines. Evaluate complete effects: less CPU in one component can cause much more network or storage work elsewhere. Environmental claims need actual evidence about the relevant hardware, place, time, and lifecycle. Do not invent energy or carbon measurements. Useful engineering improvements can be explained by the resources they reduce while keeping broader sustainability conclusions within the available evidence.

    21.3.3 · Unit, integration, contract, end-to-end, and performance tests

    A unit test can check fee arithmetic with controlled inputs. A database integration test can check a transaction. A contract test checks boundary expectations, and an end-to-end test follows a complete journey. Performance tests examine behaviour under load.

    Choose each test for the failure it can detect. A fake provider helps exercise declines, but cannot establish real serialization or commit behaviour. A suite that asserts every private call may hinder harmless refactoring while missing a lost reply. The test pyramid is guidance about feedback cost and scope, not a mandatory numerical ratio. Useful evidence matters more than raw test count.

    21.3.4 · Fault-injection tests

    A process killed before it starts work says little about a crash after commit but before acknowledgment. Place faults at the boundary whose guarantee is in question.

    Inject delays, unavailability, interruptions, or invalid responses with explicit acceptable outcomes and stop conditions. Test a resumed worker after lease expiry and an interrupted data move where relevant. Combine serving observations with data checks: the application can start responding again while a promised job remains lost. A fault test passes the business contract only when both the recovered service and its required state are accounted for.

    Think further · When could a more expensive architecture be simpler to operate overall?

    Compare total work for people as well as the invoice. A managed service may reduce patching, backup, or recovery burden while adding charges and leaving application responsibilities. Evaluate the same correctness and service goals with explicit staffing assumptions. Choose the design the team can understand, change, and recover reliably.

    Remember: Efficiency and validation should reduce real work or uncertainty without weakening the required contract.

    Try applying it: Which failure window would a process kill before work begins leave untested?

    PART 5 / UNIT 21 / CHAPTER 21.4

    Fitness functions and design validation

    Prerequisites: 21.3 · Efficiency and a useful test portfolio4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A migration has matching row counts but wrong tenant ownership. Validate identities and invariants, preserve important regressions, and return to the requirements that justified the design.

    21.4.1 · Data consistency validation

    Source and destination each contain a thousand rows, but some rows belong to the wrong tenant. Equal counts missed the error. Data consistency validation must compare identities, versions, and domain rules as well as totals.

    For a ledger, check balanced postings and operation uniqueness. For a search index, check the source version and deletion state. Run suitable checks after migration, replay, and restoration. Sampling can reduce cost but supports a weaker claim than examining every relevant record. State the coverage of the evidence so a useful sample is not presented as complete equivalence.

    21.4.2 · Architecture fitness functions

    An import rule can prevent the orders module from depending on private payment storage. A runtime test can check tenant-scoped queries. These are architecture fitness functions: repeatable checks for properties the architecture needs to preserve.

    Protect the reason for the boundary instead of freezing every incidental class relationship. Some qualities require drills or manual review rather than static inspection. Update a check when a legitimate decision changes the required property. Passing the set provides evidence for its covered behaviours, not a general certificate of architectural correctness. Choose checks that can reveal a meaningful erosion of the intended design.

    21.4.3 · Regression testing

    A regression test keeps an important behaviour visible while the implementation changes. Include relevant errors, concurrency, compatibility, and recovery sequences, especially those that previously caused harm.

    Use representative data and preserve the test's purpose through refactoring. Performance checks need sufficiently stable conditions and tolerances to avoid treating noise as a defect. If a requirement changes, revise the expected outcome explicitly. Deleting a failing test without naming the changed contract loses the reason it existed. The suite should preserve useful obligations while allowing the code that fulfils them to improve.

    21.4.4 · Evaluating a design against its original requirements

    Return to the original brief. For each promised behaviour, identify its test, measurement, review, or still-unresolved assumption. This creates a traceable link from the design choice to its evidence.

    Check function, timing distributions, capacity, recovery, access, cost, and operating burden under the stated workload. A diagram review and a load test answer different questions. If a target has not been measured, keep calling it a target. Record the remaining uncertainty rather than treating completed coverage as completed validation. The final evaluation asks whether the chosen system meets the needs that justified building it.

    Try the mechanism in code

    Python · fictional comparison

    from mechanisms import cost_options
totals = {name:sum(parts.values()) for name,parts in cost_options().items()}
assert totals == {"single":371, "replicated_app":551, "partitioned":1402}

    The monthly totals are 371, 551, and 1,402 fictional units. They show how component costs add, rather than how the deployments actually perform.

    Check equal requirements before ranking price. The additional latency and availability models have explicit synthetic inputs; real capacity, tails, and recovery require corresponding tests.

    Think further · When could a more expensive architecture be simpler to operate overall?

    Compare total work for people as well as the invoice. A managed service may reduce patching, backup, or recovery burden while adding charges and leaving application responsibilities. Evaluate the same correctness and service goals with explicit staffing assumptions. Choose the design the team can understand, change, and recover reliably.

    Remember: Pair each requirement with evidence and keep unresolved targets clearly labelled.
