    PART 6 / UNIT 22 / CHAPTER 22.1

    URL Shortener

    Prerequisites: API Design and Communication Contracts, Data Models and Storage Technologies, Caching and Content Delivery, Scalability, Load Balancing, and Data Distribution4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A short link hides a lookup, an ownership rule, and a cache-freshness decision. Follow one mapping from creation through redirect and revocation.

    The workload, timing, and prices in this design are teaching assumptions. They are not measured benchmarks or a description of a particular company.

    22.1.1 · Functional requirements

    A user submits a long URL and receives a short code. Later, a visitor opens that code and is redirected to the original target. The owner can expire or revoke the link and manage it through an authenticated interface.

    Keep the original target and creation identity. Click analytics is secondary work: a failed analytics database should not make an otherwise valid redirect wait indefinitely. Abuse handling and the correctness of the redirect remain part of the main product.

    22.1.2 · Nonfunctional requirements

    For this example, target redirect p99 below 100 ms under the supported peak. An acknowledged mapping must survive the selected single-storage-node failure, and management operations must preserve ownership.

    Specify how soon revocation and expiry take effect. A long-lived cached redirect can remain usable after the source changes unless another mechanism prevents it. The latency target, storage acknowledgment policy, and cache freshness rule therefore need to be checked together rather than promised independently.

    22.1.3 · Explicit assumptions and workload numbers

    Assume 100 creations/s and 10,000 redirects/s on average, with a tenfold redirect peak. Assume 200 stored bytes per mapping before indexes and extra copies. Daily raw growth is 100×86,400×200 = 1.728 GB.

    For transfer calculations, assume a 500-byte redirect response. These quantities are teaching inputs. Actual record size, traffic duration, and transport overhead must be measured before using them to provision a service.

    22.1.4 · Naive initial architecture

    Begin with one web application, one relational mapping table, and a unique code constraint. A background job handles analytics. Local uniqueness is straightforward, and this arrangement is suitable for an initial small workload.

    Its weaknesses are visible: the application host can fail, and every miss reaches the one data path. Measure lookup and write behaviour before distributing data. A sharded design adds routing and uniqueness work that may not yet solve the actual bottleneck.

    22.1.5 · Core API contracts

    POST /links accepts a target, expiry, and idempotency key. GET /{code} returns the permitted redirect or the defined expired/revoked result. DELETE /links/{id} checks the owner before changing state.

    Validate supported URL schemes and syntax without fetching arbitrary destinations. Reusing a key with different content conflicts; retrying an identical creation can recover its original result. State whether redirects are permanent or temporary, since that affects how clients may keep copies after later changes.

    22.1.6 · Data model and schema

    A link record contains id, unique code, target, owner_id, creation time, expiry, state, and version. An operation record binds the owner and operation key to a request fingerprint and result link. The key is unique within the owner scope.

    The code must be unique across its intended namespace. If mappings are later sharded, routing or allocation must preserve that rule across owners. A uniqueness constraint applied independently to unrelated shards is insufficient. Keep revocation and expiry attached to authoritative versioned state.

    22.1.7 · Low-level component organization

    LinkService checks the target and caller. CodeAllocator proposes a code. LinkRepository commits the mapping and its operation result together. RedirectResolver decides whether the link is usable, and AnalyticsPublisher records secondary events.

    The allocator can encode an appropriately unique integer in base62 or propose random codes and retry collisions. The repository's uniqueness check is the decisive boundary. A random proposal is not proof of uniqueness, and a provider-specific storage error should not leak through every application caller.

    22.1.8 · High-level system architecture

    Put an edge or reverse proxy before replaceable application instances. A cache serves representations whose expiry and revocation policy permits reuse. The authoritative replicated store owns mappings and recovery; a queue or log carries analytics separately.

    The cache can improve reads but must not become the only recoverable copy. Bound fallback traffic when it is unavailable. Extra application instances protect some serving capacity, while storage placement and acknowledgment determine which mapping history survives a failure.

    22.1.9 · Data and control flows

    For creation, validate the request, atomically commit the mapping and deduplication result, then reply. For redirect, check usable state, obtain a permitted cached or source value, and send the response. Record analytics independently of the visitor's required result.

    Combine concurrent misses for a code where useful. Keep private management representations out of the public redirect cache. The write, read, and analytics paths have different responsibilities and should remain distinguishable in the implementation.

    22.1.10 · Capacity estimates

    With an assumed 90% hit ratio, 10,000 redirects/s cause 1,000 source reads/s before retries or coalescing. At 100,000 redirects/s, the same ratio implies 10,000 source reads/s. Response traffic is 100,000×500 = 50 MB/s before transport overhead.

    Also test a cold cache, when the nominal miss calculation no longer applies. The source and admission policy need a defined response to that workload; ordinary warm-cache success does not establish it.

    22.1.11 · End-to-end latency estimates

    Assume a warm path spends 20 ms at the edge/network, 10 ms in the application, 5 ms in cache access, and 20 ms returning the result. The sum is 55 ms.

    This is a proposed budget, not measured p99. A miss adds source lookup and possible queueing. Measure the tail under hot links, cache loss, storage failover, and required revocation checks before claiming the 100 ms objective. Adding average stage times does not by itself establish an end-to-end percentile.

    22.1.12 · Failure scenarios

    Two creations propose the same code. The second insert must fail atomically and retry, preserving the first target. A lost creation reply should recover the stored operation result instead of creating another mapping.

    Cache outage needs origin admission controls. A stale cache can redirect a revoked link unless the freshness rule prevents it. Analytics failure should affect analytics progress rather than valid redirect service. Test these separate histories; one successful create-and-open demonstration leaves all of them unexamined.

    22.1.13 · Scalability improvements

    Add application capacity when independent application work is limiting. Add shared or edge caching when measured reads justify it. Partition mappings only when the authoritative storage path needs division.

    A globally popular code may need permitted read copies instead of more cold partitions. Every added copy retains the expiry and revocation obligation. Data movement needs routing, version, and recovery rules, so expansion should preserve both global code ownership and the supported state of existing operations.

    22.1.14 · Consistency requirements

    Creating a code needs one atomic uniqueness decision. The owner-facing read should meet the chosen read-after-write rule. Public redirects may tolerate delayed target changes only within the stated expiry and revocation contract.

    Analytics can be processed later with stable event identities. These operations therefore have different consistency needs. Calling the whole system “eventually consistent” hides the exclusive code insertion and the permitted delay of a click count. State the observable rule for each path.

    22.1.15 · Security model

    Authorise owner management and limit creation abuse. Accept only supported target schemes. If previews fetch destinations, restrict egress and validate redirect hops so a public URL field does not become access to private services.

    Protect credentials and avoid leaking private targets through logs or analytics. A short code that is difficult to guess is still a link, not a complete permission system for confidential content. If restricted destinations are supported, define authentication and access checking for those redirects separately.

    22.1.16 · Deployment approach

    Start with a region and a clear failure contract. Use compatible rolling application releases, a suitably replicated authoritative store, and tested backups. Preserve operation identities through replacement and drain connections as needed.

    New code must understand existing mapping versions. A later second region needs a deliberate write-authority and possible-loss policy. Add it for a named locality or recovery requirement, rather than assuming that more geography automatically preserves every acknowledged mapping.

    22.1.17 · Observability design

    Measure redirect outcomes and latency, separating hits from misses. Track origin admission, hot codes, code conflicts, storage progress, and how long revocation takes to reach permitted readers.

    Observe analytics lag separately. A good cache hit ratio does not show whether a newly created or revoked link is correct. Alert on useful request failures and rapid budget consumption, and use traces or sampled histories to locate the affected path without exposing private target data unnecessarily.

    22.1.18 · Infrastructure cost considerations

    Model compute as instance-hours times unit rate, storage as retained bytes times copy factor and rate, and transfer as response bytes times rate. Keep the duration assumption explicit.

    For example, sustaining 100,000 redirects/s for 30 days at 500 bytes produces 129.6 TB before overhead. That is a different workload from a brief peak of the same height. Use actual traffic durations and current rates for spending decisions; these formulas only expose the inputs the estimate requires.

    22.1.19 · Alternative architectures and trade-offs

    Allocated sequential identifiers simplify code generation but need a valid allocator and can reveal order. Random codes reduce that predictability but still need collision detection. Neither option grants access control.

    Permanent redirects can let clients reuse responses more aggressively, making later changes harder to enforce. Temporary redirects retain more server control at a traffic cost. Compare the alternatives using revocation, mutation, privacy, and load requirements. The right choice is the smallest mechanism that preserves those meanings, not the most familiar coding trick.

    22.1.20 · Architecture evolution from small scale to large scale

    Use traffic levels as teaching checkpoints rather than hardware promises. Around 100 requests/s, begin with one application and transactional store. Around 1,000, inspect plans and indexes. Around 10,000, consider measured application and cache needs.

    At 100,000, expand the actual bottleneck and verify cold-cache and degraded operation. A given machine may reach a limit earlier or later. Preserve stable code and operation identities at every stage so scaling does not change the meaning of existing links or retries.

    22.1.21 · Design review identifying weaknesses and improvements

    The main uncertainties are revocation freshness, source capacity after cache loss, and global uniqueness during partitioning. Pair each with a specific check: revoke under load, empty or disable the cache, and force a collision across the real ownership boundary.

    Record acceptable degraded outcomes and unresolved evidence. Replicating the cache alone does not answer these questions. A useful review ends with the failure behaviour the design supports and the test that could show its assumption wrong.

    22.1.22 · A short implementation exercise

    Implement base62 encoding and a repository with an atomic unique-code constraint. Force two proposals to use one code and check that the original target remains unchanged.

    Then stop execution after commit but before returning the creation result. Retry with the same owner and operation key. The expected result is the existing mapping, with no second logical creation. Also check that changing the target under that key returns the documented conflict.

    A small implementation of the key rule

    PSEUDOCODE · ONE PART OF THE DESIGN

    def allocate(target, operation_key):
    prior = operations.find(operation_key)
    if prior: return prior
    while attempts_remaining():
        code = propose_code()
        try:
            with transaction():
                link = insert_unique_code(code, target)
                save_operation_result(operation_key, link.id)
            return link
        except CodeConflict:
            continue
        except OperationConflict:
            return load_and_validate_prior_result(operation_key, target)
    raise AllocationUnavailable

    Use the implementation exercise to test the rule and the failure described above. You can also run local examples of seat claims, duplicate handling, ledger balance, and workflow epochs in the mechanism collection.

    PART 6 / UNIT 22 / CHAPTER 22.2

    Rate Limiter

    Prerequisites: Requirements, Estimation, and Engineering Trade-offs, Runtime, Processes, Threads, and Concurrency, Scalability, Load Balancing, and Data Distribution, Reliability, Fault Tolerance, and Disaster Recovery4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Three application instances each grant a full bucket of tokens. We need to decide whether the policy is local, globally strict, or a bounded allocation shared among regions.

    The workload, timing, and prices in this design are teaching assumptions. They are not measured benchmarks or a description of a particular company.

    22.2.1 · Functional requirements

    A request arrives from a caller and asks to perform work with a known cost. The limiter decides whether the current policy permits it and returns useful guidance if it must wait or be rejected.

    Distinguish continuing rate, permitted burst, and cumulative quota. For a distributed deployment, state whether the limit is exact globally or a bounded regional approximation. Giving every region a full independent global bucket silently creates a different policy.

    22.2.2 · Nonfunctional requirements

    Admission should add little delay while keeping protected resources within their allowance. Preserve tenant fairness and specify how the limiter behaves when its state is unavailable.

    An exact global cap can require rejection or waiting during a partition. Failing open cannot preserve that cap unless previously allocated safe budgets cover the admitted work. Choose the failure rule alongside the availability goal. “Always fast and always exact” needs a protocol and assumptions, rather than two independent targets.

    22.2.3 · Explicit assumptions and workload numbers

    Assume 100,000 checks/s and one million active keys. A sample policy holds ten tokens and refills two per second. At an assumed 64 bytes of raw state per key, the raw total is 64 MB.

    Engine allocation, expiry metadata, replication, and network requests add to this. These are teaching inputs, not product benchmarks. State size is only one capacity dimension; the update rate and contention of a popular key may become limiting sooner.

    22.2.4 · Naive initial architecture

    Begin with a dictionary in one process and protect each bucket transition with a suitable lock. This provides one local atomic decision for the callers sharing that process.

    Starting a second unrelated process gives it another full allowance. Restart may reset the bucket too. The simple version is appropriate only if this scope and reset behaviour meet the requirement. Demonstrating correct arithmetic locally does not establish a shared cap across instances.

    22.2.5 · Core API contracts

    check(key,cost,policy_version) returns the admission decision, remaining allowance, and meaningful retry delay. Derive the key from trusted caller and resource identity; a caller must not evade its policy by inventing another key.

    Require a positive bounded cost. Policy administration needs authorisation and an effective-version rule. Distinguish overload from invalid business input, and state whether rejected attempts consume a separate abuse budget. These meanings let callers react without immediately recreating the same excessive demand.

    22.2.6 · Data model and schema

    Keep a bucket record with scope_key, policy_version, tokens, last_refill, and expiry. Refill and spending share one atomic update. A cumulative daily quota can require separate state and rules.

    Fixed-point or integer units can avoid unnecessary numeric drift. A policy change needs defined treatment of existing tokens and capacity. The elapsed-time basis must be trusted; client timestamps must not let a caller refill early. Expiring state also changes allowance, so it belongs in the contract.

    22.2.7 · Low-level component organization

    KeyResolver derives trusted scope, PolicyResolver supplies validated policy, and Clock supplies the time basis. BucketStore performs the coordinated transition. AdmissionService translates the result for the caller.

    These roles make deterministic tests practical, but do not replace atomic state access. Two pure calculations using the same old token count can both admit work. Keep the refill/check/debit decision under one owner or supported transaction. The decisive property concerns the combined operation, not merely each helper's correctness.

    22.2.8 · High-level system architecture

    Use coarse admission near ingress and more specific protection before expensive resources. Independent keys can have different owners. A strict shared bucket needs one suitable atomic authority or a reviewed distributed protocol.

    Regional budgets can avoid a remote check on each request, but need bounded allocation and replenishment. State the allowed overshoot or outstanding-budget rule. Protect the limiter's own capacity and define emergency controls. A protection service can otherwise become the first component overloaded by the traffic it was meant to regulate.

    22.2.9 · Data and control flows

    Derive the request's scope and current policy. Under coordinated access, load its bucket, calculate nonnegative elapsed time, refill no further than capacity, compare the cost, and debit only if allowed.

    Compute retry delay from the deficit and refill rate when that advice is meaningful. Record bounded metrics. Splitting the read and final write into unprotected calls lets two requests spend the same last token. The atomic transition is what connects correct arithmetic to a correct concurrent decision.

    22.2.10 · Capacity estimates

    One million 64-byte records require 64 MB raw. A remote check per incoming request also means 100,000 limiter requests/s under the assumed workload, before replica work and retries.

    A single hot key can serialise many updates despite evenly distributed storage. Measure check rate, active state, contention, and replicated write cost. Batching or local budgets may reduce traffic, but their changed timing and precision must be stated. A memory estimate alone is not a complete limiter capacity plan.

    22.2.11 · End-to-end latency estimates

    Assume a 100 ms application target and allocate 5 ms to admission. This is a budget to validate under contention, not a measured guarantee.

    A strict cross-region decision adds propagation and queueing and may not fit it. Local preallocated budgets can reduce that delay while adding an allocation protocol. Measure the complete path, including store failover and policy retrieval, against the required precision. Changing the consistency contract can change latency, so present those choices together.

    22.2.12 · Failure scenarios

    Two requests read one token and both pass. Repair that race by combining the read, refill, and debit atomically. Backward time must not create extra refill, and state expiry must not grant an unintended unsafe burst.

    Test key spoofing and policy disagreement as well as arithmetic. During owner failure, apply the documented reject, safe-local-budget, or bounded fail-open policy. A mathematically correct bucket can still fail to protect the resource if identities or deployment scopes are wrong.

    22.2.13 · Scalability improvements

    Partition independent keys while keeping a bucket's decision coordinated. Cache versioned policy definitions where suitable, while maintaining the authority needed for spending.

    One strict hot bucket cannot be divided freely without a budget-allocation protocol. Hierarchical limits or local allowances can help when their semantics fit the resource. Different operations may deserve different costs. Scale according to protected work and measured limiter contention, rather than increasing the key count while leaving the hot decision unchanged.

    22.2.14 · Consistency requirements

    A strict bucket preserves one policy's refill-and-debit rule under its time model. An approximate distributed version needs a stated bound, such as the total independently outstanding regional allowance.

    Token buckets permit bursts. Fixed windows have boundary effects, while sliding windows model recent history differently. These are different admission contracts. Converging usage metrics later cannot repair requests already admitted beyond a mandatory cap. Name the invariant the live decision must preserve instead of treating eventual counter agreement as equivalent protection.

    22.2.15 · Security model

    Bind scope keys to authenticated tenant or service identity. Guard policy changes and cap key creation so arbitrary callers cannot exhaust state memory. Do not trust client time, policy names, or tenant headers without validation.

    Limit what usage information responses reveal about other callers. Admission and permission remain separate: possessing tokens does not authorise a read of another tenant's document. Apply the resource access rule after, or as part of, the relevant protected operation.

    22.2.16 · Deployment approach

    Deploy the policy and bucket owners with specified state-loss and failover behaviour. A restart that grants every caller a new full bucket changes the protection contract.

    Roll out policy versions compatibly and test time behaviour, old clients, and shared-owner loss. A local fallback must have an acceptable bound. Preserve state or allocate safe replacement allowance according to the chosen design, rather than relying on the assumption that protection state is disposable merely because individual records are small.

    22.2.17 · Observability design

    Measure allowed and rejected cost, check latency, owner errors, active keys, hot-key pressure, and policy-version differences. Compare these with the resource the limiter protects.

    Many rejections can indicate effective protection or a bad configuration blocking legitimate users. Few rejections can hide fail-open behaviour during store failure. Observe both protection failures and unnecessary denial. Use bounded dimensions for metrics so tenant or key cardinality does not make the monitoring system the next capacity problem.

    22.2.18 · Infrastructure cost considerations

    The cost includes state memory, check traffic, replicated updates, transfer, and operating work. A remote strict decision on every cheap business request can cost more than the operation being protected.

    Compare strict and local-budget designs with their guarantees stated. Use symbolic or explicitly fictional rates for teaching. If the cheaper choice permits more overshoot or fails differently, show that difference. A reduced bill does not establish equal protection when the policy has changed.

    22.2.19 · Alternative architectures and trade-offs

    Token bucket admits bounded bursts. A leaky-bucket shaper smooths output by adding waiting. Fixed-window counters are simple but permit bursts around boundaries. Sliding approaches model recent traffic at additional state or computation cost.

    Regional budgets trade precision and allocation work for local delay and availability. Choose according to the protected resource and acceptable behaviour, not a universally preferred algorithm name. Include what a caller sees when rejected and how its retries interact with the limit.

    22.2.20 · Architecture evolution from small scale to large scale

    First build a deterministic local bucket with an atomic owner. Move to shared state when several processes need one cap. Partition keys only when measured load requires it.

    Introduce regional allocation for a named latency or failure need, with an explicit bound. Preserve the original policy meaning through each step or version the changed contract. Evolution is safest when each addition answers a demonstrated scope or capacity problem rather than silently multiplying the allowance.

    22.2.21 · Design review identifying weaknesses and improvements

    Ask whether the advertised scope matches enforcement, whether a policy update creates unintended tokens, and what happens to the hottest key. These are protocol questions beyond the basic refill formula.

    Test simultaneous spending of the last token, backward time, expiry, policy replacement, owner failure, and regional reconnection. Reject an exact-global claim implemented as full independent buckets. Record unresolved evidence instead of assuming a shared product name establishes all these behaviours.

    22.2.22 · A short implementation exercise

    Use an injected monotonic clock to build the sample bucket. Spend its ten initial tokens, reject an immediate eleventh spend, advance three seconds, and verify that six tokens have returned under capacity ten.

    Reject invalid costs and ensure rollback in elapsed time adds no allowance. Then reproduce two unprotected readers spending one token and fix it with a coordinated transition. The test should show both the incorrect history and why the corrected ownership permits only one winner.

    A small implementation of the key rule

    PSEUDOCODE · ONE PART OF THE DESIGN

    def spend(bucket, now, cost):
    require(cost > 0)
    elapsed = max(0, now - bucket.last)
    available = min(bucket.capacity,
                    bucket.tokens + elapsed * bucket.rate)
    allowed = available >= cost
    bucket.tokens = available - cost if allowed else available
    bucket.last = max(bucket.last, now)
    return allowed
# Entire transition executes atomically for this bucket.

    Use the implementation exercise to test the rule and the failure described above. You can also run local examples of seat claims, duplicate handling, ledger balance, and workflow epochs in the mechanism collection.

    THE WORKBENCH · TRY CHANGING THE INPUTS

    Use a burst of tokens, then let the bucket refill

    The bucket holds at most ten tokens and gains two per second. Spend tokens, then advance the simulated clock. One browser owns this bucket. A shared implementation must update the balance atomically; several independent owners need a protocol to enforce a global limit.

    PART 6 / UNIT 22 / CHAPTER 22.3

    Chat Application

    Prerequisites: Networking Foundations for System Design, Data Models and Storage Technologies, Distributed Systems Fundamentals, Message Queues, Events, and Distributed Workflows4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A message can be safely stored while its live frame never reaches a device. Build chat around that distinction so reconnecting repairs delivery without creating another message.

    The workload, timing, and prices in this design are teaching assumptions. They are not measured benchmarks or a description of a particular company.

    22.3.1 · Functional requirements

    Two people send messages in an authorised conversation. Online devices should receive updates, and a disconnected device should later fetch what it missed. The system also supports bounded groups and a defined retention policy.

    Name the receipts carefully. A message can be accepted, persisted, delivered to a device, and read by a person at different times. Presence is only an approximate indication of connectivity. Opening a WebSocket supplies a live path, not evidence of human reading or durable history.

    22.3.2 · Nonfunctional requirements

    Retain acknowledged messages under the chosen storage-failure contract and protect conversation privacy. Define ordering per conversation or state a deliberately weaker alternative. Target online delivery below one second for the assumed supported workload.

    A disconnected client catches up later, so its delivery delay differs from that target. Presence can expire approximately without being treated as a strict allocation invariant. Moderation, deletion, and offline history need their own retention and visibility rules, including what returning devices may fetch.

    22.3.3 · Explicit assumptions and workload numbers

    Assume 100,000 concurrent connections and 10,000 accepted messages/s. Each stored message averages 500 bytes and produces five recipient deliveries in the simplified workload.

    Raw ingestion is 5 MB/s, or 432 GB/day. Five deliveries per message produce about 25 MB/s of body traffic before framing and overhead. Model device multiplicity, large groups, connection memory, and reconnect bursts separately. These assumptions do not establish the capacity of a particular gateway or database.

    22.3.4 · Naive initial architecture

    Begin with one connection server and one transactional history store. Save a message before returning its persistence receipt, then attempt delivery to online clients.

    A gateway crash loses live connections but need not lose committed history. Clients reconnect and request missing messages. This first design makes ownership clear, while exposing the server's availability and capacity limits. A database commit establishes persistence under its contract; it does not establish that any particular device received the message.

    22.3.5 · Core API contracts

    A send operation includes conversation_id, client_message_id, and bounded content. A history request continues after a sequence, for example GET /conversations/{id}/messages?after=sequence.

    Receipts identify a device or user and the highest relevant delivered or read sequence under the product's policy. Check membership on reads and writes. Reusing a client message identifier within its sender scope returns the earlier message. This lets a client recover a lost send reply without adding another history record for the same logical message.

    22.3.6 · Data model and schema

    Keep conversations and membership separately from message records. A message includes conversation_id, sequence, sender, client_message_id, body, and version. Receipt records track delivered and read progress for the appropriate user or device.

    Enforce the intended client-identity uniqueness scope. Presence uses a separate expiring heartbeat record. Conversation order needs a sequence authority or a supported conflict model; timestamps from client clocks do not automatically provide a stable total order. State which identity remains valid through reconnect and retry.

    22.3.7 · Low-level component organization

    ConnectionGateway manages connections. MembershipPolicy checks access. MessageService coordinates identity and persistence, SequenceOwner establishes order, and HistoryRepository serves bounded pages. DeliveryWorker handles committed fan-out.

    ReceiptAggregator combines progress without moving backward under the chosen device policy. Large-group work belongs in an explicit bounded operation instead of a long synchronous loop inside the message transaction. These components can begin together in one deployment. Their contracts should make clear which state is durable and which routing information may disappear.

    22.3.8 · High-level system architecture

    Use replaceable connection gateways and a conversation-routed durable message path. A log or outbox carries delivery intent to workers. Routing metadata identifies currently connected recipient devices, while history storage remains authoritative.

    A route can be stale, so clients recover missing frames from their last known sequence. If publication intent commits with the message, a broker outage can delay live delivery without discarding acknowledged history. Gateway state is then a recoverable convenience for reaching a device, rather than the only record of what should be delivered.

    22.3.9 · Data and control flows

    The client sends a stable message identity. The service checks membership, assigns order, and commits the message with its delivery intent. It then returns the persistence result.

    Workers send live frames and process valid receipts. On reconnect, the client supplies its last observed sequence, fetches missing pages, and detects gaps. Repeated frames are recognised by message identity. This separates two questions: what the service has safely retained and what this device currently displays. Losing a live frame is repaired through history rather than assumed impossible.

    22.3.10 · Capacity estimates

    At 10,000 messages/s and 500 bytes each, raw storage grows by 5 MB/s, or 432 GB/day. Five recipients imply 50,000 deliveries/s and 25 MB/s of bodies.

    Connection memory needs measurement. At an illustrative 20 kB per connection, 100,000 connections require 2 GB before other process memory and queued content. Bound outbound buffers for slow devices. A sender can otherwise make an idle-looking connection server run out of memory while the message database remains within its own limits.

    22.3.11 · End-to-end latency estimates

    Assume 20 ms ingress, 30 ms for commit coordination, 20 ms in delivery queues, and 80 ms on the recipient path. The sum is 150 ms before rendering.

    This budget is not measured online p99. Test hot conversations, congestion, failover, and slow-client buffers. Offline delivery has a different timeline. Keep persistence-receipt delay, device-delivery delay, and human-read delay as distinct indicators. One successful transport response cannot establish all three outcomes.

    22.3.12 · Failure scenarios

    If the send reply is lost after commit, recognise the client's repeated identity. If a gateway stops, reconnect and recover from history. If a client is too slow, disconnect or reduce its service before buffers consume the gateway's resources.

    A revoked membership can race with cached access information, so enforce the defined policy for delivery and history. Reconnect storms need admission and staggered retries. Test these event sequences directly rather than only testing two clients that stay connected throughout a normal exchange.

    22.3.13 · Scalability improvements

    Distribute independent gateway connections and partition history and ordering by conversation where suitable. Use bounded fan-out workers for groups.

    One extremely popular conversation can still concentrate ordering or distribution work. It may need different large-channel semantics rather than forcing every recipient into a low-latency acknowledgment chain. Preserve sequence and deduplication identity during ownership movement. Add capacity for the measured limit, with history catch-up included in the workload. Ordinary message averages do not account for every device returning after a gateway event.

    22.3.14 · Consistency requirements

    Provide a defined per-conversation order and a sender confirmation that agrees with the stored message. History catch-up must allow a client to resume without silently skipping required records.

    Cross-conversation total order is unnecessary unless the product requires it. Frames can repeat, so devices deduplicate. Presence and receipt updates can propagate later, while delivered/read progress follows the chosen monotonic model. State the guarantees at these different boundaries instead of describing WebSocket delivery as exactly-once messaging.

    22.3.15 · Security model

    Check membership on send, history, fan-out, search, and media access. Limit abusive sending, group size, and payloads. Avoid putting message bodies into routine telemetry.

    If end-to-end encryption is required, design device keys, recovery, and membership changes, and explain the resulting limits on server features. TLS protects a connection but does not implement that product guarantee. File attachments need access and retention rules too. Treat each content path as part of conversation privacy rather than assuming an authorised chat page protects every derived URL.

    22.3.16 · Deployment approach

    Drain gateways during rollout and support reconnecting old clients. Evolve message and receipt formats compatibly, and preserve history according to the selected replication and promotion rules.

    Load-test reconnect and catch-up alongside normal sending. Restarting every gateway together can generate a larger burst than ordinary chat traffic. A new region also needs explicit ordering and membership behaviour. State how existing client identities and progress survive replacement so deployment does not turn uncertain sends into duplicated messages.

    22.3.17 · Observability design

    Measure persistence delay, live-delivery lag, missing sequence recovery, reconnect rate, fan-out backlog, and hot conversations. Observe slow-client limits and membership denials.

    Correlate client and server message identities in suitable detailed evidence, without creating an unbounded metric label for every message. Synthetic clients can send, disconnect, reconnect, and check history and forbidden access. This tests the complete journey. A healthy connection count alone cannot show that an accepted message reached history or that a revoked device is blocked.

    22.3.18 · Infrastructure cost considerations

    Separate connection capacity, message history, fan-out transfer, indexes, replicas, media, and telemetry. Under the assumptions, thirty days of raw messages need 432 GB/day×30 = 12.96 TB before indexes and copies.

    Media can dominate storage and transfer and needs its own quota and lifecycle. Use explicit rates or symbolic calculations rather than assumed provider prices. Cost per retained message and cost per delivered body explain different work, particularly when many recipients or devices multiply the live path.

    22.3.19 · Alternative architectures and trade-offs

    WebSockets supports bidirectional low-latency messaging with connection-management work. SSE with HTTP sends may fit some clients; polling is simpler but creates requests during idle periods.

    A single conversation sequence authority simplifies order while creating a hot-key boundary. Conflict-tolerant regional writing changes that contract and needs a suitable merge and ordering model. Compare alternatives against the actual offline, receipt, and privacy requirements. The least complex transport that meets those behaviours can be preferable to one offering features the product never uses.

    22.3.20 · Architecture evolution from small scale to large scale

    First make durable history and reconnect recovery correct. Add gateway replicas with explicit connection routing. Introduce durable fan-out for higher volume or groups, then partition conversation ownership when storage or ordering measurements justify it.

    Regional placement comes with another authority and failure decision. Preserve message identity at every step. A client retry should retain the same logical meaning after a shard move or gateway replacement. Evolution that loses this identity can duplicate messages even while increasing connection capacity.

    22.3.21 · Design review identifying weaknesses and improvements

    Review the meanings of “sent” and “delivered,” the hottest conversation, slow-client memory, and revocation. Each needs a specific supported history.

    Test commit followed by a lost send reply, a dropped frame, gateway loss, a stale route, and a history read after membership is removed. Confirm the resulting list and receipts. A demo with two permanent online connections proves little about catch-up, privacy during change, or the storage contract that makes messages durable.

    22.3.22 · A short implementation exercise

    Build a client model that recognises message identities and detects sequence gaps. Save a message but suppress its live frame. Reconnect from the earlier sequence and verify that history supplies it once in the visible list.

    Repeat the same client_message_id and check that storage does not add another logical message. Distinguish deduplicating displayed frames from deduplicating history creation: both are useful, and each protects a different boundary.

    A small implementation of the key rule

    PSEUDOCODE · ONE PART OF THE DESIGN

    with transaction():
    existing = find_by_client_id(sender, client_message_id)
    if existing: return existing
    require_member(sender, conversation)
    seq = allocate_conversation_sequence(conversation)
    msg = insert_message(conversation, seq, body)
    insert_outbox(msg.id, "deliver")
return persisted_receipt(msg)
# Device delivery and read receipt happen later.

    Use the implementation exercise to test the rule and the failure described above. You can also run local examples of seat claims, duplicate handling, ledger balance, and workflow epochs in the mechanism collection.

    PART 6 / UNIT 22 / CHAPTER 22.4

    Notification Platform

    Prerequisites: Design Patterns, Dependency Injection, and Object Lifecycles, API Design and Communication Contracts, Message Queues, Events, and Distributed Workflows, Reliability, Fault Tolerance, and Disaster Recovery4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    The notification provider may accept a message just before its reply disappears. Track intent, attempts, and evidence so retries do not become unsupported delivery claims.

    The workload, timing, and prices in this design are teaching assumptions. They are not measured benchmarks or a description of a particular company.

    22.4.1 · Functional requirements

    An application submits a notification intent. The service selects permitted channels, renders a versioned template, sends through email, SMS, or push, and tracks what happened. Some messages may be scheduled or cancelled within a defined window.

    Provider acceptance, device delivery, and human viewing are separate outcomes. Preference rules can also differ by message purpose. Keep that policy explicit rather than letting a channel adapter decide whether a particular user may receive an operational or product message.

    22.4.2 · Nonfunctional requirements

    Preserve accepted intents and make delayed, expired, or permanently failed work visible. Define a business expiry: a password-reset message delivered hours late may be useless or harmful.

    Isolate critical and bulk work so a marketing batch does not consume every delivery resource. Avoid duplicate relevant effects where provider contracts support that promise, and expose residual uncertainty where they do not. The service should state the outcome it can establish rather than equating a submitted request with a delivered message.

    22.4.3 · Explicit assumptions and workload numbers

    Assume ten million intents/day. Dividing by 86,400 gives about 115.7/s average. An assumed tenfold peak is about 1,157/s. At 1 kB of initial intent and attempt metadata per item, raw growth is 10 GB/day.

    Repeated attempts, indexes, copies, and retained content add costs. Channel quotas are separate configured inputs that must be checked with the actual provider. An overall average cannot establish the submission capacity or delay of a specific route.

    22.4.4 · Naive initial architecture

    A first version calls one provider directly after a user action. It is simple, but the user's request now waits for that provider. If the business action commits and the process dies before sending, the notification intent can disappear.

    Persist required intent in the business transaction or an outbox, then let a worker send it. This separates accepted work from a temporary provider problem. It adds queued state and recovery rules, which should be visible rather than hidden inside an untracked background call.

    22.4.5 · Core API contracts

    POST /notifications accepts the recipient, template version, variables, channel policy, expiry, and idempotency key. GET /notifications/{id} reports a state such as pending, submitted, delivered, expired, failed, or cancelled.

    Define cancellation's boundary: it cannot recall a message already accepted by a provider. Callback endpoints verify authenticity and recognise repeated events. State transitions must reflect provider evidence. A delivered label should not merely mean that a worker returned without an exception.

    22.4.6 · Data model and schema

    Store the logical intent, template version, relevant preference information, channel/recipient delivery tasks, attempts, and provider-event inbox. Uniqueness binds each intended effect to its stable identity under the chosen policy.

    Keep provider references and uncertain outcomes. Retain sensitive message content separately from minimal progress or audit metadata. Decide what a new preference setting means for already queued tasks. Consent or cancellation rules may require a current check at send time rather than relying only on the submission snapshot.

    22.4.7 · Low-level component organization

    NotificationService records intent. PreferencePolicy selects allowed channels. TemplateRenderer builds the message, SenderStrategy chooses channel behaviour, and ProviderAdapter maps its protocol and outcomes. DeliveryRepository owns durable attempts and progress.

    Metrics decorators and factories can support genuine variation without changing result meanings. Keep construction and resource lifetimes clear. A retry wrapper needs more than the same method name: it must preserve operation identity and account for uncertainty about a prior submission.

    22.4.8 · High-level system architecture

    Use durable ingress, preference and template access, channel-specific queues, bounded workers, callback inboxes, and an outcome store. Separate resources for critical and bulk traffic where their priorities require it.

    A failed provider should occupy only its allocated capacity. A queue helps recovery only when intent, attempts, acknowledgment, and progress records agree about ownership. Draw these state boundaries alongside the normal sending path so it is clear what survives a worker or broker interruption.

    22.4.9 · Data and control flows

    Accept and deduplicate the intent, choose permitted channel and template, and persist the delivery task. A worker checks its current authority, expiry, and required preference policy before submission.

    Use a stable provider operation identity where supported. Save the returned result or an uncertain state, then acknowledge according to the task protocol. Apply verified callbacks idempotently, with rules preventing an older event from incorrectly reversing progress. An attempt and a callback can arrive out of order, so state transitions need evidence and identity rather than arrival order alone.

    22.4.10 · Capacity estimates

    Overall average traffic is about 115.7 intents/s, but each channel has its own capacity. Suppose SMS arrivals are 100/s and its route submits 40/s. Backlog grows by 60/s.

    Over ten minutes that adds 60×600 = 36,000 waiting submissions if the rates persist. Model retries, recipient fan-out, and expiry too. The queued work may become useless before capacity catches up. Admission, priority, or supported alternate routes must respond to the channel's real limit rather than the service-wide daily average.

    22.4.11 · End-to-end latency estimates

    Assume acceptance takes 50 ms, queue wait 2 seconds, and provider submission 500 ms. Provider acceptance then occurs around 2.55 seconds after submission to our API.

    The short API latency and delivery journey are different measurements. These inputs are illustrative budgets, not measured percentiles. Actual delivery and human viewing depend on further systems and evidence. Do not advertise a 50 ms notification outcome merely because durable acceptance was quick. Track the completion event that matters for the message's purpose.

    22.4.12 · Failure scenarios

    A worker sends a message, then dies before recording the provider reply. The provider may already have accepted it. Query or use provider idempotency where available; otherwise state the remaining duplicate risk.

    Malformed templates need review, outages need bounded retries and expiry, and callbacks need authenticity checks. Reconcile old submitted or uncertain tasks. A second provider does not automatically resolve uncertainty: sending there can create another message if the first provider's effect already occurred.

    22.4.13 · Scalability improvements

    Distribute independent recipients and channel tasks, with bounds and any required per-recipient order. Add routes only with a deliberate selection, rate, and uncertainty policy.

    Extra providers can improve some outage paths while increasing content and reconciliation work. A timeout followed by route switching can produce two messages. Measure the actual channel bottleneck before adding workers, and keep downstream quotas and critical-message capacity visible. Safe progress is the goal, rather than maximum parallel submissions regardless of expiry or duplicate effects.

    22.4.14 · Consistency requirements

    Persisting intent and the deduplication result needs an atomic local boundary. Task deliveries may repeat, while local transitions recognise stable identities. Provider acceptance and final delivery have separate evidence.

    Retain the template version so a retry does not silently send different content. Apply the chosen current-preference policy at the correct boundary. A general exactly-once label would hide the different guarantees supported by email, SMS, and push providers. State which local record or external effect the specific mechanism protects.

    22.4.15 · Security model

    Authorise which actor may send which template to which recipients. Validate variables and escape or encode them appropriately for the target channel. Protect recipient data, provider credentials, and callback authenticity.

    Avoid leaking tokens or message bodies through logs. Limit intent creation to prevent abuse. Signed links inside messages need an appropriate audience and lifetime; the delivery system should not broaden their capability accidentally. Include adapter-level protections such as preventing unsafe header or content construction.

    22.4.16 · Deployment approach

    Deploy workers with durable attempt state and graceful draining. Scale-down must not abandon unrecorded work. Template edits create new versions rather than changing content under an existing retry identity.

    Roll task schemas out compatibly and plan credential rotation. Test deployment during a provider outage so accumulated work does not overwhelm the recovering route. Verify that critical-channel and acceptance policies still work while another channel is saturated or being replaced.

    22.4.17 · Observability design

    Track accepted intents, queue age by channel, expiry, provider submission delay, uncertain outcomes, callbacks, and duplicate recognition. Separate critical and bulk outcomes so an apparently good total cannot hide important delayed messages.

    Alert on old unresolved tasks and rapid budget consumption. A growing queue without worker exceptions can still be a delivery incident. Correlate attempts and provider evidence while keeping private content out of general telemetry. Enqueue success is one stage of the journey, not its final outcome.

    22.4.18 · Infrastructure cost considerations

    Include intent and attempt storage, provider-submitted units, workers, callbacks, transfer, and operating effort. Retries can create billable work even when they do not produce a useful delivery.

    Model channel_unit_price×submitted_units using explicit inputs. Content length and character encoding may change SMS billing under the provider contract, which must be checked rather than assumed. Compare cost per accepted intent and per relevant successful delivery. They explain different parts of the service and should not be mixed in one denominator.

    22.4.19 · Alternative architectures and trade-offs

    Direct synchronous sending has little infrastructure but ties the user path to the provider. Durable queued delivery adds recoverable state and a separate delay. Orchestration can make multi-channel escalation explicit; event reactions may distribute coordination but make total progress harder to see.

    A backup provider adds another recovery option and another uncertainty boundary. Choose using message expiry, criticality, and the evidence each provider supplies. A solution that eventually sends something is insufficient when the message must be timely, permitted, and meaningfully tracked.

    22.4.20 · Architecture evolution from small scale to large scale

    Start with one sender behind a contract. Add durable intent and a worker when required work must survive failure or leave the user's latency path. Add channel strategies and factories for real variation.

    Separate critical and bulk resources as volume and harm justify it. Provider failover and escalation come after the uncertain-outcome policy is explicit. Preserve stable task, template, and attempt identities through these changes, rather than treating scaling as permission to create fresh effects for the same intent.

    22.4.21 · Design review identifying weaknesses and improvements

    Review whether “delivered” overstates the evidence, whether expiry and current preferences are checked, and whether failover can duplicate a message. These are product and protocol questions.

    Test send-then-crash, forged or repeated callbacks, preference revocation after enqueue, template updates, and channel saturation. Confirm terminal progress does not regress under late events. A dashboard of successful submission requests cannot establish that the intended people received timely messages under the chosen policy.

    22.4.22 · A short implementation exercise

    Build a recording sender that stores a submission but returns uncertainty. Process the same task again and inspect the local attempt identities and resulting state. It must not invent evidence of delivery.

    Add expiry and current-preference checks. Then switch provider after the uncertain attempt and show why this can produce a second external effect. Implement only the recovery behaviour your mock provider contract supports, and make any residual duplicate risk explicit in the result.

    A small implementation of the key rule

    PSEUDOCODE · ONE PART OF THE DESIGN

    def deliver(task, now):
    require_current_attempt(task)
    if now >= task.expires_at: return mark_expired(task)
    if not permitted_now(task): return mark_cancelled(task)
    sender = sender_factory.for_channel(task.channel)
    result = sender.send(task.stable_provider_key, render(task))
    if result.uncertain:
        return persist_uncertain(task, result.reference)
    return persist_submission_result(task, result)
# A provider acknowledgment is not a human-read receipt.

    Use the implementation exercise to test the rule and the failure described above. You can also run local examples of seat claims, duplicate handling, ledger balance, and workflow epochs in the mechanism collection.

    PART 6 / UNIT 22 / CHAPTER 22.5

    Social Media Feed

    Prerequisites: Data Models and Storage Technologies, Caching and Content Delivery, Scalability, Load Balancing, and Data Distribution, Message Queues, Events, and Distributed Workflows4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Preparing every follower feed makes reads cheaper but multiplies writes. Compare where the work belongs while keeping private and deleted posts out of every served page.

    The workload, timing, and prices in this design are teaching assumptions. They are not measured benchmarks or a description of a particular company.

    22.5.1 · Functional requirements

    Users publish posts, follow accounts, and read a ranked home feed. The feed must support bounded continuation and obey privacy, blocking, moderation, and deletion rules.

    Ranking chooses among posts the viewer is allowed to see. A high score cannot override denial. Engagement counts and candidate lists can update later than the original post, but the product needs to state what freshness those derived views permit. Separate finding interesting content from deciding which content is authorised.

    22.5.2 · Nonfunctional requirements

    Assume a 300 ms p99 feed target under the supported workload. Retain accepted posts and define how quickly access changes must take effect. Pagination should have understandable duplicate and omission behaviour.

    Ranking can change between refreshes. Decide whether each refresh begins a new generation and what a continuation cursor preserves. Cached candidates may be old, so specify which properties are rechecked at serving time. These conditions are part of a useful feed response alongside its latency.

    22.5.3 · Explicit assumptions and workload numbers

    Assume ten million daily readers, twenty feed reads each, and one million posts/day. The read total is 200 million/day, or about 2,315/s on average.

    For a simplified ordinary-author model, assume one hundred followers per author and 32 bytes per materialised candidate reference. Fan-out creates one hundred million references/day, or 3.2 GB raw. A celebrity with millions of followers is a different traffic class. The average cannot describe that author's burst or inactive followers' unused work.

    22.5.4 · Naive initial architecture

    Begin with indexed posts and follow relationships, building the feed when requested. This avoids writing a copy for every follower and keeps the initial system small.

    As users follow more authors, candidate retrieval and ranking can require too much work per read. Measure those costs and the follower distribution. Materialising every feed immediately can replace read pressure with large unused write pressure. Introduce that trade-off only when the repeated read work justifies maintaining another representation.

    22.5.5 · Core API contracts

    POST /posts creates a versioned post; POST /follows changes the relationship. GET /feed returns a bounded page, continuation cursor, and relevant ranking generation. DELETE /posts/{id} records authoritative removal.

    Bind cursors to the viewer and applicable filters, and explain their snapshot or continuation semantics. A cursor does not grant continuing permission to content after access changes. Validate it and reapply the required visibility policy whenever the next page is served.

    22.5.6 · Data model and schema

    Post records include identity, author, version, visibility, state, and creation time. Follow records connect follower and author. Optional feed candidates connect a reader to a post and source version with ranking information.

    Keep model version or generation where reproducibility needs it. Candidates are derived references, while posts and access relationships remain authoritative. Stable source identity lets workers recognise repeated work, remove or suppress old results, and rebuild views. State whether copied features are snapshots or values expected to follow updates.

    22.5.7 · Low-level component organization

    PostService owns publication and FollowService owns relationship changes. CandidateGenerator retrieves or prepares references. FeatureFetcher supplies bounded ranking inputs, Ranker scores them, and VisibilityFilter enforces access. FeedAssembler combines results, removes duplicates, and produces pages.

    Keep the access decision independent of desirability. Missing features can change order; they must not broaden visibility. These roles let performance work focus on candidate or feature costs while preserving a separate rule for what the viewer may receive.

    22.5.8 · High-level system architecture

    Use a durable publication path with an outbox. Workers prepare candidates for ordinary authors; high-fan-out authors can be pulled at read time. Candidate storage, ranking compute, and permitted caches complete the serving path.

    This hybrid avoids immediately writing to every celebrity follower while making common reads cheaper. It adds strategy-selection and reconciliation work. Separate model deployment decisions from the live data path, and preserve source state and access checks when cached or materialised results lag.

    22.5.9 · Data and control flows

    Publication commits the post and fan-out intent. Workers add candidate references under stable identity. A read combines prepared and pulled candidates, checks current required permissions and post state, obtains bounded features, ranks, deduplicates, and returns a continuation.

    Track the generation involved. A deleted candidate may physically remain while serving correctly rejects it. That is acceptable only under the chosen deletion policy. Storage cleanup and permission to expose the reference are separate events with different completion requirements.

    22.5.10 · Capacity estimates

    The assumed 200 million daily reads average about 2,315/s. With an illustrative fivefold peak, the rate becomes about 11,574/s. One million posts times one hundred followers produces one hundred million candidate writes/day.

    A single post by an author with ten million followers creates a separate burst. Also estimate candidates ranked per read and feature-lookup amplification. API rates alone miss much of the storage and compute work, especially when an apparently small feed request fans out to many dependencies.

    22.5.11 · End-to-end latency estimates

    Assume 20 ms at the edge, 50 ms retrieving candidates, 80 ms fetching features, 70 ms ranking, and 30 ms preparing the response. The proposed path sums to 250 ms before additional tail and queue allowance.

    Measure against the 300 ms objective rather than calling this sum p99. A required slow feature call can dominate the request. Define a safe missing-feature response, and measure publication freshness separately from read latency. Fast reads can still show an outdated or empty feed.

    22.5.12 · Failure scenarios

    A worker can repeat fan-out after a crash, so candidate identity must suppress duplicate effects. A celebrity burst needs the selected pull or controlled distribution path rather than unlimited queue growth.

    Candidate cleanup can lag privacy changes, making current serving checks important. If ranking fails, an authorised chronological feed may be an acceptable fallback. It must still reject deleted or forbidden content. Test the fallback's semantics as well as its speed; returning something quickly does not make it a valid feed.

    22.5.13 · Scalability improvements

    Partition candidate work by a measured ownership key, batch feature reads, and cache values within their freshness scope. Bound how many candidates a read retrieves and ranks. Give rebuilds separate budgets so they do not consume all live-serving capacity.

    Do not increase workers past storage capacity. Choose the hybrid threshold from observed write amplification, reader activity, and read cost. Moving an author between push and pull needs a transition that prevents missing or duplicated candidates. A threshold is a design parameter to revisit, not a universal follower count.

    22.5.14 · Consistency requirements

    Post identity, updates, and deletion need a suitable local transactional authority. Feed projections and engagement totals may propagate later. An author expecting to see their own new post may need a direct-source overlay or another supported path.

    Access policy must still meet its own freshness rule when candidates are stale. Specify which parts of a page belong to a ranking snapshot and which are revalidated. The feed has several consistency boundaries, so one label cannot describe all its accepted observations.

    22.5.15 · Security model

    Enforce author permissions, viewer visibility, blocks, and moderation on each relevant path. Validate cursors, bound scraping and feature-query amplification, and keep client-provided scores from influencing permission.

    Ranking logs can contain private behaviour, so retain only justified information with controlled access. Propagate required deletion into feature and analytical copies as well as post storage. The model's input and output paths need the same tenant and content-scope discipline as the main feed response.

    22.5.16 · Deployment approach

    Version rankers and use representative canary cohorts, checking rollback compatibility with stored features. Roll fan-out formats out so mixed-version readers remain valid.

    Keep rebuilding capacity separate from live publication and reads. A region-local feed needs a defined route for source and access-policy changes before it can promise both locality and the required privacy behaviour. Model release is another kind of serving change, so observe it with the same care as application code and schema deployment.

    22.5.17 · Observability design

    Track publication-to-candidate delay, candidate counts, denied visibility, read latency, feature tails, model version, duplication, and hot-author backlog. Measure relevance and useful content separately from infrastructure timing.

    A low p99 does not establish that pages contain correct, varied, current results. Pair operational indicators with suitable content and privacy checks. Detailed evidence should identify generations and source versions without making every post or user an unbounded metric label.

    22.5.18 · Infrastructure cost considerations

    Costs include candidate-write amplification, feature storage and reads, ranking CPU, responses, and rebuilds. The simplified 3.2 GB/day of raw references excludes indexes and other metadata.

    Compare push and pull using how many followers actually read. Preparing feeds for inactive users can spend work that is never used. Use explicit fictional rates or current verified quotes. A cost comparison is meaningful only when visibility, retention, freshness, and recovery requirements are equal.

    22.5.19 · Alternative architectures and trade-offs

    Fan-out-on-write spends more when posts arrive to make reads cheaper. Fan-out-on-read avoids unused preparation but adds work to each read. A hybrid targets different traffic classes while adding policy and transition complexity.

    Precomputed ranking can reduce serving CPU and introduce another freshness delay. Compare these choices against actual active-reader ratios and author skew. A lower average read time obtained by weakening deletion or privacy is a different contract. Keep that distinction visible when evaluating the trade-off.

    22.5.20 · Architecture evolution from small scale to large scale

    Start with indexed pull reads, then add bounded ranking and useful caching. Materialise ordinary-author candidates when repeated read work becomes the limiting cost. Introduce a separate high-fan-out path after observing skew.

    Regional copies require source-version and privacy-update rules. Revisit thresholds as posting, reading, and follow distributions change. Stable candidate identity and explicit generation boundaries should survive each stage so the new arrangement preserves continuation and duplicate behaviour.

    22.5.21 · Design review identifying weaknesses and improvements

    Test the assumptions about inactive readers, high-degree authors, and revoked access. Place a post in cached candidate pages, then delete it or make it private. Verify that later serving follows the required rule.

    Replay a fan-out event, pause a worker, and disable a feature dependency. Check both the resulting feed and fallback access. A drained queue does not prove that every intended reader received one usable authorised candidate; validate the identities and source versions involved.

    22.5.22 · A short implementation exercise

    Build push and pull candidate generation over a small follow graph with one very high-degree author. Count writes and reads for explicit user journeys rather than relying only on averages.

    After materialising candidates, delete a post and check the serving filter. Replay a fan-out event and verify there is no visible duplicate. Explain which strategy spends work for inactive readers and which moves it into active reads, keeping privacy checks identical in both.

    A small implementation of the key rule

    PSEUDOCODE · ONE PART OF THE DESIGN

    def feed(reader, cursor):
    candidates = materialized(reader) + pull_hot_authors(reader)
    unique = deduplicate_by_post_id(candidates)
    permitted = [p for p in unique if visible_now(reader, p)]
    features = fetch_bounded_features(permitted)
    ranked = rank(permitted, features, model_version)
    return page(ranked, validated_cursor(cursor, reader))

    Use the implementation exercise to test the rule and the failure described above. You can also run local examples of seat claims, duplicate handling, ledger balance, and workflow epochs in the mechanism collection.
