    PART 6 / UNIT 22 / CHAPTER 22.6

    Video Streaming Platform

    Prerequisites: Networking Foundations for System Design, Caching and Content Delivery, File Systems, Search Infrastructure, and Data Pipelines, Deployment, Cloud Infrastructure, and Platform Architecture4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    An encoder has written two of three required segments. Decide what makes the video ready, how a retry resumes, and which references a viewer is permitted to fetch.

    The workload, timing, and prices in this design are teaching assumptions. They are not measured benchmarks or a description of a particular company.

    22.6.1 · Functional requirements

    An owner uploads a video, the service validates and converts it, and viewers receive an authorised playback manifest and media segments. Support resumable uploads, processing progress, and deletion.

    Adaptive playback chooses among available renditions as conditions change. It cannot correct a missing segment or a manifest published before its required outputs exist. The product therefore needs both a byte-transformation workflow and a clear decision that a particular generation is ready to play.

    22.6.2 · Nonfunctional requirements

    Preserve original and required derived media according to stated durability and retention rules. Set playback-start and smoothness objectives for supported clients, measured through the delivery journey.

    Asynchronous processing must expose failed and review states, not leave users waiting on an unexplained spinner. Protect private manifests, segments, thumbnails, and download links as well as the player page. A private metadata row cannot compensate for public media objects that anyone can fetch directly.

    22.6.3 · Explicit assumptions and workload numbers

    Assume 1,000 uploads/day, each averaging 1 GB and thirty minutes. Raw input is 1 TB/day and 500 source-hours/day. Assume the chosen renditions produce five output GB for each source GB, giving 5 TB/day derived data.

    For 10,000 simultaneous viewers averaging 3 Mb/s each, delivery is 30 Gb/s, or 3.75 GB/s, before overhead. Encoding, retention, and playback therefore impose different capacity needs. These ratios are teaching assumptions rather than codec or infrastructure benchmarks.

    22.6.4 · Naive initial architecture

    A prototype can accept an upload and have one worker produce one playback file. It is simple but places large transfer and computation behind fragile local execution and offers little adaptation to changing networks.

    Direct upload to storage removes much of the byte traffic from application workers. Durable encoding tasks preserve required progress. Begin with a small supported rendition set. Producing every possible format immediately adds compute and storage that may never be useful to the intended viewers.

    22.6.5 · Core API contracts

    POST /videos creates an upload intent. Scoped multipart authorisation permits the byte transfer. A completion operation validates the stored content, a status endpoint reports processing, and a playback endpoint returns an authorised manifest reference.

    Deletion tracks the required cleanup. Define the scope, lifetime, and cache behaviour of playback capabilities. An old page URL should not silently grant indefinite access. The status contract must distinguish upload complete, processing, playable, and failed rather than treating every accepted byte as ready media.

    22.6.6 · Data model and schema

    Store video identity, owner, source version, and state. Upload sessions track unfinished transfers. Encoding jobs identify input digest, profile version, and attempt epoch. Renditions identify profile, version, object key, and checksum; a manifest generation names its required artifacts.

    Publish only when that set is verified. Do not change bytes behind an immutable published reference without a version transition. Link derived objects to their source and owner so deletion, repair, and inventory reconciliation can find the whole media lifecycle.

    22.6.7 · Low-level component organization

    UploadService owns upload permission. MediaValidator checks supported bounded input. EncodingPlanner chooses profiles, WorkerLease manages attempts, and TranscoderAdapter performs isolated conversion. ArtifactPublisher advances published metadata when the required outputs are verified.

    PlaybackService checks access and issues scoped delivery references. Keep transformation separate from publication. A worker can finish writing one file without making the video's complete generation playable. The metadata transition needs evidence about the entire required artifact set.

    22.6.8 · High-level system architecture

    Use object storage for immutable sources and segments, a durable workflow and task queue, isolated transcoders, metadata storage, and an edge delivery path. The application handles control and access while large bytes flow directly through storage and CDN facilities.

    Keep source and derived retention policies explicit. Untrusted media parsers need limited resources and suitable execution and egress permissions. The source store, workflow state, and published generation each have recovery responsibilities that a task queue alone does not supply.

    22.6.9 · Data and control flows

    Validate completed upload identity, choose a versioned encoding plan, and produce artifacts under an attempt identity. Verify the required segment and manifest set, then atomically publish the playable metadata generation.

    Failed attempts leave unpublished outputs for cleanup or safe reuse. A client obtains an authorised manifest and fetches supported renditions through the delivery path. Marking ready after the first output is valid only if progressive publication is an explicit supported contract. Otherwise it exposes a partially usable video as complete.

    22.6.10 · Capacity estimates

    Thirty days under the assumptions need 30 TB of original data plus 150 TB of renditions before extra copies and overhead. Viewer delivery at 30 Gb/s is far larger than the metadata API's transfer.

    Encoding cost needs measured source-duration and codec ratios. If an assumed two compute-hours are needed per source-hour, 500 source-hours/day require 1,000 compute-hours/day. This is a model input, not a performance result. Use real content and profiles to measure the ratio before sizing workers.

    22.6.11 · End-to-end latency estimates

    Assume 50 ms for playback authorisation, 30 ms for manifest delivery, and 800 ms for initial buffering. That path totals 880 ms in the example.

    A cache miss or a constrained client changes it. Measure startup, rebuffering, rendition switches, and failures independently of the metadata API's p99. The viewer's experience includes segment delivery and player behaviour. A fast permission endpoint establishes little about a missing or slowly delivered first segment.

    22.6.12 · Failure scenarios

    An upload stops halfway. An input is corrupt. A worker writes two segments and crashes before the third. A manifest points to a deleted object. Each needs a distinct state and supported repair path.

    Keep unfinished generations unpublished and validate the final set. Protect the origin if the edge path fails; fallback can suddenly send enormous video traffic to it. Deletion and revoked access must affect playable references and copies according to the chosen capability and cache policy. Test through the actual media path.

    22.6.13 · Scalability improvements

    Scale upload bytes, encoding jobs, and viewer delivery separately. Bound worker concurrency and prioritise encoding according to deadlines. Immutable segments are suitable for caching where access policy permits it.

    A viral video creates hot-object delivery pressure, not necessarily a metadata-sharding problem. Plan origin protection and regional copy cost during cache loss. Adding profiles or transcoders can also increase storage and backfill load. Improve the measured limiting path rather than expanding every component together.

    22.6.14 · Consistency requirements

    The published metadata generation must name a usable artifact set. Encoding attempts can repeat using stable output identities and conditional completion, so an old worker cannot replace a newer generation.

    Playback caches have a declared reuse interval; private access and deletion have their own requirements. Before using regional copies for recovery, ensure the publication protocol establishes the required objects there. Merely copying some bytes does not make a region an authoritative complete failover source.

    22.6.15 · Security model

    Authorise upload and playback, limit size and supported formats, and isolate parsers and encoders. Give workers narrowly scoped storage access. Protect signed capabilities and keep them out of routine logs.

    Check manifest, segment, and thumbnail delivery: private metadata can coexist accidentally with public objects. Test capability expiry, cache keys, membership revocation, and deletion end to end. The player's page is only one route to the content and should not be the only place enforcing its privacy.

    22.6.16 · Deployment approach

    Version encoding profiles and retain usable older outputs until a validated transition permits removal. Workers need durable claims and graceful shutdown. Expensive backfills should not consume playback or live-processing capacity.

    Test recovery when source bytes survive but metadata is restored to an older point. Artifact inventories and source identities must let the application reconcile what exists. A rollout that preserves running containers but loses the link between metadata and media can still leave acknowledged videos unusable.

    22.6.17 · Observability design

    Observe upload completion, oldest encoding jobs, failed profiles, compute-to-media ratios, and ready-generation integrity. For playback, track edge hits, origin transfer, startup delay, rebuffering, and access outcomes.

    Correlate source, profile, and playback generation in appropriate detail. Alert on missing segments and videos stuck processing, even if workers report few exceptions. A synthetic private-video journey should include permitted playback and later revocation, so monitoring covers content access as well as infrastructure availability.

    22.6.18 · Infrastructure cost considerations

    Include originals, renditions, repeated encoding, compute, delivery requests, transfer, metadata, and telemetry. Sustaining the assumed 3.75 GB/s for an hour delivers 13.5 TB before overhead.

    The duration of viewer demand matters as much as a peak concurrency label. Compare profile count and retention with quality needs. Use fictional labelled rates for examples or verified current quotes for spending. A smaller rendition set can save costs while changing playback choices, so evaluate the user effect as well as the storage total.

    22.6.19 · Alternative architectures and trade-offs

    A single file is easy to manage but adapts poorly to varying delivery conditions. Segmented adaptive delivery adds manifests and a larger artifact lifecycle. Pre-encoding offers readiness while consuming work and storage for profiles that may never be used.

    On-demand encoding can reduce unused work and create startup or burst risk. Managed conversion moves selected operations to a provider while leaving publication, access, and reconciliation decisions. Compare alternatives with the same supported-client, privacy, and recovery requirements.

    22.6.20 · Architecture evolution from small scale to large scale

    Start with resumable upload and durable processing identity. Add a small tested adaptive set and versioned publication. Then introduce suitable edge delivery and scale encoding separately from playback.

    Add regional objects or more profiles for demonstrated locality, recovery, or quality needs. Keep exact source and profile identities so every result remains explainable and reproducible. More delivery capacity should not change what ready, private, or deleted means for an existing video.

    22.6.21 · Design review identifying weaknesses and improvements

    Ask whether every ready generation is actually playable, whether its private segments remain protected, and whether origin survives edge loss. These are separate claims requiring separate evidence.

    Test corrupt input, worker interruption between artifacts and publication, repeated completion, a missing segment, expired access, and deletion after caching. A video that played once through a warm public URL proves little about private recovery, partial encoding, or the failed-delivery path.

    22.6.22 · A short implementation exercise

    Build a toy publisher requiring three segments. Write two and stop. The manifest must remain unpublished. Resume using the same job identity, write the third, validate checksums, and advance one metadata generation atomically.

    Then remove a segment deliberately and run an integrity check. The check should identify the broken published set. Explain which boundary establishes ready state and which later failure the integrity check detects, rather than using one success flag for both.

    A small implementation of the key rule

    PSEUDOCODE · ONE PART OF THE DESIGN

    def publish(job):
    require_current_epoch(job)
    artifacts = expected_artifacts(job.source, job.profile)
    require(all(exists_and_valid(a) for a in artifacts))
    with transaction():
        assert_current_epoch(job)
        generation = record_complete_manifest(artifacts)
        mark_playable(job.video, generation)
# Partial worker output is never silently declared ready.

    Use the implementation exercise to test the rule and the failure described above. You can also run local examples of seat claims, duplicate handling, ledger balance, and workflow epochs in the mechanism collection.

    PART 6 / UNIT 22 / CHAPTER 22.7

    Ride-Hailing System

    Prerequisites: Data Models and Storage Technologies, Scalability, Load Balancing, and Data Distribution, Distributed Systems Fundamentals, Message Queues, Events, and Distributed Workflows4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Two riders select the same nearby driver. Spatial search can find candidates; an authoritative claim must decide who actually receives the assignment.

    The workload, timing, and prices in this design are teaching assumptions. They are not measured benchmarks or a description of a particular company.

    22.7.1 · Functional requirements

    A driver reports location and availability. A rider requests a trip; the system finds candidates, offers work, and records one accepted assignment. It also tracks trip progress and cancellation.

    Being nearby makes a driver a candidate, not a confirmed owner of the trip. Define offer expiry and the rider's view while matching is unresolved. The same driver must not become actively assigned to incompatible trips merely because two matchers saw an old available state.

    22.7.2 · Nonfunctional requirements

    Set a bounded machine-side dispatch target for the assumed region and preserve exclusive active assignments. Protect precise location information. Treat the freshness and accuracy of reported positions as uncertainty, not ground truth.

    Trip transitions must survive retries and temporary disconnection. A missing heartbeat does not establish that a trip ended. Human offer acceptance and provider payment status also have different timelines. Keep these states visible rather than collapsing every delay into one failed trip outcome.

    22.7.3 · Explicit assumptions and workload numbers

    Assume 100,000 online drivers report every five seconds. The rate is 20,000 updates/s. At 100 raw bytes per position, that is 2 MB/s, or 172.8 GB/day if every update is retained.

    Assume 100 new trip requests/s. Map calls, candidate evaluation, regional skew, and location retention require separate estimates. The large location stream and the smaller authoritative assignment workload do not need the same storage or coordination mechanism.

    22.7.4 · Naive initial architecture

    Begin with one service that stores recent positions and selects a nearby available driver. It is straightforward while requests are handled sequentially, but concurrent matchers can select the same driver.

    Separate the location projection used for search from authoritative assignment state. Preserve exclusive claims before optimising spatial queries. A better nearest-neighbour lookup improves candidates; it cannot resolve two buyers of the same driver's availability. Stale positions can also reduce match quality even when the assignment invariant remains correct.

    22.7.5 · Core API contracts

    A driver location update carries position, source sequence, and observed time. POST /trips creates a stable rider request. POST /offers/{id}/accept attempts a valid claim, while trip status and cancellation expose explicit transitions.

    Derive driver identity from authentication and validate plausible input. An expired or superseded offer returns a defined conflict. A repeated accept can recover the existing result. The API must not permit a caller-supplied driver identifier to replace another assignment without passing the ownership rule.

    22.7.6 · Data model and schema

    Keep driver_state with availability, assignment_id, and version. Trip records contain rider, state, driver, and version. Offers identify the trip, driver, expiry, and status. Latest positions carry driver sequence, spatial cell, and observation time.

    Retained location history has a separate restricted lifecycle. A conditional transition or appropriate uniqueness constraint protects active assignment. The spatial index is derived candidate state; it must not become a second independent authority for whether a driver is free.

    22.7.7 · Low-level component organization

    LocationIngestor validates updates and their order. SpatialIndex finds candidates, Matcher ranks a bounded set, and OfferService manages offer validity. AssignmentRepository performs the authoritative claim, while TripStateMachine controls later transitions.

    Map and ETA adapters have their own deadlines. Their failure must not corrupt assignment. Stable trip and acceptance identities let clients retry without starting different logical work. Keep the availability decision at its atomic owner even when candidate selection runs on many workers.

    22.7.8 · High-level system architecture

    Use a regional location stream and spatial projection, a durable trip/assignment store, matching workers, offer delivery, and trip events. Partition geography for useful query locality while defining driver movement across boundaries.

    Configuration can come from a control plane, but stale independent availability copies must not each accept the same driver. The placement needs one valid authority or transfer protocol for assignment. Region-local candidate reads and exclusive ownership are different paths and should appear separately in the design.

    22.7.9 · Data and control flows

    Commit one rider request identity. Search for sufficiently fresh candidates, recheck authoritative availability, and create a bounded-lifetime offer. Acceptance verifies that the offer and ownership conditions still hold.

    Atomically bind the driver and trip under the chosen transaction model. Replay repeated accepts or reject stale ones. If the reply is lost, trip status resolves the client's uncertainty. Receiving an offer is not itself the assignment decision; the conditional acceptance is the point that prevents incompatible winners.

    22.7.10 · Capacity estimates

    The example ingests 20,000 locations/s and receives 100 dispatches/s. If each dispatch evaluates twenty candidates, that adds 2,000 candidate evaluations/s before retries or ETA calls.

    Do not call a route service for every location update without justification. Busy centres and major events can concentrate work in one area while global averages look mild. Estimate regional peaks, hot cells, and movement across their edges. Candidate pruning can reduce map cost without changing the exclusive assignment rule.

    22.7.11 · End-to-end latency estimates

    Assume 30 ms ingress, 40 ms candidate lookup, 80 ms bounded ETA evaluation, and 30 ms assignment work. The machine-side planning budget sums to 180 ms.

    Human acceptance is a separate interval. Missing candidates, offer expiry, communication delays, and retries can extend the matching journey. Measure these states rather than announcing one optimistic dispatch latency. The budget is illustrative and needs validation for actual city shapes, traffic, and provider behaviour.

    22.7.12 · Failure scenarios

    Reject late location updates that would move the serving projection backward under its sequence rule. When two requests select one driver, only one authoritative claim may succeed. A paused worker cannot accept a superseded offer after it resumes.

    Lost offers or replies need status recovery. A map outage may permit a justified simpler ranking or require pausing matching. It must not bypass exclusive assignment. Test each failure at the relevant state boundary so a candidate-search problem does not become a conflicting trip commitment.

    22.7.13 · Scalability improvements

    Scale the location stream and spatial serving independently from assignment transactions. Batch or prune ETA calls. Partition regions or cells with an explicit handoff that preserves the current driver's authority.

    Candidate caches need freshness information. More matchers do not divide a hot serialised claim owner automatically; changing that model must still preserve one active assignment. Observe the actual concentrated work before choosing finer partitions, since they also increase cross-cell queries and movement coordination.

    22.7.14 · Consistency requirements

    Location can update through a delayed projection with an explicit age policy. Driver and trip assignment require a coordinated conditional transition. Crossing a regional boundary needs authority transfer rather than independent acceptance in both regions.

    Give trip status the required read-after-accept behaviour. Time helps judge whether a position is recent, but sequence and fencing rules handle stale updates and owners. These different forms of state should not all be given the same broad consistency label.

    22.7.15 · Security model

    Authenticate driver updates and restrict rider and driver views to the relevant trip context. Limit access to precise location history, including support and administrative paths. Retain only justified history and audit privileged use.

    Bound geographic scraping and expensive map requests. A rider cannot select an arbitrary driver identity as authority to claim them. Keep raw coordinates out of broad telemetry where unnecessary. Privacy follows locations through streams, candidate caches, exports, and retained logs, not just the map displayed to the user.

    22.7.16 · Deployment approach

    Use regional placement with a stated failure model and durable assignment state. Roll releases compatibly with old clients and offers already in progress. Drain new work while preserving existing offer and trip records.

    Disaster recovery must reconcile active assignments and uncertain provider outcomes. Restoring an old snapshot must not reoffer drivers still assigned elsewhere. The replacement needs valid history and fencing before it acts, even if the API has resumed responding. Test the recovery path with active trips rather than only an empty system.

    22.7.17 · Observability design

    Track location age, stale-update rejection, cell skew, candidate counts, claim conflicts, expiry, matching outcomes, and time spent in each dispatch state. Observe map-provider errors separately.

    Correlate stable creation and acceptance identities across attempts. Alert on unresolved assignments and invariant violations, not only HTTP errors. Simulated drivers can move across cells, disconnect, and accept near expiry while concurrent riders compete. These journeys test the distinction between fresh candidates and correct exclusive outcomes.

    22.7.18 · Infrastructure cost considerations

    Include ingestion, hot location state, maps/ETA calls, assignments, offer attempts, history retention, transfer, and operations. A route lookup for every position update could dominate the cost despite efficient state storage.

    Model calls per candidate and dispatch, then compare pruning and batching. Use explicit fictional rates or verified commercial terms. The example does not claim a real company's internal bill. Keep the accuracy and latency effects of a cheaper candidate strategy visible alongside its savings.

    22.7.19 · Alternative architectures and trade-offs

    Straight-line proximity is cheap but may ignore road travel. Route-based ETA can improve ranking while adding delay and an external dependency. Sequential offers reduce simultaneous acceptance opportunities; multi-offer designs need a controlled single winner.

    Fine spatial cells improve some lookup locality but add boundary queries and handoff work. Compare fairness and rider outcomes too. Candidate quality, human wait, and machine cost all matter, while none can justify weakening the active-assignment invariant.

    22.7.20 · Architecture evolution from small scale to large scale

    First establish a correct regional claim and basic proximity search. Add streamed positions and spatial indexing when lookup work requires it. Then distribute matching with bounded ETA evaluation.

    Split geographic ownership after measuring hot areas, using a safe transfer procedure. Regional serving adds another partition and failure policy for active trips. Preserve stable identities and claims as the deployment grows. Replicating an apparently stateless matcher does not replicate the assignment authority it depends on.

    22.7.21 · Design review identifying weaknesses and improvements

    Review the meanings of nearby, recently observed, available, offered, and assigned. The spatial index answers only some of those questions.

    Test two riders choosing one driver, out-of-order positions, acceptance after expiry, paused workers, and ownership handoff. One claim should win and losers should receive a meaningful state. Confirm the search projection never acts as an independent writer of authoritative availability. A fast matching demo can otherwise hide the most consequential race.

    22.7.22 · A short implementation exercise

    Build an optimistic driver claim with expected version and offer expiry. Start two requests using the same initial version. Verify one claim succeeds locally and one returns conflict.

    Then deliver an older location and a delayed acceptance after the winner commits. Neither should overwrite the active assignment. Explain the actual protected boundary: the local transaction can establish one local owner, while external trip or payment effects still need their own contracts and recovery evidence.

    A small implementation of the key rule

    PSEUDOCODE · ONE PART OF THE DESIGN

    def accept_offer(offer, driver, now):
    with transaction():
        current = lock_offer(offer.id)
        require(current.pending and now < current.expires_at)
        won = claim_driver_if_available(driver, current.expected_version)
        if not won: raise AssignmentConflict
        bind_trip_and_offer(offer.trip, driver, offer.id)
    return current_trip_state(offer.trip)

    Use the implementation exercise to test the rule and the failure described above. You can also run local examples of seat claims, duplicate handling, ledger balance, and workflow epochs in the mechanism collection.

    PART 6 / UNIT 22 / CHAPTER 22.8

    Online Ticket Booking

    Prerequisites: API Design and Communication Contracts, Database Internals, Transactions, and Concurrency Control, Message Queues, Events, and Distributed Workflows, Security Architecture and Privacy4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A payment succeeds just after a seat hold expires. Follow the reservation, current seat owner, and provider evidence to find an outcome that does not sell the seat twice.

    The workload, timing, and prices in this design are teaching assumptions. They are not measured benchmarks or a description of a particular company.

    22.8.1 · Functional requirements

    A buyer browses an event, holds selected seats, pays, and receives tickets. Holds last for a defined period; cancellation and refunds follow an explicit policy.

    The displayed seat map is advisory. The authoritative reservation decides who owns the opportunity to buy a seat. Retries, expiry tasks, and payment callbacks may overlap, but must not confirm the same seat for two buyers. Design that invariant before optimising the map or launching a waiting room.

    22.8.2 · Nonfunctional requirements

    Prevent duplicate confirmed ownership and retain accepted payment and ticket records under the chosen failure contract. Pending reservations must resolve through supported confirmation, expiry, or recovery.

    Set booking and waiting-room objectives for launches, including the intended fairness policy. Fixed inventory cannot satisfy every simultaneous request. Reject or queue excess demand clearly instead of promising universal acceptance and overselling. Separate an admitted transaction's latency from the user's total time waiting for admission and payment.

    22.8.3 · Explicit assumptions and workload numbers

    Assume 50,000 seats and a short peak of 100,000 reservation attempts/s. At 200 raw bytes per seat, seat records occupy about 10 MB before indexes.

    The small byte total does not make the launch easy. Many callers compete for the same limited ownership transitions. Assume two-minute holds and a bounded number of seats per user. Retry volume, transaction conflicts, and expiry work need their own capacity estimates. These assumptions are a launch scenario, not a benchmark for a particular database.

    22.8.4 · Naive initial architecture

    Start with a transactional seat table. Claim a seat using a conditional change from available to reserved, and insert its reservation in the same transaction.

    A read followed by an unconditional update can let both callers report success. The conditional claim must check its result. This first correct boundary handles simpler traffic; flash demand, payment uncertainty, and expiry races motivate further controls. Fixing concurrency first prevents a faster interface from merely producing incorrect tickets more quickly.

    22.8.5 · Core API contracts

    POST /reservations includes event, seat identities, and an idempotency key. The returned resource exposes status and expiry. A payment operation belongs to that reservation, and authorised ticket reads show committed issuance.

    Repeat keys recover the established result rather than claiming another seat. Bind them to the trusted actor and request content. Payment states distinguish authorisation, capture, decline, and uncertainty according to the provider. An expired reservation and an uncertain payment are different conditions needing different next actions.

    22.8.6 · Data model and schema

    A seat identifies event and seat, state, reservation owner, and version. Reservation records hold owner, state, expiry, and version, with a relationship to selected seats. Payment operations and ticket records have their own identities.

    Enforce one relevant confirmed active ticket per seat. Expiry and confirmation check the reservation identity and current state/version. An old expiry task must not release a seat now held by a later reservation. These relationships need actual constraints or atomic checks, not just matching names in a diagram.

    22.8.7 · Low-level component organization

    SeatRepository performs conditional claims or locks. ReservationService manages selection and hold rules. PaymentWorkflow handles external effects, TicketIssuer commits valid issuance, and ExpiryWorker conditionally releases old holds.

    Pricing and refund rules use explicit amounts and units. Enforce ownership at the shared state boundary so callbacks and workers cannot bypass a check implemented only in an HTTP handler. Each role should return enough state to distinguish conflict, expiry, confirmed success, and an uncertain provider result.

    22.8.8 · High-level system architecture

    Place bounded admission or a waiting room before the ownership store. Keep durable reservation state, the payment adapter, a workflow or outbox path, and a ticket read model. Cache descriptions and advisory maps separately.

    Event partitioning can keep one event's seat operations local, but a popular event remains hot. Admission and contention control still matter. The cache answers what may be available; the transaction answers what this buyer actually reserved. Do not let those paths become competing allocation authorities.

    22.8.9 · Data and control flows

    Atomically claim seats and create the hold, then return its expiry after commit. Submit payment with stable provider identity. Confirmation verifies a still-valid transition and commits the required reservation, seat, and ticket changes.

    If payment succeeds after expiry, follow a defined recovery policy: reacquire only if safe or refund according to the contract. Never issue against a seat already owned by someone else. Expiry checks current identity and version before release, so delayed tasks cannot undo a later valid outcome.

    22.8.10 · Capacity estimates

    Assume admission is configured to allow 2,000 reservation attempts/s out of a 100,000/s launch. The remaining callers wait or receive rejection under the stated policy. That 2,000 limit is an input to validate, not demonstrated capacity.

    A two-minute hold is bounded by the number of seats, but the surrounding retry traffic is not. Estimate writes per attempt, repeated-key checks, conflicts, and expiry scans. Web concurrency can grow rapidly while the small inventory remains the same.

    22.8.11 · End-to-end latency estimates

    Assume 20 ms edge time, 30 ms acquiring the transaction resources, 40 ms for conditional seat/reservation work, and 20 ms returning the result. The admitted path totals 110 ms in this scenario.

    Contention can exceed that budget, so bound waiting and stop work that is no longer useful. Report waiting-room time separately. Payment has its own expiry-sensitive timeline. Fast admitted requests do not establish a fast journey for users still queued outside the allocation boundary.

    22.8.12 · Failure scenarios

    Two buyers must not both win after reading available. A crash after reservation commit but before reply needs repeat-key recovery. Duplicate payment evidence must not issue another ticket.

    Also test payment after hold expiry and stale expiry after confirmation or reassignment. Conditional current-state transitions and reconciliation protect these overlaps. If email fails after a ticket commits, the ticket still exists and needs another delivery path. Communication failure must not be mistaken for failure of the already accepted ownership transition.

    22.8.13 · Scalability improvements

    Cache advisory data, bound launch admission, and shorten the correct seat transaction. Partition independent events when measured load justifies it.

    Multi-seat claims need a deliberate all-or-nothing rule and consistent lock order. Splitting an event across shards can make group bookings harder. Extra shards do not split contention over one particular seat. Scale the work around the invariant while preserving its atomic owner, and introduce a more complex allocation protocol only when its benefit exceeds the added transaction and recovery burden.

    22.8.14 · Consistency requirements

    Seat ownership and ticket issuance need an atomic authoritative rule. Availability displays may lag if that is clear to the buyer. Payment and email are external effects with stable identities and tracked workflow state.

    A serializable local transaction can help with local concurrency but does not include the provider automatically. Handle retryable serialization failures with bounded whole-transaction retries and safe external-effect placement. State which records move together and which later outcomes are reconciled, rather than claiming the entire booking journey is one database transaction.

    22.8.15 · Security model

    Authorise holds, payments, tickets, transfers, and refunds. Calculate prices on the server, verify provider callbacks, and protect credentials. Limit automated and bulk abuse under a defined identity policy.

    Scope idempotency keys so one actor cannot recover another's result. If tickets use download capabilities, set their scope and lifetime and audit important changes. A waiting room protects capacity; it is not proof of authorised identity or fairness. Those policies still need their own enforcement and tests.

    22.8.16 · Deployment approach

    Keep reservation states and expiry meanings compatible during rollout. Durable scheduled expiry survives worker replacement. Database promotion must respect the acknowledged-data policy.

    After recovery, reconcile provider results before declaring all bookings resolved. When write authority is uncertain, temporarily pausing allocation can protect exclusive ownership while descriptions remain readable. Test these transitions with live holds and callbacks, not only an empty event. A newly running server must not treat an old snapshot as permission to sell seats already confirmed elsewhere.

    22.8.17 · Observability design

    Track admitted attempts, claim conflicts, transaction waits, hold age, expiry backlog, payment uncertainty, late success, and ticket uniqueness. Follow one logical booking through repeated requests and callbacks.

    Run appropriate invariant checks over seats, reservations, and tickets, with reconciliation against payment evidence. Empty error logs cannot establish that the relationships agree. Keep user-visible waiting and completion times separate from raw API times so operational dashboards reflect the actual booking journey.

    22.8.18 · Infrastructure cost considerations

    Include burst admission, transactional work, abandoned holds, payment calls, delivery, retention, telemetry, and recovery capacity. Model the duration of a launch rather than charging its peak rate for every hour of the month.

    More web workers cannot remove contention on one seat. Compare alternatives using the same no-double-ticket and recovery requirements. Use explicit fictional rates or verified prices, and include retry and expiry work that occurs even for buyers who never complete a purchase.

    22.8.19 · Alternative architectures and trade-offs

    Pessimistic locking serialises access early but can create waiting and deadlocks. Conditional optimistic claims return conflicts quickly but require clear retry and user handling. One event owner can simplify order while imposing a capacity boundary.

    Distributed allocation can reduce some central work and complicate multi-seat atomicity and fairness. Choose by the actual seat and hold contract. The mechanism must explain one winner under concurrent attempts, then integrate that winner with payment and expiry rather than stopping at a successful lock acquisition.

    22.8.20 · Architecture evolution from small scale to large scale

    First implement the seat transaction and repeat-key result. Add durable expiry and provider reconciliation. Then protect launches with admission and advisory caching.

    Partition independent events after measuring the workload. Change one-event allocation only when its demonstrated constraints justify the added protocol. Recheck no-double-ticket behaviour at every stage. Increasing traffic capacity is not progress if an earlier safe expiry or retry becomes an uncoordinated write in the new arrangement.

    22.8.21 · Design review identifying weaknesses and improvements

    Check that expiry and confirmation refer to the same reservation identity and current state. Review the recovery for a successful payment after the hold is gone, and confirm that display state never grants ownership.

    Test competing buyers, repeated callbacks, commit-then-crash, stale expiry after reassignment, and late payment. A correct happy-path seat update answers only part of the workflow. The review must also account for money and tickets that remain uncertain after the visible request ends.

    22.8.22 · A short implementation exercise

    Reproduce the last-seat race using two connections or an explicit interleaving. Show both buyers reporting success under naive reads and writes. Replace it with a conditional claim and reservation transaction, checking affected rows.

    Add versioned expiry. Confirm or reassign the seat, then deliver the old expiry task. It must leave the current owner's seat unchanged. Explain the condition that prevents the stale release, rather than relying on the test's usual timing.

    A small implementation of the key rule

    PSEUDOCODE · ONE PART OF THE DESIGN

    with transaction():
    insert_reservation(reservation_id, owner, expires_at)
    updated = reserve_if_available(event, seat, reservation_id)
    if updated != 1: raise SeatUnavailable
# Expiry later releases only the same current reservation version.
# Provider payment is coordinated outside this local transaction.

    Use the implementation exercise to test the rule and the failure described above. You can also run local examples of seat claims, duplicate handling, ledger balance, and workflow epochs in the mechanism collection.

    PART 6 / UNIT 22 / CHAPTER 22.9

    Payment System

    Prerequisites: API Design and Communication Contracts, Database Internals, Transactions, and Concurrency Control, Message Queues, Events, and Distributed Workflows, Reliability, Fault Tolerance, and Disaster Recovery, Security Architecture and Privacy4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A provider charges successfully, but the local service stops before recording the reply. Use stable identity and reconciliation to connect the external result to one valid local posting set.

    The workload, timing, and prices in this design are teaching assumptions. They are not measured benchmarks or a description of a particular company.

    22.9.1 · Functional requirements

    A client creates a payment intent, the service requests authorisation or capture, and later reports the supported outcome. It records balanced accounting entries, reconciles provider evidence, and tracks refunds as separate operations.

    An order's status, a provider's operation, and the ledger are related but different records. Represent money with currency and integer minor units plus an explicit rounding policy. A single paid flag cannot explain the sequence, uncertainty, or accounting consequences of moving money.

    22.9.2 · Nonfunctional requirements

    Preserve financial invariants and auditable state. Prevent duplicate relevant provider effects where its contract supports that guarantee, and resolve uncertain outcomes rather than inventing success or decline.

    Set intent-acceptance timing separately from completion. Each settled amount should have unique balanced postings and authorised corrections under the chosen accounting model. A provider outage may leave work pending. Safe pending state is preferable to a fast unsupported final result that the system cannot later explain.

    22.9.3 · Explicit assumptions and workload numbers

    Assume one million intents/day, about 11.6/s on average, with an illustrative peak of 200/s. Suppose each initially produces six 1 kB operational/audit records: raw growth is 6 GB/day.

    Ledger details, indexes, copies, callbacks, and retention add to this. The model uses synthetic amounts and does not assert actual provider prices or institutional architecture. Estimate provider concurrency and reconciliation traffic separately from the daily average, especially under long waits and retries.

    22.9.4 · Naive initial architecture

    A first service calls the provider, sets an order flag, and replies. If the provider charges and the process dies before saving the result, a retry can repeat the charge.

    Before scaling, add a durable operation identity and explicit states including uncertainty. Local transactions protect related local changes. Provider keys, status queries, and reconciliation address the external gap. They solve different parts of the history. A larger deployment cannot repair an ambiguous operation for which no stable identity was recorded.

    22.9.5 · Core API contracts

    POST /payment-intents accepts amount_minor, currency, business reference, and idempotency key. The status resource reports explicitly supported states such as pending, authorised, captured, declined, or uncertain. A refund endpoint creates a separately keyed refund.

    Bind keys to actor and financial payload; changed content under the same key conflicts. Verify provider webhooks rather than trusting client approval fields. Define how clients wait or query after uncertainty, so a missing reply does not automatically become another financial attempt.

    22.9.6 · Data model and schema

    Keep payment_intent and operation records with actor, key, fingerprint, progress, and result. Provider attempts retain stable keys, references, and outcomes. A verified-event inbox recognises repeated evidence.

    The ledger has transactions and entries identifying account, currency, and signed amount. Required entries balance within the relevant currency and accounting scope. Enforce external-operation linkage and correction identity. An authorised correction creates a new accounting event instead of silently rewriting past evidence. These constraints make the relationship between provider facts and local postings reviewable.

    22.9.7 · Low-level component organization

    PaymentService owns allowed transitions. Money and policy values check amounts. ProviderAdapter maps explicit outcomes, OperationRepository handles duplicate identity, and LedgerService validates and commits postings. Reconciler compares external evidence; RefundWorkflow owns refund progress.

    These responsibilities can begin in one application. A timeout maps to uncertainty, not a definite decline. Keep provider-specific details at the adapter while exposing enough evidence for recovery. A component boundary is useful when it preserves meaning and ownership, rather than requiring a network service for every role.

    22.9.8 · High-level system architecture

    Use an authenticated API, durable intent and operation state, bounded provider workers, a verified callback inbox, a ledger boundary, and scheduled reconciliation. Where downstream updates are required, commit their publication intent with the relevant local state.

    Reserve capacity for reconciliation rather than letting optional analytics consume it. Regional serving must preserve the chosen ledger and provider-operation authority. Draw external calls outside the local transaction boundary so the uncertainty and recovery path remain visible.

    22.9.9 · Data and control flows

    Commit the intent and logical operation identity. Submit the stable provider key, then record either supported evidence or uncertainty. Capture or settlement evidence drives an idempotent transition creating the required balanced postings once.

    Callbacks may arrive before or after a synchronous reply, so transitions must not regress incorrectly. Reconciliation queries the stable reference and repairs discrepancies. It must not blindly resend a charge merely because a local status is still pending. Trace evidence and local updates in order to see where a crash can leave work unresolved.

    22.9.10 · Capacity estimates

    At a stable 200 calls/s and an assumed 500 ms provider wait, Little's Law gives 200×0.5 = 100 in-flight provider calls in that boundary. The average daily rate of 11.6/s does not describe this peak.

    The calculation is not a safe pool recommendation: allow for variance, deadlines, provider limits, and failures. Initial operational records total 6 GB/day before other storage. Callback and reconciliation work can continue after original traffic subsides and need capacity of their own.

    22.9.11 · End-to-end latency estimates

    Assume 20 ms ingress, 20 ms committing the intent, 500 ms with the provider, and 20 ms for the final local update. The successful synchronous path totals 560 ms.

    These are assumed stage times, not p99 or guaranteed completion. Returning a durable pending intent after about 40 ms is a different API contract with later completion. A timeout requires status recovery or reconciliation. It supplies no reliable basis for converting an attempted payment into a definite failed business outcome.

    22.9.12 · Failure scenarios

    Test a lost reply after local commit, provider execution followed by process loss, repeated or reordered callbacks, refund uncertainty, and failure to commit postings.

    Persist unknown outcomes and repeat only with a supported safe identity or established evidence. If the ledger is unavailable, do not bypass it by setting paid. Recovery must explain provider state and required postings before claiming the complete outcome resolved. A healthy API response after restart does not establish that the money histories now agree.

    22.9.13 · Scalability improvements

    Scale independent acceptance and operation workers, while bounding provider concurrency and retaining per-payment and relevant per-account invariants. Keep reconciliation resources isolated enough to repair uncertainty during an incident.

    Status projections can serve reads with a stated freshness rule. Ledger partitioning needs a deliberate balance and transaction scope; one hot account can remain concentrated. A modest average daily rate alone is no reason to shard. Make the added ownership and recovery complexity answer an observed bottleneck.

    22.9.14 · Consistency requirements

    Local duplicate recognition, payment transitions, and required postings need appropriate atomic boundaries. A provider is outside those local transactions and requires its own identity and recovery contract.

    Uniqueness and transaction semantics can protect one local posting set. They do not prove the provider executed exactly once. Refunds have separate states and may not reverse timing, fees, or downstream consequences perfectly. State what each accepted result means and preserve uncertainty until there is evidence for a final transition.

    22.9.15 · Security model

    Authorise payments and refunds, validate values server-side, verify callbacks, and protect credentials. Minimise sensitive data through reviewed provider tokenisation or integration where appropriate, rather than keeping unnecessary raw credentials.

    Restrict and audit privileged corrections. An operator is not automatically permitted to rewrite accounting history. Bind every effect and query to its tenant and account scope. Logs should preserve relevant identity and outcomes without exposing secrets. These are architecture controls, not a claim of compliance with any particular financial or legal regime.

    22.9.16 · Deployment approach

    Roll states and event formats out compatibly. Preserve operation identities through releases and recovery, and control provider configuration and key changes.

    An old database restore can forget keys for effects the provider already executed. Recovery therefore needs replay protection and reconciliation before resubmission. Test delayed callbacks from an older release and return after an outage. The new process's local view must be brought into agreement with external evidence instead of treating restored pending rows as untouched work.

    22.9.17 · Observability design

    Separate acceptance and completion delay. Track pending/uncertain age, provider attempts, repeated-event recognition, callback verification, imbalances, unmatched settlements, refund progress, and reconciliation outcomes.

    Alert on invariant violations and old unresolved money movement, even when HTTP success rates are good. Evidence should distinguish attempted, provider-accepted, and locally posted states. Stable identities let an investigator reconstruct the operation without pretending that one log line or response code proves the complete financial journey.

    22.9.18 · Infrastructure cost considerations

    Costs include provider attempts, secure records, ledger work, retained audit evidence, telemetry, reconciliation, and operation. Use symbolic fees and labelled hypothetical infrastructure inputs unless current prices are verified.

    A cheaper arrangement that cannot explain uncertain charges is a different and insufficient service. Cost per reconciled successful business payment is often more useful than cost per HTTP attempt. Retries can increase the attempt denominator precisely when useful outcomes decline. Keep the supported financial invariants equal when comparing alternatives.

    22.9.19 · Alternative architectures and trade-offs

    Synchronous completion can suit a client expecting an immediate result but exposes provider waits and uncertainty. Asynchronous intents make pending progress explicit while adding workflow state.

    One local transactional application simplifies related invariants. Separating provider and ledger services can give organisational or isolation benefits and adds coordination. Append-only accounting history and mutable operational projections can complement each other. Do not force one paid record to serve every status, audit, and accounting need. Compare boundaries by the work they clarify and the recovery they require.

    22.9.20 · Architecture evolution from small scale to large scale

    Begin with explicit states, currency-aware integer values, local transactions, and stable provider operation identity. Add durable callback handling and reconciliation before introducing more traffic paths.

    Then use projections and bounded workers for measured needs. Partition only when a demonstrated limit justifies a preserved invariant boundary. Every earlier payment must remain explainable through its provider evidence and postings after the topology changes. Scaling is successful when it expands supported work without losing that meaning.

    22.9.21 · Design review identifying weaknesses and improvements

    Ask which evidence establishes financial success, who commits required postings, and how recovery handles an old deduplication snapshot beside newer provider effects.

    Test charge-then-crash, callback-before-reply, duplicate evidence, partial refunds, and restore from earlier local state. Check for one valid local posting set and explicit unresolved states where evidence is missing. A provider timeout must not become a convenient decline merely to make the normal request path appear finished.

    22.9.22 · A short implementation exercise

    Build a synthetic provider that remembers stable operation keys and a local ledger that accepts only balanced entries. Stop after provider execution but before recording the result locally.

    Reconcile by key and verify one logical operation leads to one balanced local posting set. Replay the provider event, and reject a changed financial payload under the old key. Explain that this demonstrates the synthetic contract and local boundary, rather than a guarantee for an arbitrary real provider.

    A small implementation of the key rule

    PSEUDOCODE · ONE PART OF THE DESIGN

    def apply_settlement(event):
    with transaction():
        if inbox_contains(event.id): return prior_outcome(event.id)
        payment = lock_payment(event.payment_id)
        validate_transition_and_amount(payment, event)
        entries = [debit_entry(event), credit_entry(event)]
        require_balanced_by_currency(entries)
        insert_unique_posting_set(event.operation_id, entries)
        update_payment_and_insert_inbox(payment, event)
# Provider execution is reconciled separately from this transaction.

    Use the implementation exercise to test the rule and the failure described above. You can also run local examples of seat claims, duplicate handling, ledger balance, and workflow epochs in the mechanism collection.

    PART 6 / UNIT 22 / CHAPTER 22.10

    Distributed Job Scheduler

    Prerequisites: Runtime, Processes, Threads, and Concurrency, Replication, Leader Election, and Consensus, Message Queues, Events, and Distributed Workflows, Reliability, Fault Tolerance, and Disaster Recovery4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A scheduler and its worker can both restart around a due job. Give the schedule, occurrence, attempt, and effect separate identities so recovery knows what it is resuming.

    The workload, timing, and prices in this design are teaching assumptions. They are not measured benchmarks or a description of a particular company.

    22.10.1 · Functional requirements

    A user creates a schedule, the service identifies due occurrences, and workers execute the jobs. The user can inspect history, configure retries, and cancel supported future work.

    Define fixed times versus intervals, timezones, missed runs, and overlap. A schedule and one occurrence are different identities. Restarting a worker or scheduler must not invent a new logical occurrence for the same due time. Timing semantics need to be explicit before choosing a timer or queue implementation.

    22.10.2 · Nonfunctional requirements

    Keep accepted schedules and required runs recoverable under the supported failures. Bound scheduling delay and prevent stale attempts from overwriting newer results. Execution can start repeatedly around failures, so external effects need appropriate identity or fencing.

    Cancellation also needs a boundary: future dispatch, pending work, and best-effort interruption of a running effect are different promises. A local cancellation flag cannot prove a remote effect was undone. Make these distinctions visible in run status.

    22.10.3 · Explicit assumptions and workload numbers

    Assume one million schedules and 100,000 occurrences/hour. The average rate is 100,000/3,600 ≈ 27.8 runs/s. At an initial 2 kB of run state each, raw growth is 200 MB/hour.

    With ten-second mean execution at a stable rate, average active work is about 27.8×10 = 278 runs. Top-of-hour bursts, long jobs, retries, and retention add requirements. The number of saved schedules alone does not describe due-time concentration or required execution capacity.

    22.10.4 · Naive initial architecture

    One process scans due schedules and launches local functions. If it creates a run and advances the schedule in separate commits, a crash between them can repeat or miss the occurrence.

    Create a stable occurrence record and advance due state transactionally. A leader can simplify scanning, but leadership alone does not make worker effects execute once. The first improvement is durable identity and atomic progress, not simply adding a second process to repeat the same unsafe loop.

    22.10.5 · Core API contracts

    POST /schedules accepts timing, timezone, payload reference, retry rules, and overlap policy. Cancellation changes the documented future behaviour. GET /runs/{id} reports attempts and outcome. A run-once operation has its own idempotency identity.

    Bound timing-expression and payload complexity. Return durable acceptance separately from execution completion. Where an external effect remains uncertain, status should say so rather than treating a worker's missing reply as proof it never happened.

    22.10.6 · Data model and schema

    A schedule stores id, version, next_due, timing policy, and state. A run binds a unique (schedule_id,occurrence) to input version and progress. Attempts record epoch, lease deadline, worker, and result.

    Preserve original due time separately from dispatch time. Runs and attempts are not interchangeable: another attempt does not create another logical occurrence. Conditional progress prevents a superseded attempt from replacing newer state. Use outbox or effect records where durable dispatch and external identity require them.

    22.10.7 · Low-level component organization

    ScheduleParser and TimePolicy calculate occurrences. DueScanner finds candidates. RunRepository inserts the run and advances schedule state atomically. Dispatcher routes work, LeaseManager grants attempts, and WorkerAdapter executes it.

    Reconciler finds stuck or uncertain outcomes. The scheduler owns when work is due; workers execute under a bounded current claim. Each effect adapter needs a stated repetition or fencing contract. The component split helps test time decisions separately from executing a potentially irreversible external operation.

    22.10.8 · High-level system architecture

    Keep durable schedules, coordinated scanners or partition owners, dispatch records, bounded workers, attempt state, and reconciliation. Store large versioned payloads separately rather than copying them into every retry message.

    Timing control and execution capacity are different paths. Losing the control plane may delay new dispatch while already running work continues. Losing a worker should leave a recoverable run. These behaviours require explicit state and ownership rules, not just a queue attached to a cron loop.

    22.10.9 · Data and control flows

    A scanner locks or conditionally claims due state, creates the unique occurrence and dispatch intent, advances next_due, and commits. The worker then claims an attempt epoch and executes under the stable run identity.

    It renews a lease where supported and records completion only if still current. A replacement can take over expired work, while effect-side identity or fencing limits harmful stale execution. Reconcile runs whose progress never reaches an acceptable terminal state. This closes the history beyond merely starting a callback.

    22.10.10 · Capacity estimates

    The assumed 27.8 runs/s and ten-second average yield about 278 active executions. If one worker can sustain four independent I/O jobs, the arithmetic minimum is roughly seventy workers before headroom and other limits.

    CPU jobs need measured compute capacity instead. A round-hour burst can be far larger than the average, so estimate due-time distribution and queue delay. Include retries and catch-up. A worker count derived from steady averages is not evidence that launch or outage recovery meets its scheduling objective.

    22.10.11 · End-to-end latency estimates

    Scheduling delay measures due time to dispatch or start. Runtime measures how long the job takes afterward. An illustrative target is that 95% of eligible runs start within five seconds under supported load.

    Scanning intervals, claim coordination, queue waits, cold starts, and concurrency limits all consume that budget. A ten-minute task can still meet a five-second start target, so completion deadlines need another rule. Measure both where the business requires them rather than describing every duration as “job latency.”

    22.10.12 · Failure scenarios

    Test crashes between occurrence creation and schedule advancement; the atomic boundary should prevent a partial accepted result. Lease expiry can overlap a resumed old worker with a replacement.

    Clock changes, timezone transitions, malformed inputs, and poison jobs need policies. Reject stale local completions by epoch. External effects accepted before ownership changes remain a separate reconciliation concern. A timer can be correct about due time while the workflow is still incorrect about identity or repeated execution.

    22.10.13 · Scalability improvements

    Index due time, claim bounded batches, and partition schedules with stable ownership when scan work becomes limiting. Scale independent workers by their actual CPU, memory, and I/O use.

    Keep long, high-priority, and CPU-heavy work from consuming each other's whole budget. Catch-up after an outage also needs limits so millions of overdue runs do not starve current critical jobs. Replacing a global lock requires preserving atomic occurrence creation, not merely removing the contention point and hoping duplicates will be rare.

    22.10.14 · Consistency requirements

    Advancing the schedule and creating its occurrence need uniqueness and atomicity. Delivery to workers may repeat. Current-epoch completion protects local progress; side-effect identity or enforced fencing protects the relevant external effect.

    A lease alone does not establish exactly-once execution. Define missed-run and overlap policy so timing races do not decide which logical runs exist. The accepted schedule, occurrence, attempt, and effect are separate scopes with connected but different consistency requirements.

    22.10.15 · Security model

    Authorise schedule ownership, payload references, run views, and cancellation. Validate supported executable work types rather than permitting arbitrary code or unrestricted URLs through the API.

    Bind each run to tenant and immutable input. Give the worker only the required capabilities and audit administration. A global administrator credential in every worker would make one malformed or compromised job unnecessarily powerful. Follow access from stored schedule through dispatched task to the actual resource used by the job.

    22.10.16 · Deployment approach

    Roll schedule and run formats out compatibly, including lease and epoch meanings. Drain new claims and preserve progress before workers terminate. Reconcile queues against authoritative run state during recovery.

    An older restored schedule table can lag external effects already executed. Stable occurrence identity and evidence are needed before replay. Test control-plane interruption separately from worker loss. Recovery must restore the meaning of due work and prior outcomes, rather than simply restart scanning.

    22.10.17 · Observability design

    Measure due-to-dispatch and due-to-start delay, oldest eligible work, repeated occurrence attempts, lease expiry, stale completion rejection, retries, duration, and tenant fairness.

    Check that one occurrence maps to one logical run. CPU can stay low while a broken scanner creates no work, so monitor generation and completion directly. Alert on accepted jobs with no progress. Detailed histories should distinguish one run from its attempts, allowing operators to recognise repetition without interpreting it as new scheduled demand.

    22.10.18 · Infrastructure cost considerations

    Costs include scanning, indexes, history, dispatch, workers, spare capacity, external calls, and recovery. At 2 kB per run and 100,000 runs/hour, raw daily history is 4.8 GB before attempts and indexes.

    Compare scan frequency and batching against the start-delay target. A cheaper design that silently misses due runs offers a different service. Use explicit rates and include catch-up and idle headroom so normal execution cost does not hide the work required after a failure.

    22.10.19 · Alternative architectures and trade-offs

    Polling a due-time index is simple and recoverable. Timer wheels or delayed-message facilities may improve some timing workloads while needing durable reconstruction. Central scanning simplifies ownership; partitioned scanning divides work and adds coordination.

    Long-lived workers reduce startup costs, while managed invocation can fit bursts under different limits. Compare timing precision, job duration, recovery, and effects. The timer data structure answers only part of the design; a fast due lookup does not establish safe occurrence or worker semantics.

    22.10.20 · Architecture evolution from small scale to large scale

    First implement deterministic time policy and atomic occurrence creation. Add durable dispatch and bounded execution. Introduce leases and epochs together with a safe effect identity before claiming worker takeover.

    Partition whichever scan or execution path measurements identify. Regional ownership requires a supported transfer and partition policy for due work. Preserve stable identities throughout so the next deployment does not reinterpret retries as new occurrences or lose the evidence needed to resolve old runs.

    22.10.21 · Design review identifying weaknesses and improvements

    Review stable occurrence identity, atomic next_due advancement, stale workers, cancellation, and recovery from old state. Each is a separate potential failure gap.

    Run competing scanners at commit boundaries, pause a worker past its lease, cancel during execution, cross a timezone transition, and recover after a long outage. Check which runs should exist and which effects remain uncertain. A callback firing on time once is evidence of timing for one run, not a durable scheduler's full contract.

    22.10.22 · A short implementation exercise

    Use an injected clock and transactional run table. Start two scanners against the same due occurrence and verify that the unique logical run is created once.

    Pause an attempt at epoch 7, replace it with epoch 8, then submit the old completion. The local store must reject it. Identify the further key or fencing enforcement needed at an external effect receiver. This separates the local progress guarantee from unsupported claims about physically executing the job once.

    A small implementation of the key rule

    PSEUDOCODE · ONE PART OF THE DESIGN

    with transaction():
    schedule = claim_due_schedule(now)
    run = insert_unique_run(schedule.id, schedule.next_due)
    insert_dispatch_outbox(run.id)
    advance_next_due(schedule)
# Worker completion compares the current attempt epoch atomically.
# A stale worker's external effects need resource-side protection.

    Use the implementation exercise to test the rule and the failure described above. You can also run local examples of seat claims, duplicate handling, ledger balance, and workflow epochs in the mechanism collection.
